HNSW vs GraphRAG distinction: HNSW = geometric proximity (fast approximate nearest neighbor in Phase 2-3). It clusters topics automatically via statistical co-occurrence in the embedding space (e.g., 'neural network' maps near 'deep learning'). GraphRAG = named, typed, directional relationships (CITES, DERIVES_FROM, CONTRADICTS) built by an LLM parsing text in Phase 4+. They are complementary: HNSW finds 'what is near', GraphRAG finds 'how things connect'. Do not expect HNSW to answer causal or multi-hop relational questions.

ChromaDB has 4 mutation ops: (1) add() -- insert only, crashes if ID exists. (2) update(ids, metadatas) -- patches metadata only, NO re-embedding, vectors unchanged, ~0.01s per chunk regardless of scale. (3) upsert() -- update-or-insert; re-embeds text if replacing a document. (4) delete(). Rule: metadata field additions = update() only. Text content change = upsert(). Embedding model change = wipe entire collection. Idempotent migration pattern: collection.get(where=filter) -> patch meta with {**meta, new_field: val} -> collection.update(ids, new_metas). Guard with if new_field not in meta for idempotency.

Every manual edit to a generated file is a future regression — when the codegen runs again, it overwrites or conflicts. If you find yourself editing generated output, the source config is wrong; fix the config and regenerate.

Two-job pattern is mandatory when a pipeline mixes arbitrary Python (dbutils.fs, file ops, validation) with streaming CDC: notebook job for general-purpose work, DLT job for streaming/CDC, chain via depends_on. Reasons (in priority order): (1) DLT cannot run arbitrary Python — full stop; (2) different compute profiles — single-node notebook vs autoscale DLT; (3) independent failure domains — preprocessing failure shouldn't block streaming, and vice versa. Forcing them into one job creates compute waste, unclear failure boundaries, and DLT-graph violations. Apollo Gen2 follows this; generalize to any project mixing imperative + declarative steps.

Streaming Delta tables retain columns from ALL writers forever. When a DLT streaming table is written by multiple @dp.append_flow flows (e.g., historical Parquet + ongoing CloudFiles), Delta unions their schemas. Once any writer produces a column, it is permanent in the table — subsequent writes that don't produce it land NULL. Removing the column requires drop+recreate because DLT-managed streaming tables don't enable column mapping mode. Lesson: NORMALIZE column schemas across all writers BEFORE they ever run, or accept permanent NULL-padding. Common manifestation: historical loader produces a deprecated column, you remove it from the incremental loader, but it stays in the table forever as a NULL graveyard.

CDC mode choice by source shape, not preference. APPLY CHANGES INTO (mode: cdc): for partial feeds (CDC streams, API deltas) — each row is an upsert event, deletes need an explicit operation column or track_deletions. APPLY CHANGES FROM SNAPSHOT (mode: snapshot_cdc): for full snapshots — compares consecutive snapshots; absent key = soft delete automatic. CRITICAL TRAP: feeding partial data to snapshot_cdc compares the partial batch against the full Bronze table, soft-deleting EVERY row not in the batch. 5-row 'snapshot' fed to a 10K-row table -> 9,995 soft-deletes silently. Decision rule: does your source deliver complete state or incremental events? Wrong choice causes silent corruption, not errors.

create_auto_cdc_flow with stored_as_scd_type=1 implements per-key overwrite ONLY: key in source not in target = INSERT; key in both = UPDATE/overwrite; key in target NOT in source = UNTOUCHED (row persists forever). There is NO equivalent to MERGE WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE DELETE. SCD1 specifies history behavior for matched keys; it says nothing about orphan target rows. When this bites: (a) authoritative snapshot sources where key disappearance should propagate as delete; (b) PK-column restatement where business-column change shifts the key hash, inserting NEW row while old orphans. Options for delete-if-missing: switch to snapshot_cdc, OR union with anti-join + apply_as_deletes view, OR accept drift and monitor.

CDC has two orthogonal mechanics: sequence_by (decides per-batch winner among same-PK records) and track_history_except (excludes columns from change detection). They apply together. sequence_by needs real per-row granularity — sequencing by file_modification_time when multiple rows can come from the same file leaves CDC to pick arbitrarily on ties. track_history_except must list every operational metadata column (_processing_timestamp, _source_file_path, etc.) — without it, every pipeline re-run creates a false SCD2 version because metadata changes even when business data doesn't. Independent issues, both required.

ROW_NUMBER() dedup pattern feeding streaming CDC target: keep BATCH all the way until the CDC write. Streaming + ROW_NUMBER raises NON_TIME_WINDOW_NOT_SUPPORTED_IN_STREAMING. Pattern: type:sql load (always batch) -> transform_type:sql dedup with ROW_NUMBER (batch) -> streaming_table + mode:cdc write. create_auto_cdc_flow accepts batch sources — each pipeline update is a discrete batch CDC merge. Within-batch dedup in transform; cross-batch dedup via sequence_by. Diagnostic for the streaming-window error: inspect generated .py — should show @dp.temporary_view (not @dp.temporary_streaming_view) upstream, no spark.readStream anywhere.

Testing strategy: focus exclusively on what can produce wrong data without errors. Silent failures to test: wrong-cast NULL columns, count mismatches that need interpretation (e.g., STG > BRZ for snapshot CDC is normal), composite-key correctness, edge cases (midnight, single-digit months, timezone offsets). Do NOT test hard gates — enforcement:strict drops, expect_all_or_drop, raise ValueError on column-count mismatch — these crash loudly and tests add noise. Warn-vs-fail progression: start with warn during dev (observability), promote to fail in prod once baseline is established and false positives tuned out.

SUM/AVG/MAX over zero rows returns NULL, not 0. Downstream comparisons like result = 0 evaluate to NULL (falsy in WHERE) — tests 'fail' silently because NULL is neither equal nor not-equal to 0. Manifests as: a data-quality test that should catch a problem reports passing when the violating row count is zero (because the violating SELECT returned NULL not 0). Fix: always wrap aggregations with COALESCE(SUM(...), 0) when the WHERE clause could legitimately match zero rows. Universal across SQL engines, not Spark-specific.

In DLT/streaming architectures, data writes and validation queries run in parallel within a pipeline. A test querying a streaming target may see zero rows on the first run because @dp.append_flow hasn't committed yet. Specifically: on first run or full refresh, target_count=0 is expected, not a bug. Two design choices: (a) accept first-run failures as expected and only alert on persistent failure; (b) require a completed run before running tests, design tests against stable state only. Same gotcha applies to any pipeline that mixes write and read in one DAG step.

Test applicability is determined by source shape, not pipeline layer. CloudFiles-specific tests (PK uniqueness per file batch, file-modification freshness, _rescued_data schema-drift detection) don't apply to API/custom-datasource ingestion (no batch boundary, no file metadata) or to materialized views (no batch column, no timestamp). Mapping: PK uniqueness per batch -> CloudFiles only; row count source-vs-target -> CloudFiles, NOT API (streaming mismatch); freshness via file timestamp -> CloudFiles only; SCD2 integrity -> applies at BRZ regardless of source. Build per-source-type test catalogs, not layer-uniform ones.

DLT load-source streaming semantics differ by type. type:delta -> generates @dp.temporary_view wrapping spark.read.table OR spark.readStream.table — batch by default, streams when readMode:stream is set. type:sql -> generates @dp.temporary_view wrapping spark.sql(...) — ALWAYS batch, readMode:stream has no effect. transform_type:sql is also always batch. Streaming inheritance cascades: a SQL transform downstream of a streaming source IS streaming, and non-time window functions (ROW_NUMBER) get rejected. Only reliable way to keep a SQL transform batch: make its upstream batch too. For UNION-of-multiple-BRZ feeding a streaming CDC target, type:sql with UNION inlined is correct; five type:delta loads + UNION transform forces the streaming constraint everywhere.

Spark/PySpark high-frequency gotchas: (1) spark.conf.get('key') raises SparkNoSuchElementException if missing — always provide default: spark.conf.get('key', 'default'). (2) df.coalesce(1).write.csv(path) writes a DIRECTORY of part files, not a single CSV — coalesce(1) gives one part file but the directory wrapper remains; copy/rename the part-*.csv outside if you need a named file. (3) spark.read.csv(header=False) names columns _c0, _c1, _c2... — match by position, not name. (4) COUNT(*) and COUNT(1) have identical physical plans in Spark; only COUNT(column_name) differs (excludes NULLs). (5) DLT expectations use SQL syntax = not == — common mistake from Python/Scala. (6) Inject Python timestamps with explicit TIMESTAMP 'literal' wrapper — never rely on implicit string->timestamp coercion. (7) SELECT * EXCEPT(colA, colB), transform(colA), transform(colB) keeps multi-column transforms concise and robust to source schema changes.

Cross-job pipeline overlap fails immediately, not queued. max_concurrent_runs:1 only serializes runs of THE SAME job. Two different jobs triggering the same DLT pipeline at overlapping times = the second update gets rejected in ~1s with 'pipeline busy'. There is no cross-job pipeline queue at the platform level. No DAB-native clean solution. Mitigation menu (pick at least two): (a) staggered schedules, but manual triggers still break it; (b) task-level retries with 2-min backoff, but codegen regeneration wipes them; (c) master-job orchestrator using run_job_task to serialize; (d) consolidate to one owning job. Plan retries + staggered schedules from day one when a pipeline is shared across jobs.

DAB ACL/permissions hygiene: (1) Permission-level vocabularies differ per resource: jobs use IS_OWNER/CAN_MANAGE/CAN_MANAGE_RUN/CAN_VIEW; DLT pipelines use IS_OWNER/CAN_MANAGE/CAN_RUN/CAN_VIEW. CAN_MANAGE_RUN is jobs-only; pipelines use CAN_RUN (same intent, different spelling). Bundle-level permissions: fans to every resource, breaks deploy if level is invalid for any target. (2) 'Cannot remove permissions: allowed permissions levels: CAN_MANAGE, IS_OWNER' has TWO root causes: invalid level for resource type, OR caller lacks CAN_MANAGE/IS_OWNER on the existing ACL. The error always lists the same authorizing levels regardless of which root cause — diagnose YAML first, UI ACLs second. (3) Three ACL sources collide: bundle YAML, resource YAML (often not emitted by codegen), manual UI grants. DAB doesn't know about UI; later deploys notice drift and try to remove it -> authority error. Pick ONE source of truth. (4) YAML duplicate keys silently collapse — last wins. Use list-of-items per grantee, not multiple user_name keys under one item.

File-arrival trigger pattern (DAB-native): the trigger block goes on the JOB resource (not the pipeline). Required: url must be a UC volume path (/Volumes/<catalog>/<schema>/...); subfolder recursion supported. Use min_time_between_triggers_seconds + wait_after_last_change_seconds to prevent rapid-fire on multi-file landings. Constraint: a job has EITHER schedule: OR trigger:, never both. Codegen frameworks (LHP and similar) emit job YAML from a documented schema; non-documented fields like trigger:, custom retry policies, and run_job_task are silently DROPPED. If you need them, plan for manual post-edit OR a wrapper script from day one — every codegen re-run wipes manual edits unless the YAML is one the codegen never emits (e.g., a master orchestrator with no flowgroup references).

Secrets policy: (1) Plaintext credentials anywhere beyond local dev = security risk the moment the repo is shared, backed up, or pushed. Mandatory gate before promoting beyond dev: move all sensitive values to a secret store (Azure Key Vault, Databricks secrets) and reference via placeholder syntax like ${secret:keyvault-name/secret-name}. (2) Not all secrets are static. OAuth refresh tokens get OVERWRITTEN by the auth server on each successful exchange — storing them as static secrets means they're stale by the next pipeline run. Build write-back logic: after each auth exchange, write the new refresh token back to the secret store. Identify which secrets rotate (OAuth refresh, session keys, time-bounded tokens) and add write-back for those.

Silent CSV/path quirks (defend BEFORE column-count validation): (1) Trailing commas on every row (Synapse Link, many ERP exports) -> Spark reads an extra empty _c<n> column. Defense: if len(df.columns) == len(expected_columns) + 1: df = df.drop(df.columns[-1]). (2) Leading/trailing spaces in folder/file names from upstream systems -> entity-lookup code that matches on name silently fails (entity not found). Defense: .strip() in lookup code; never trust upstream names to be clean. (3) schemaEvolutionMode: addNewColumns ONLY adds — never removes, renames, or changes types. Source removes a column -> Autoloader doesn't catch it -> column starts landing NULL silently. Schema-drift test should flag unexpected NULL patterns in previously-populated columns.

DE meta-aphorisms (each distilled from concrete production incidents): (1) Silent failures > loud failures — a clear crash tells you where to look. (2) Enforce schema once, at one layer; trust both sides. (3) Every row needs operational metadata (processing timestamp, source path, source modification time) — you'll need them for debugging eventually. (4) Fail fast, fail specific — raise ValueError with context beats /unprocessed/ folders nobody monitors. (5) Design around framework limitations, don't fight them — workarounds editing generated code are future regressions. (6) Generated code is artifact, not source of truth — edit config and regenerate. (7) Batch-generate at scale — 200 entities = 1 script generating 200 YAMLs. (8) Test small data first, scale second. (9) Document the type-mapping chain — Source -> CSV -> Spark -> STG -> BRZ. (10) Don't test hard gates, test silent failures. (11) Browse raw data 30 min before building pipelines — saves days. (12) When source is already SCD2, don't run CDC on top — collapse to current-only or preserve via direct column mapping. (13) Two-job pattern beats forcing mixed workloads into one. (14) Layer responsibility separation — each layer has ONE job. (15) Developer isolation needs full-stack namespacing — missing the suffix in ONE reference breaks everything.

They correctly framed the input as 'consolidated learnings' (signaling they want compressed indexable entries, not 1:1 copy of every bullet) and trusted JARVIS to dedupe against existing entries. Query expansion (Stage 2.4.3) — bridge the lexical gap between short user queries and long corpus chunks. HyDE: LLM generates a hypothetical answer paragraph, embed THAT instead of the query; the answer-style embedding aligns with answer-style corpus chunks. Verified on 156-chunk research_papers collection: baseline distances 0.77-0.90, HyDE distances 0.35-0.46 (~50% closer). Multi-Query: LLM generates 3+ paraphrasings, retrieve top-k for each query (incl. original), fuse via Reciprocal Rank Fusion: score(d) = sum_q 1/(60+rank_q(d)); chunks appearing in many queries get promoted (consensus = relevance signal). Cost: 1 LLM call per HyDE; 1 LLM call + N retrievals per Multi-Query. ADAPTIVE USE: skip for queries with exact identifiers (function names, error codes, chemical formulas) — expansion hurts precision there. Demo + production wrapper in js-learning/stage_2_memory/sub_2.4_retrieval_strategies/03_query_expansion.py. Production placement: Memory Layer pre-retrieval hook, before JarvisMemoryStore.query_collection.

User forward-simulated query expansion (HyDE / Multi-Query) against actual prompt style and pushed back: 90% of their prompts are detailed (~200 words, technical vocab, multi-claim contextual paragraphs). HyDE/Multi-Query are designed for SHORT/SPARSE queries — applying them by default to detailed prompts wastes LLM cost + latency for marginal or negative recall gain. DIRECTIVE: when designing any auto-applied retrieval/reasoning primitive (query expansion, reranking thresholds, RRF fusion, cross-encoder re-scoring), build it as a standalone module first, then gate it with an explicit should_X(query) predicate — adaptive, not always-on. Default callers map: /learn, /research, /dev, direct CLI = expansion off; agent-generated sub-queries (Stage 3+) and cold-start exploratory retrievals = expansion on. Apply this lens to all Stage 2.5+ retrieval components. The user's natural prompt mode is long-and-detailed; short-query primitives only earn their keep on machine-emitted queries.

Production query expansion lives at jarvis_core/memory/expansion.py. Public API: should_expand(query) gate, hyde_query/multi_query_search primitives, expand_then_query orchestrator with strategy=auto|hyde|multi_query and force flag, FusedHit frozen dataclass for RRF results, LLMCall = Callable[[str], str] type alias. Module is layer-pure: never instantiates an LLM client; caller injects llm_call. Stage 3+ Brain agents wire OpenRouter/Ollama/etc. when integrating. Lesson at js-learning/stage_2_memory/sub_2.4_retrieval_strategies/03_query_expansion.py imports from production rather than redefining — single source of truth. Smoke test in __main__ uses stub LLM + stub store, no live ChromaDB or API key required.

Decision: jarvis_core/memory/expansion.py uses dependency injection (llm_call: Callable[[str], str]) rather than owning an LLM client directly. Rationale: per JARVIS_ENDGAME.md, LLMs are a Brain-layer primitive; Memory is RAG/vector-store. Query expansion structurally sits in Memory (between query and store) but invokes LLM. DI preserves the layer boundary: caller passes the function; module never imports anthropic/openai/httpx. Tradeoff: each caller wires its own LLM, slight friction. Win: trivially mockable in tests (stub_llm in expansion.py __main__), no transitive dependencies, swap providers without touching Memory code. DIRECTIVE: any future Memory-layer code that needs LLM-or-equivalent (e.g., contextual compression, LLM-as-judge for RAGAS) follows the same DI pattern.

DIRECTIVE for all Stage 2.5+ retrieval adaptivity: adaptive feature gates (should_expand today; future BM25 enable threshold, cross-encoder rescore-K threshold, GraphRAG when-to-traverse, contextual compression on/off) MUST fail closed. Any unexpected condition — LLM error, parse failure, ambiguous classification, dependency raised — returns the unexpanded baseline behavior, never an exception. The caller never has to defend against the gate failing. Pattern: try-the-gate, on-fallthrough-or-exception go to baseline retrieval. Implemented in jarvis_core.memory.expansion.expand_then_query: should_expand returns False = baseline; force=False is the safe default. Generalizes: every adaptive primitive in the Memory layer follows this rule. Rationale: agent loops (Stage 3+) will issue thousands of retrieval calls; one gate exception per session destroys the latency budget and causes hard-to-debug intermittent failures. Failing closed = degraded quality, not broken pipeline.

Observability spec for jarvis_core.memory.expansion (instrument when Stage 4 tracing/structlog lands). METRICS: (1) expansion.gate.skipped_ratio — % of calls where should_expand returns False; high = good calibration to user prompt style. (2) expansion.hyde.distance_delta_avg — mean cosine-distance reduction (baseline -> HyDE); validates HyDE earns its keep. Empirical baseline today: 0.85 -> 0.40 on agentic-RAG demo (~50% reduction). (3) expansion.multi_query.consensus_avg — mean appeared_in/n_queries across fused hits; high = robust paraphrasings, low = paraphrasings diverged too much. (4) expansion.llm.latency_p95 — dominant latency component (~500ms typical for DeepSeek-V4 via OpenRouter). LOGGING HOOKS to add: hyde_query post-llm_call (debug: hypothetical length), multi_query_search post-parse (debug: paraphrasing count), expand_then_query post-gate (info: expanded, strategy, query_word_count). Currently uses print() per surrounding Memory-layer convention; upgrade to structlog when observability stack ships.

Production contextual compression lives at jarvis_core/memory/compression.py. Public API: should_compress(query, k, total_words) gate, embeddings_filter (cheap baseline, lossless, ~10-50ms CPU, no LLM call), llm_filter (escalation, lossless, K small LLM calls), compress_results orchestrator with strategy=embeddings|llm_filter|auto and force flag, CompressedHit frozen dataclass, LLMCall = Callable[[str], str] type alias (matches expansion.py). Module is layer-pure: never instantiates an LLM client; caller injects llm_call. Stage 3+ pipeline composition: result = expand_then_query(...); result = compress_results(result, ...). Verified end-to-end against research_papers collection (156 chunks): embeddings filter at threshold 0.30 retains all 5/5 on-topic chunks (sims 0.42-0.67); auto-strategy correctly falls to baseline when total_words<1000 (gate floor). Lesson at js-learning/stage_2_memory/sub_2.4_retrieval_strategies/04_contextual_compression.py imports from production.

Decision (2026-04-27): jarvis_core/memory/compression.py ships TWO strategies — embeddings_filter (default) and llm_filter (escalation). LLM Extractor (the lossy rewriter that compresses each chunk via LLM-generated extraction) is DEFERRED until 2.5.6 RAGAS measurements demonstrate llm_filter isn't precise enough. Rationale: extractor carries hallucination risk (LLM can invent text not in source) and requires post-process substring validation to be safe; that's complexity we shouldn't build until justified. Embeddings filter (cost $0) covers the cheap-default case; LLM filter (cost ~$0.0001/chunk) covers semantic-intent cases the embeddings can't see; both are LOSSLESS. DIRECTIVE: when adding any LLM-rewriting step to Memory layer (extractor here, future contextual summarization, etc.), require empirical justification + post-process validation; don't build speculatively.

DIRECTIVE for Memory-layer adaptive primitives: default to the cheapest strategy that works at all, escalate only when measurements show the cheap baseline isn't enough. Implemented in compression.compress_results auto-strategy: embeddings_filter (cheap, $0, lossless) is default; llm_filter (K small calls, lossless) is auto-picked only when total_words >= _AUTO_LLM_FILTER_WORD_FLOOR (1500) AND llm_call is provided. Calibration knobs: DEFAULT_EMBEDDINGS_THRESHOLD=0.30 (permissive for MiniLM range 0.2-0.7 on relevant chunks), _MIN_K_FOR_COMPRESSION=4, _MIN_WORDS_FOR_COMPRESSION=1000, _AUTO_LLM_FILTER_WORD_FLOOR=1500. These are tunable per-corpus — current research_papers (140-word chunks, K=5 = 750 words) is below most thresholds, so compression rarely fires today; will fire more once K or chunk size grows in Stage 4. Generalizes: query-time compression in any Stage 2.5+ retrieval primitive should follow this pattern.

Observability spec for jarvis_core.memory.compression (instrument when Stage 4 tracing lands). METRICS: (1) compression.gate.skipped_ratio — % calls bypassing compression; high = good calibration to current corpus volume. (2) compression.tokens_kept_ratio_avg — mean fraction of original words surviving filter; lower = more aggressive compression earning its keep. (3) compression.llm_filter.drop_rate — % chunks rejected by LLM filter; very high (>80%) suggests retrieval was poor; very low (<10%) suggests LLM is over-permissive (model too small). (4) compression.embeddings_filter.below_threshold_rate — % chunks below threshold; same diagnostic as (3) for the cheap path. (5) compression.llm.latency_p95 — dominant cost of the llm_filter path. LOGGING HOOKS at: should_compress entry (gate inputs/decision), embeddings_filter post-encode (sims distribution), llm_filter per chunk (verdict), compress_results return (final ratio + strategy). When the LLM Extractor is added later, also instrument its hallucination_drop_rate (% chunks where post-process substring validation rejected LLM output).

BM25 (Stage 2.5.1) — TF-IDF + saturation (k1) + length normalization (b). Score: sum_t IDF(t) · TF(t,D)·(k1+1) / (TF(t,D) + k1·(1-b+b·|D|/avgdl)). IDF formulation differs by library: Lucene/Pyserini ship the smoothed form ln(1 + (N-df+0.5)/(df+0.5)) which never goes negative; rank_bm25 0.2.2 ships the raw Robertson-Sparck-Jones form ln((N-df+0.5)/(df+0.5)) and clamps negative IDFs (when df > N/2) to epsilon·avg_idf (epsilon=0.25 default). Both produce equivalent ranking on practical corpora; absolute scores diverge. k1 (default 1.5) = TF saturation knob; asymptote = IDF·(k1+1); half-saturation at TF=k1. b (default 0.75) = length penalty; b=0 disables, b=1 maximally punishes long docs. NOTHING is gradient-trained — k1/b are tuned by grid search on labeled test set, df/avgdl are corpus statistics. Library: rank_bm25.BM25Okapi (pure NumPy, ~100 LOC, CPU-ms per query on 10K docs). KEY GOTCHA: tokenization MUST match between index and query — same lowercasing, same regex, same stemming policy, or recall silently collapses. JARVIS hybrid-retriever role (next lesson 2.5.2): BM25 catches identifier/exact-match queries (`store.query_collection`, `$contains`, `AWQ`) where MiniLM blurs sub-word tokens; semantic catches concept queries where BM25 has no synonym awareness. RRF fuses the two ranked lists. Failure modes: synonyms invisible; tokenizer drift kills recall; default rank_bm25 keeps stopwords (fine for prose, wrong for code corpora — never strip identifiers); stemming changes precision/recall trade. Calibration note for our research_papers corpus: avgdl is high (~400 chunked tokens); b=0.75 may over-penalize long chunks — sweep once 2.5.5 metrics + 2.5.6 RAGAS provide a labeled test set.

Decision: production BM25 uses rank_bm25 0.2.2 which ships the un-smoothed Robertson-Sparck-Jones IDF (ln((N-df+0.5)/(df+0.5))) with negative-IDF clamping (eps·avg_idf, eps=0.25). Lucene/Pyserini ship the smoothed form ln(1+...) which never goes negative; the Stage 2.5.1 lesson hand-computation used the Lucene form for pedagogical clarity. Same module documents both. DIRECTIVE: never compare absolute BM25 scores across implementations — only ranks. For Stage 2.5.5 evaluation, recall@k is implementation-agnostic and the only valid quality metric across libraries. For Stage 2.5.2 hybrid RRF fusion, score normalization is irrelevant because RRF uses ranks, not raw scores — the IDF-formula divergence is invisible to the fused output.

BM25 improves upon standard TF-IDF for RAG by introducing term frequency saturation (parameter k1, preventing keyword stuffing dominance) and document length normalization (parameter b, valuing concise chunks).

Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) is the established pattern for merging semantic (ChromaDB) and lexical (BM25) search results. Compute score as 1 / (RRF_K_CONSTANT + rank), where rank is 0-indexed and RRF_K_CONSTANT is typically 60. Accumulate scores per unique chunk_id across all retrieval streams.

Cross-Encoder Pipeline: Bi-Encoder (Chroma) rapidly retrieves top-k candidates (e.g., 20); Cross-Encoder (e.g., MiniLM) re-scores them via joint self-attention to output top-n (e.g., 5) for LLM context. Avoids computational explosion while maximizing relevance.

DIRECTIVE: Explain that DL models require batched matrices (Lists/Tensors) for parallelization speed. A batch of 1 (via yield) destroys throughput. The real OOM risk is VRAM, mitigated by chunked batch processing, not element-by-element streaming.

Deep Learning Inference Safety: Never use Big Data streaming patterns (yield/generators single elements) to feed a DL model, as Batch Size 1 destroys matrix-math throughput. To prevent VRAM OOM on large datasets, accumulate in RAM and use chunked batch processing (e.g., batch_size=32).

ColBERT vs Bi-Encoder: ColBERT stores a vector for every token, enabling late interaction (MaxSim matrix multiplication) for Cross-Encoder precision at near Bi-Encoder speed, but explodes vector storage costs by ~100x compared to flat Bi-Encoders.

Skipped productionizing ColBERT (Late Interaction). Rationale: The ~100x storage explosion per document violates the local-first footprint constraint. Hybrid search (BM25 + Chroma) + Cross-Encoder reranking provides sufficient precision with acceptable latency for Stage 2.

Evaluation Physics: Recall@K measures retrieval existence (did we find it?), MRR measures top-heavy sorting (how deep is the first hit?), NDCG measures graded sorting (is the list optimally ordered?). Rule: Recall proves the DB works, MRR/NDCG proves the prompt engineering will work without Lost-in-the-Middle syndrome.

LLM-as-Judge (Stage 2.5.7) — Mechanics: one LLM (judge) scores another LLM's (subject) output against (a) ground-truth reference [graded mode], (b) retrieved context [faithfulness mode — RAG-canonical], or (c) just the query [self-grade]. Output: structured score (1-5 or pass/fail) + free-text reason. Prompt template: SYSTEM=role+scale; USER=QUERY+CONTEXT+ANSWER+output JSON schema. The whole mechanism is prompt + structured-output discipline; no model magic. FOUR DOCUMENTED BIASES + mitigations: (1) Self-grading bias — if judge==subject, scores inflated +15-20%; mitigation: stronger or different model (Kimi K2.6 subject -> Opus 4.7 judge for high-stakes; Qwen3-235B for routine). (2) Position bias — A-vs-B comparisons favor first answer ~55%; mitigation: shuffle order or run both orders + average. (3) Verbosity bias — judges prefer longer/more confident answers even when wrong; mitigation: 'penalize unnecessary length' in judge prompt + truncate subject answers to fixed length. (4) Math/code blind spots — judge unreliable on math derivations or code correctness; mitigation: use deterministic test runners (pytest, sympy.simplify), reserve LaaJ for natural-language tasks. Production module = jarvis_core/evaluation/judge.py (Stage 4 land); Stage 2.5.7 = design + KB only. Per Decision line 161: judge LLM call uses dependency injection (judge_call: Callable[[str], str]); module never imports anthropic/openai.

Langfuse Tracing (Stage 2.5.7) — Architecture: open-source MIT-equivalent observability for multi-LLM pipelines; self-hostable matches JARVIS privacy stance. Vocabulary: TRACE = one user request end-to-end (trace_id); SPAN = one step inside (retrieval, rerank, LLM call) with parent-child nesting; GENERATION = LLM-call span recording model+in_tokens+out_tokens+latency+cost. Self-host stack: Postgres (metadata) + ClickHouse (column-store for high-volume span data) + Langfuse Node server (~200MB RAM); ~1hr docker-compose setup. JARVIS instrumentation plan: (a) Memory layer emits spans for retrieval_dense, retrieval_bm25, rrf_fuse, rerank, embedding_cache; (b) Brain layer emits llm_call generations + judge generations (offline). Compactor Design Pattern (kb_compact.py reference, reusable for future ChromaDB / GraphRAG / extracted-images compactors): SEVEN reusable primitives. (1) DI'd embedder: Embedder = Callable[[Sequence[str]], np.ndarray]; module never imports sentence-transformers/anthropic — caller wires it (per Decision line 161 layer-boundary discipline). (2) Type-isolated pairwise dedup: same_type_only=True default; a Decision and a Failure on the same topic capture different signals and must both stay; cross-type collapse is dangerous. (3) Structural rule: cosine >= threshold AND tag_jaccard >= overlap_threshold; either alone is insufficient (cosine=0.95 with tag_jaccard=0 = false positive). (4) Quality-aware merge: pick winner by tuple (DIRECTIVE-in-content, content-length, tag-count); ties broken by earliest-timestamp (provenance preservation). Tag-union into winner via merge_tags_into_winner. (5) Transitive redirect resolution: state[line]->current-winner, redirects[loser]->winner, resolve(line) follows chains with cycle break. Handles A->B then B->C correctly. (6) Atomic write: tempfile.mkstemp in same dir + fsync + os.replace (POSIX-atomic rename); .bak preserved before write; on exception unlink tmp + reraise (original KB intact). (7) Default safety: dry-run is default; --force required; audit log appends to compaction_log.jsonl (machine-local, gitignored) every run. SMOKE TESTS via --self-test arg: 6 pure-functional checks (expiry parsing, tag_jaccard math, _pick_winner ordering, provenance tiebreak, tag merge, dedup integration with stub embedder). DIRECTIVE: when building the Stage 4.6 GraphRAG compactor or any future Memory-hygiene tool, port these 7 primitives directly. Do not reinvent. The dedup core is pure-functional and trivially unit-testable; the embedder and KB-IO are the only side-effecting layers.

Decision: parse_tool_call in jarvis_core/agent/parser.py normalizes LLM outputs into an immutable ToolCall dataclass. dispatch() resolves calls against the Tool registry and executes them via safe_invoke. dispatch_batch() partitions calls by is_concurrency_safe, running stateless tools (e.g. calculator) in parallel via asyncio.gather and stateful tools serially. This guarantees maximum concurrency safety and speed without downstream ReAct modifications.

Procedural: Robust JSON extraction from LLM output: First attempt to strip markdown code blocks using _FENCE_PATTERN (r"```(?:json)?\s*\n?(.*?)\n?\s*```", re.DOTALL). If no fence is present, fallback to _BRACE_PATTERN (r"\{[^{}]*(?:\{[^{}]*\}[^{}]*)*\}", re.DOTALL) to extract the outermost JSON object out of surrounding natural language text, making tool parsers resilient to conversational conversational models.

Decision: Error handling for tool calls is implemented as a stateful recovery policy layer (ErrorHandler) above the parser. It classifies ParseError/ToolResult into 5 ToolErrorKinds, tracks per-tool retry budgets via RetryPolicy, and generates targeted LLM repair hints (RecoveryDecision). This separates failure mechanics from the LLM prompt formatting, ensuring infinite loops are prevented via BUDGET_EXCEEDED aborts.

Tool Architecture 3-Category Taxonomy (foundational framing for Stage 3 build). Confirms Iron-Man-like behavior comes 80% from B+C, 20% from A. CATEGORY A (Callable Tool, Stage 3.2): registered via Tool.register(), invoked when LLM emits {tool, input} JSON, dispatched through dispatch_batch() concurrency partition (STEAL #8). Examples: memory_*, calculator, web_search, code_exec, file_read, shell_run, cognitive_mirror callable form, bear_case_devil, portfolio_state, trigger_monitor callable form, pre_mortem, multi_specialist_consult. CATEGORY B (Middleware/Interceptor, Stage 3.4 ReAct pipeline): fires automatically on every relevant agent step, NOT in tool registry, cannot be skipped by LLM. Hooks: pre-system-prompt, pre-LLM-call, pre-tool-dispatch, post-tool-result, pre-response-finalize. Examples: voice_persona (every output), cognitive_mirror middleware form (pre-prompt), integrity_check (pre-commit), leak_check (pre-cloud-call), response_calibration (post-draft), flow_state_detector (every N turns), pattern_witness (session-end). CATEGORY C (Daemon/Ambient): runs independently of agent invocation via TaskScheduler tick loop (OpenJarvis STEAL #4). Triggers: cron, file-change, session-boundary, error-trace-pattern-match, laptop-switch. Stage 3.5 minimal backbone piggybacks on MemGPT heartbeat (session_resume_context, failure_pattern_alarm, narrate_progress, cross_runtime_sync_check, attention_handoff). Stage 6 full scheduler adds world_state_briefing, decision_deadline_tracker, trigger_monitor daemon, screen_observer, voice_command, stage_gate_check pre-commit hook, shadow_search, etc. DIRECTIVE: when describing any Stage 3+ feature, explicitly classify A/B/C. Conflating callable tools with daemons obscures WHEN code fires - the primary source of architectural bugs. Iron-Man feel = B + C, not just A.

NEW 8th Category-B middleware: temporal_grounding (AUGMENTS Decision 2026-05-19 Category B Inventory). Closes the Iron-Man 'ambient time-awareness' gap — JARVIS knows WHEN code fired without procedural CoT reasoning. Eliminates the failure mode where Claude/JARVIS iteratively debugs differences that are trivially explained by 'a commit happened between then and now'. HOOK: PRE_PROMPT (fires before LLM sees user message). INPUTS: current user message, last N=20 conversation turns, KB entries from last 90 days, git log (full), telemetry gap_seconds + local_hour. ALGORITHM: (1) regex + spaCy NER scan for temporal/causal markers — explicit dates ('yesterday' / 'last week'), relative refs ('before X' / 'after Y' / 'since Z'), pronouns referring to past events ('the test' / 'that bug' / 'the fix'), causal language ('because' / 'after' / 'before'); (2) for each marker, call temporal_resolver utility (jarvis_core/agent/temporal.py, Stage 3.2 lib) to resolve to specific timestamp / commit SHA / KB entry; (3) build TEMPORAL_CONTEXT block: per-ref resolution + relevant KB excerpts + commit summaries + causal frame; (4) inject block into system prompt BEFORE user message. OUTPUT SCHEMA: 'TEMPORAL_CONTEXT (auto-resolved):' followed by per-ref lines 'User mention X -> resolved Y (timestamp T, commit SHA, KB entries [L_a, L_b])'; then causal-frame summary. COMPOSITION ORDER: fires FIRST in middleware chain — BEFORE cognitive_mirror (temporal context informs which Cognitive_Patterns are relevant). PERFORMANCE BUDGET: <100ms p95 (typical <5 refs/message), <500ms p99 (>10 refs); per-session resolution cache. FAILURE MODES: (a) ambiguous ref ('the bug' with 3 candidates) -> include all with confidence scores, let LLM disambiguate via context; (b) no markers found -> silent passthrough (no injection); (c) git log >10k commits -> sliding window last 1000 commits; (d) corrupt git_kb_correlator index -> fall back to live scan (slower but correct). ORDERING NOTE: Stage 3.4 ships BEFORE Stage 3.5 — temporal_grounding initially runs live scan; git_kb_correlator (Stage 3.5) makes it fast retroactively. DIRECTIVE: this is the SINGLE highest-leverage interceptor for Iron-Man feel — every response with temporal reasoning saves 5-15 tokens of CoT and avoids procedural-reasoning-arrives-at-wrong-conclusion. NEVER ship Stage 3.4 without this.

NEW 6th Stage-3.5 Category-C daemon: git_kb_correlator (AUGMENTS Decision 2026-05-19 Daemon Inventory L285; slots alongside session_resume_context + failure_pattern_alarm + narrate_progress + cross_runtime_sync_check + attention_handoff on the MemGPT heartbeat backbone). Pre-computes the correlation index that temporal_grounding middleware queries at request time. Keeps middleware p95 <100ms by avoiding live git+KB scan per request. TRIGGERS: (a) post-commit git hook on every commit to main (primary); (b) full backfill on first run (walks all commits since 2026-03-01); (c) hourly cron belt-and-suspenders catch-up. MECHANISM: for each commit C with modified_paths P[]: (1) walks KB entries in last 7 days; (2) for each entry E, checks if E.content mentions any file / feature name / symbol in P[] (substring + fuzzy match); (3) records correlation: {kb_timestamp, commit_sha, modified_paths, correlation_score 0.0-1.0 (path-mention strength), evidence_substring (the matching span)}. OUTPUT FILE: jarvis_data/git_kb_correlations.jsonl (GITIGNORED — derivable index, treated as regenerable like ChromaDB; rebuild via --backfill). Schema per line: {kb_timestamp: ISO, commit_sha: str, modified_paths: List[str], correlation_score: float, evidence: str, indexed_at: ISO}. Append-only; --backfill flag rebuilds from scratch. SCHEMA-PORT: NOT loaded into main KB — KB stays semantic insights; this is structural correlation index. Add to .gitignore alongside chromadb/. PERFORMANCE BUDGET: post-commit hook <1s p95 (most commits touch <5 files, <20 KB entries in scan window); backfill <60s for typical 200 commits + 300 KB entries. FAILURE MODES: (a) corrupt index -> temporal_grounding falls back to live git log + KB scan (slow but correct); (b) commit during indexing -> defer to next hook fire (idempotent); (c) symbol-mention ambiguity -> record all candidates with low confidence, middleware disambiguates; (d) KB compaction shifts line numbers -> index uses timestamps as IDs, not line numbers, so compaction-stable. DIRECTIVE: install post-commit git hook at Stage 3.5 entry alongside MemGPT heartbeat; full backfill is the activation gate. After 3.5 ships, temporal_grounding middleware switches from live-scan (slow) to index-lookup (fast) automatically via fallback chain.

NEW Utility Library: temporal_resolver (Stage 3.2 ships alongside Tool ABC + memory tools). Pure-functional library used BY temporal_grounding middleware (Stage 3.4) and optionally callable from agent (Stage 3.2 tools/cognitive.py addition). NOT a Category A/B/C primary — shared utility, analogous to how jarvis_core/memory/chunking.py is to ingestion. FILE: jarvis_core/agent/temporal.py (~400 lines target). PUBLIC API (pure functions, no LLM call, no network): (1) resolve_relative_date(expr: str, reference: datetime, locale: str = 'en-IN') -> Optional[datetime]: parses 'yesterday', 'last week', '3 days ago', 'this morning', 'Monday', 'before lunch' etc. Returns None on unparseable. Uses dateparser library + custom Indian-English regex extensions (lunch/dinner/IST 9-5). (2) resolve_event_reference(expr: str, git_log: Sequence[Commit], kb_index: Sequence[KBEntry]) -> List[ResolvedRef]: parses 'before X was pushed', 'since the feature landed', 'after the rerank fix'. Searches commit messages + KB content via fuzzy match (rapidfuzz, ratio>=70); returns ranked candidates with confidence 0.0-1.0. (3) resolve_pronoun(expr: str, conversation: Sequence[Message]) -> Optional[ResolvedRef]: resolves 'the test', 'that bug', 'the fix' against recent conversation; last-mention + coreference heuristics. (4) detect_temporal_markers(text: str) -> List[Marker]: dispatcher — returns [(start_idx, end_idx, marker_type, raw_text)] used to route to (1)/(2)/(3) per marker_type. DATA TYPES: @dataclass(frozen=True) Marker, ResolvedRef, Commit (lightweight git log shim — sha, timestamp, message, modified_paths). TEST COVERAGE: 100% pure-function smoke tests in __main__ block (per Code Style rule, no separate test file). 50+ test cases: explicit dates × 10, relative refs × 15, event refs × 15, pronouns × 10. FALLBACK BEHAVIOR: if all four return None for a marker, temporal_grounding middleware logs the unresolved marker to jarvis_data/unresolved_temporal_markers.jsonl for offline pattern expansion. LLM-based ambiguity-resolution lives IN THE MIDDLEWARE, not the resolver — resolver stays deterministic + pure. DEPENDENCIES: dateparser (pip), rapidfuzz (pip); both Apache 2.0, CPU-only, no GPU required. DIRECTIVE: land at Stage 3.2 entry sprint alongside cognitive_mirror callable + writing_voice_check (they share the 'resolve user-language to KB references' pattern). ~1 day of work — small, deterministic, smoke-tested. Becomes load-bearing at Stage 3.4 when temporal_grounding ships.

POSITIVE PATTERN: constraint_justification_probing. User tests whether a stated limitation is FUNDAMENTAL or merely INCIDENTAL by proposing the one mechanism that would refute its stated justification, rather than accepting the rule at face value. Incident (2026-05-27, DE digest): digest claimed 'snapshot CDC (create_auto_cdc_from_snapshot_flow) is incompatible with continuous mode BECAUSE .collect()/spark.sql MIN-MAX cannot run in a streaming loop.' User countered: 'what if we wrap those batch ops in foreachBatch inside the source function?' -- foreachBatch is exactly the mechanism that DOES run batch ops in a streaming loop, so the question surgically falsifies the digest's stated reason. The probe was correct: the real constraint is not 'batch ops in a loop' but (a) the source function is a DLT-owned pull-based callback returning discrete (DataFrame, version) tuples with no streaming write to attach a sink to, and (b) snapshot diffing is intrinsically discrete/bounded. Teaching implication: when documenting a constraint for this user, state the FUNDAMENTAL why (API contract / semantics), never a convenient-but-incidental why -- he will find and break the weak justification. Distinct from but related to forward_simulated_architecture (stress-testing designs against future production state); this pattern stress-tests the *justification of an existing rule*.

LoRA mechanism: freeze weight matrix W [d,k], learn Delta-W = B@A instead (A:[r,k], B:[d,r], r<<d,k). B zero-initialized, A small-random -- guarantees Delta-W=0 at step 0 so the adapted model starts IDENTICAL to base; only A,B get gradients, W.requires_grad=False throughout. Converges to the best rank-r fit SGD/Adam can find, NOT the mathematically optimal SVD-truncated approximation (common misconception -- validate empirically, don't assume the math guarantee). At d=k=4096, rank 32 (JARVIS Engineer/Scientist/Operator/Analyst's actual rank per ENDGAME Sec 3.6) = 64x fewer trainable params vs full fine-tune; rank 16 (smaller adapters) = 128x. QLoRA adds: quantize the FROZEN base to 4-bit NF4 (NormalFloat4 -- non-uniform codebook fit to the ~Gaussian weight distribution, NOT naive uniform quantization) + double quantization (quantize the quant constants too) + paged optimizers (page optimizer state to CPU RAM via NVIDIA unified memory on GPU-memory spikes) -- the 3 pillars per Dettmers et al. 2023. Dequantization happens on-the-fly every forward pass (no native 4-bit matmul hardware path) -- real memory-for-compute tradeoff. Requires bitsandbytes+CUDA -- confirmed NOT installed on this CPU-only work laptop (verified via runtime check), consistent with ENDGAME's no-local-GPU hardware reality; real training happens on RunPod. Taught + verified runnable in js-learning/stage_5_specialists/sub_5.1_fine_tuning_basics/01_lora_qlora_overview.py (lesson 5.1.1).

COMPOSITION QUESTION RESOLVED (2026-08-16) — the blocker flagged before any RunPod spend. Requirement was an always-on personalization adapter active alongside whichever specialist answers. VERIFIED FINDINGS, not assumptions: (1) vLLM CANNOT compose two LoRAs on one request -- docs verbatim: 'we only allow one LoRA per prompt'; its multi-LoRA feature routes DIFFERENT adapters to DIFFERENT requests in a batch, it does not stack adapters on one inference; single-request composition exists only as an open RFC for DIFFUSION models (vllm-omni #2149), not shipped for LLMs. (2) This codebase independently encodes the same constraint: brain/targets.py PodHandle.__init__(self, adapter_id: str, ...) is a singular string, not a list -- ENDGAME Sec3's 'one adapter at a time' is in the contract, not just prose. (3) Merging separately-trained adapters is NOT a safe fallback -- literature calls it a worst-case interference setting with highly non-uniform degradation that can collapse on specific domains. (4) Training ONE adapter on a MIXED corpus empirically BEATS merging separately-trained adapters (MathQA+Alpaca-code single-adapter > merged math+code adapters). DECISION: do not compose, do not merge -- BLEND THE CORPORA, TRAIN ONCE. Zero unsolved technology, compatible with one-LoRA-per-prompt as it actually exists, ONE training run instead of two (cheaper than the original plan), and VALIDATES ENDGAME Sec3's architecture rather than requiring a rewrite. CORRECTION to Data_Engineering_Lessons.md line 489 (found 2026-08-22 on reading the actual framework code). My 2026-08-08 lesson 'Time Travel Is Bounded by Retention' states Delta's window as 7 days / 168h and prescribes gating every resolved historical version on 'now() - commit_ts > 168h'. That is the framework's SUPERSEDED behaviour, and tst_tables_version_retention_check.py now documents at length why it was wrong. THE REAL MECHANISM IS TWO INDEPENDENT CLOCKS: deletedFileRetentionDuration (default 7d) governs how long VACUUM keeps tombstoned DATA FILES; logRetentionDuration (default 30d) governs how long _delta_log commits/checkpoints survive. Only checks that read row VALUES are bounded by 7d -- exceptAll, sampling, checksums, aggregates over a column. Everything answerable from the log (schema, column order, file count and total bytes via AddFile-minus-RemoveFile replay, tblproperties, partitioning, comments, column-mapping mode, deletion vectors, all DESCRIBE HISTORY questions) stays valid the full 30 days AFTER VACUUM has removed every data file. The code now uses RETENTION_HOURS = 720, not 168. Blast radius of my error: applying the 7d gate to all twelve checks when only two touch data files discarded ~20,000 valid log-sourced measurements PER RUN -- the user's own learnings file names this as a design bug they fixed. A THIRD store exists that neither clock governs: the Unity Catalog metastore (registration, tags, PK/FK, grants) has NO time travel at all, so pairing a live UC read against a version-pinned Delta read silently compares now-against-then. ROOT CAUSE OF MY ERROR: I distilled from a verbal description in chat and encoded the then-current implementation as the general rule, without the mechanism that would have shown the rule was over-broad. Same shape as [refusal_pattern] -- I stated a conclusion without its causal chain, which is exactly what the user rejects when I do it to them. FORWARD RULE: when distilling a lesson from a described implementation, record the MECHANISM (which store answers this?) not the THRESHOLD, because the threshold is a consequence of the mechanism and only the mechanism survives a fix.

Photon internals (RSA-prep canonical). WHAT: C++ vectorized query engine, JNI-loaded INTO the existing Spark executor JVM process (not a separate service). Paper: 'Photon: A Fast Query Engine for Lakehouse Systems', SIGMOD 2022. WHY IT EXISTS BEYOND WSCG: Whole-Stage CodeGen already killed Volcano per-row virtual dispatch, so Photon exists to break three ceilings WSCG cannot -- (1) JVM C2 JIT cannot RELIABLY auto-vectorize (bails on branches/null-checks/un-inlined calls), so you can never guarantee AVX-512; (2) HotSpot HugeMethodLimit = 8000 bytecodes silently drops WSCG's one-giant-method-per-stage to the INTERPRETER (~20-50x slower) on wide queries -- an invisible cliff with no plan-visible cause; JVM hard method cap is 64KB; (3) GC pauses + no control of cache-line layout. DESIGN CHOICE WORTH QUOTING: Databricks chose vectorized INTERPRETATION over code generation despite owning the best codegen engine in WSCG -- reasons: kernels are profileable/debuggable, and vectorization permits RUNTIME ADAPTIVITY a compile-once plan cannot do (dispatches to no-null kernel when batch has no nulls, all-ASCII kernel for strings). MECHANISM: operators return ~1000-row COLUMN BATCHES; filter writes a SELECTION VECTOR of surviving positions and passes the SAME batch downstream (no materialization, no copy); flat column array fits L1 (1000 float64 = 8KB); AVX-512 = 8 float64 lanes so 1000 compares become 125 instructions. FALLBACK RULE (the actual gate): Photon needs a hand-written C++ kernel per operator-x-datatype; where none exists the node falls back to JVM Spark AND the boundary costs a full materialization (ColumnarToRow / RowToColumnar in the plan). ZERO/NEGATIVE BENEFIT: Python+Scala UDFs (no kernel possible -- #1 killer in the wild), RDD API (opaque closures), deeply-nested complex types, stateful Structured Streaming, small data (<~1M rows, setup+JNI dominates), I/O- or shuffle-bound jobs (Amdahl: 8x on CPU moves ~5% of wall clock), small-file-heavy writes (bottleneck is PUTs + log commits). NUMBERS: ~8x on raw compute vs WSCG, 2-4x realistic end-to-end. COST TRAP: Photon bills ~2x DBU (verify current tier pricing), so Photon is a NET LOSS below ~2x speedup -- a UDF-heavy pipeline pays 2x rate for 1.0x speed. INSPECT: EXPLAIN FORMATTED for PhotonScan/PhotonProject/PhotonGroupingAgg vs plain nodes, hunt ColumnarToRow/RowToColumnar mid-plan as the transition tax, Spark UI SQL tab badges Photon nodes, photonTotalTime metric.

Serverless vs classic compute -- the ROOT CAUSE answer (RSA-prep canonical). Do NOT answer with 'faster startup'. SINGLE ROOT CAUSE: whose cloud account the data-plane VMs live in. Classic = control plane in Databricks' account, DATA PLANE VMs provisioned in YOUR subscription inside YOUR VNet/VPC (your NSGs, routes, private endpoints, vCPU quota; you pay cloud for VMs + Databricks for DBUs). Serverless = compute runs in a DATABRICKS-OWNED account and managed network; one blended DBU rate; your cloud bill shows nothing. Every other difference is a CONSEQUENCE -- frame it as a causal chain, not a feature list. CONSEQUENCE 1 NETWORKING (the real blocker): serverless cannot reach Private-Endpoint SQL/Synapse, firewalled storage, or on-prem over ExpressRoute by default. Mechanism to name: Network Connectivity Configuration (NCC), an ACCOUNT-level object with two modes -- stable outbound IPs to allowlist, or private endpoint rules where Databricks creates a managed PE from its network into your resource which YOU must approve. NO VNet injection, NO user-defined routes, NO NVA in path, NO custom DNS -- so serverless BREAKS a hub-VNet-firewall egress control model outright (a security-team conversation, not a checkbox). CONSEQUENCE 2 RESTRICTED RUNTIME (multi-tenancy forces removal of capability): no cluster-scoped init scripts (libraries only via notebook %pip / environment specs); most spark.conf locked (an entire category of 'how would you tune this' answers no longer applies); no SparkContext/RDD (UC standard-access-mode isolation kills sc.parallelize, rdd.mapPartitions); no DBFS FUSE/arbitrary local FS; Unity Catalog MANDATORY, no Hive-metastore path. HEADLINE: migrating a legacy job to serverless is a CODE-COMPATIBILITY exercise, not a config change. CONSEQUENCE 3 COST MODEL INVERTS (most-missed): classic = you provision a shape, the cluster is a physical cost CEILING, so a bad job is cheap-and-slow. Serverless = platform picks resources, so a bad job becomes EXPENSIVE instead of slow. Governance moves from cluster policies (PREVENTIVE, caps spend) to budget policies/tagging/observability (DETECTIVE, tells you after). For a client whose FinOps posture is built entirely on cluster policies, serverless INVALIDATES their cost-control model. CONSEQUENCE 4 NO VERSION PINNING: classic pins DBR (e.g. 14.3 LTS) frozen until you move; serverless has narrow environment-versions and Databricks upgrades on their cadence -- a hard blocker for a regulated client needing a validated frozen runtime. THE UNIFYING CLOSE: startup is fast because Databricks keeps a PRE-WARMED multi-tenant VM pool with the runtime image loaded -- 'starting' is really ASSIGNING you capacity + attaching identity/UC creds. That pool is only economically viable BECAUSE it is multi-tenant. So the fast startup and the restrictions are THE SAME FACT seen from two sides; there is no world where you get one without the other. PRECISION: 'serverless' is four products with different maturity/restrictions -- SQL Warehouse (oldest, Photon always on, result cache), Jobs/Workflows, Notebooks (Python+SQL first, Scala later+restricted), DLT/Lakeflow Pipelines. Asking 'which serverless?' is itself a good signal.

SILENT EMBEDDING TRUNCATION in scripts/search_memory.py -- found 2026-08-26 while VERIFYING the previous turn's work, not by looking for it. Symptom: KB 504 would not surface in semantic search even when queried with phrasing lifted verbatim out of it; the top hit was an unrelated Episodic at 0.377. ROOT CAUSE: search_memory.py embedded entry.content WHOLE through all-MiniLM-L6-v2, whose max_seq_length is 256 tokens. sentence-transformers truncates past that SILENTLY -- no exception, no warning, just a vector computed from the first 256 tokens as though the rest did not exist. PROOF IT WAS TRUNCATION AND NOT A RANKING QUIRK: two strings sharing a long head but with completely unrelated tails ('phone app, ambient, camera, Tier 0' vs 'quantum chromodynamics, bicycle repair, sourdough') embedded to cosine 1.000000. The tails were never seen at all. MEASURED BLAST RADIUS before the fix, against 505 live entries: 203 entries exceeded the 900-char chunk limit and were being partially discarded; 15 of the 15 entries written since id 490 were affected -- 100%. KB 504 at 3,220 chars had roughly its first third embedded, so every distinctive term in it sat in the dropped tail and the entry was unreachable by any query naming them. THE WORST PROPERTY: this scaled INVERSELY with entry quality. The richest, most detailed entries -- exactly the ones worth retrieving -- were the most truncated, while short entries were unaffected. Retrieval silently got worse the better the writing got. THE FIX ALREADY EXISTED IN THIS REPO AND THE SCRIPT BYPASSED IT. jarvis_core/memory/chunking.py's RecursiveWordChunker and DEFAULT_CHUNK_CHAR_LIMIT (900) exist PRECISELY to fit MiniLM's 256-token ceiling -- engineer_corpus.py's own comment says so -- and memory/store.py already chunks before embedding for the ChromaDB path. search_memory.py was the lone outlier. Fixed by chunking each entry (900 chars, 180 overlap) and reducing chunk scores to one score per entry via MAX, not mean: a long entry typically has one passage answering the query and several that do not, and averaging would penalize exactly the detailed entries most worth finding. 505 entries -> 832 chunks. VERIFIED AFTER: the previously-failing query now returns KB 504 as Result 1 at 0.478; a short-entry query is unregressed; kb_append.py --audit still runs, so the dedup caller is unbroken. FORWARD RULE: any silent-capacity limit -- token ceilings, column widths, buffer sizes -- must be asserted against, not trusted. A library that truncates rather than raising will hide the failure for months, and the only reason this surfaced at all was running a verification whose expected answer was known in advance. Verification that can only confirm success is not verification.

USER ASKED (2026-09-02): 'if i have a bond then can the company fire me in that period?' -- i.e. whether the Celebal Service Commitment Period constrains the EMPLOYER as well as them. Answered against their real terms from KB 436 (Mutual Service Agreement signed 2026-04-16, SCP 24 months to 2027-04-22, flat 3-month notice running only AFTER the SCP, early-exit liability ~Rs 2,20,000 = Rs 1,50,000 + ~Rs 70,000 half-stipend). SUBSTANCE OF THE ANSWER: yes, they can terminate during the SCP -- a service bond is a one-way covenant binding the employee, and termination rights sit in a separate clause of the same document. PYTHON GOTCHA that silently breaks log-grepping: on a str-mixin Enum, str(x) and f-string formatting DISAGREE. PermissionDecision is declared 'class PermissionDecision(str, Enum)' with DENY = 'deny'. Cost me a false test failure: the code logged the decision with an f-string ('deny') while the assertion searched for the str() form ('PermissionDecision.DENY'). The real hazard is not tests -- it is that a log line written one way and grepped the other NEVER matches, and a monitoring rule built on it silently never fires. DIRECTIVE: when logging an enum whose value must be machine-matched later, use repr() or .value explicitly, never bare interpolation. Fixed in Python 3.11+ for IntEnum via __str__ changes, but this repo runs 3.10 and the str-mixin case remains divergent regardless.

Replaying the real queue: 75 turns -> 1 candidate, 115 turns -> 0, and _deterministic_confidence was never called even once, so the 0.60 floor rejected nothing. (2) Its output was never a memory: lifetime total three sentences, all 2026-06-18, all restating one volume shift. (3) Its 'confidence' was a hand-rolled weighted sum with a free 0.35 base capped at 0.70 -- every shipped insight read '70%' because that was the cap. WHAT REPLACED IT: candidate = what the user is doing now (KB appends AND verbatim observation_queue turns); corpus = their own 305 Decision/Failure/Cognitive_Pattern entries via the EXISTING chromadb index (no re-index -- entry_type/timestamp metadata was already there); output = a RELATION (REVERSES/REPEATS/RECONFUSES/NONE) against a NAMED prior, fail-closed to NONE on every error path. Reuses ContradictionJudge's discipline from brain/reasoning.py rather than inventing a second judge. DIRECTIVE: when a detector's gate becomes harder to satisfy as data accumulates, that is a design fault, not a tuning problem -- check the monotonicity of every threshold against volume before shipping it.

ABSTENTION HAD NO LABEL, AND THAT -- NOT THE SUBSTRING BUG -- WAS THE ROOT CAUSE (found + fixed 2026-09-09, on the user's insistence). The user rejected my proposed fix outright: 'I need a permanent solution, if we keep implementing better keyword matching it will result in the same bad labels that will silently kill the training corpus.' Correct, and investigating why produced a sharper diagnosis than I had. MEASURED ROOT CAUSE: guess_domain seeded best='general' and returned it on zero matches, so 'this turn is genuinely general' and 'I have no idea' were THE SAME TOKEN. Measured on the live queue: 309 of 583 records (53%) were labelled general, and ALL 309 had ZERO keyword hits -- not one was a positive classification. An abstention was literally unrepresentable, which is why 99 days and ~15% wrong labels went unnoticed. THE TRAP I ALMOST WALKED INTO: agent/domain_classifier.py, the embedding classifier built precisely BECAUSE keywords failed, ALSO fell back to 'general' below threshold. Swapping keywords for embeddings alone would have been more accurate and equally undiagnosable. THE FIX IS FOUR PROPERTIES, only the first about accuracy: (1) semantic not lexical; (2) UNKNOWN as a distinct outcome, never 'general' -- this converts an invisible failure into a counted one; (3) the cosine SCORE persisted next to every label so a wrong threshold is inspectable; (4) a 28-turn hand-labelled GOLD SET wired into check_projections.py, which already runs on the scheduler. Property 4 is what makes it permanent: any classifier drifts as the work moves, so the durable property is not being right today but SAYING WHEN IT STOPS BEING RIGHT. The gate proved itself immediately -- first run scored 68%, refused to pass, and its misses showed the prototypes had no seeds for AWS Glue, VACUUM, ADF, SFT or RunPod. Adding seeds for that real vocabulary: 89%. DIRECTIVE: any classifier that cannot say 'I do not know' will hide its own failure rate forever. Give abstention its own label before tuning anything else.

A LONG QUERY RETRIEVES NEIGHBOURS, NOT THE THING IT CONTRADICTS (found + fixed 2026-09-09; this single fix was the difference between the detector finding nothing and working). The tension detector passed the WHOLE candidate entry as the retrieval query. Measured on the gold pair (KB 461 genuinely contradicts KB 429, confirmed by hand in KB 463): query = the full 1126-char entry -> 429 NOT IN THE TOP 15; query = its first 300 chars -> 429 at rank 9; query = one focused topic phrase -> 429 at rank 1, three times. CAUSE: a long entry covers several subjects, so its embedding is the AVERAGE of all of them and matches nothing sharply. It retrieves its own neighbours IN TIME (adjacent KB ids written the same day) rather than the specific decision it clashes with. Worse, the candidate's top TWO hits were ITSELF -- an entry is always its own strongest match, burning retrieval budget on a guaranteed non-prior. FIX: split the candidate into ~320-char overlapping windows (max 5), retrieve for each, union and dedupe; plus exclude the candidate's own entry_id explicitly rather than relying on the timestamp filter. RESULT: 461->429, 518->509 and 494->491 all now retrieve their true prior AT RANK 1, and the full pipeline (retrieval + judge, no hand-feeding) surfaces the 461/429 contradiction at 0.95 while staying silent on 518. WHAT THIS ALMOST HID: the first 30-day replay reported '0 findings'. The eval harness had passed 5/5 because I HAND-FED it the priors, so it measured the judge and not retrieval. DIRECTIVE: an eval that supplies its own inputs measures only the last stage. Instrument every stage of the funnel, and when a pipeline reports zero, prove WHICH stage produced the zero before believing it.

ONE CLASSIFIER, TWO CONSUMERS, TWO MEANINGS OF THE SAME LABEL -- caught by the Final Boss (2026-09-09). Fixing the abstention conflation, I hard-coded domain_classifier.py's below-threshold fallback from 'general' to UNKNOWN. Correct for the ACTIVITY-domain consumer, where 'general' had no prototype and was pure abstention. But brain/router.py COMPOSES the same DomainClassifier with its own ROUTING prototypes, and there 'general' IS A REAL DESTINATION -- the general model pool, present in ROUTING_LABELS and mapped in _ROUTE_MAP. Abstaining in routing legitimately means 'send it to the general pool'. So my change made the router return a label outside its own vocabulary and the 50-query frozen gate fell below 80%: FINAL BOSS 7/8, leg 3 FAILED. Caught only because that harness exists and was re-run. FIX: fallback_label is now a per-consumer constructor argument (default UNKNOWN); the router passes fallback_label='general' with the reason written at the call site. Better than reverting -- it keeps the honesty fix where abstention really is abstention, and keeps the routing semantics where it is not. Final Boss restored 8/8. DIRECTIVE: before changing a SENTINEL VALUE in a shared component, enumerate the consumers and ask what that value MEANS to each one. A label can be an abstention in one caller and a legitimate category in another; the same string is not the same semantics. Grep for construction sites, not just for the constant.

A SECURITY-RELEVANT DEPENDENCY WAS UNDECLARED, AND ITS ABSENCE WAS INVISIBLE (found 2026-09-10 by a regression run). agent/bash_classifier.py parses shell commands into a bashlex AST to decide ALLOW vs ASK vs DENY for shell_run -- it is part of the shipped permission gate. was NOT in requirements.txt and was not installed anywhere on disk. WHY IT WAS INVISIBLE: the module soft-fails correctly (bash_classifier.py:174 -- ), so nothing broke, nothing warned, and no security hole opened. The ONLY symptom was ONE smoke test flipping (permgate 13/13 -> 12/13, 'T3 shell safe ALLOW' getting ASK). Everything else -- boot, the gate, --ask -- kept working while the classifier had silently degraded to 'ask about every command', which destroys exactly the precision it exists to provide. IMPORTANT CALIBRATION: this is a CAPABILITY loss, not a safety regression. The failure direction is conservative (ASK, never ALLOW), which is the correct design. But 'fails safe' is not the same as 'fails visibly', and a permission classifier that quietly stops classifying is a real defect. FIX: installed bashlex==0.18 and declared it in requirements.txt with the consequence written next to it. DIRECTIVE: when a component soft-fails on a missing optional import, the import MUST be declared as a hard dependency if the component is security-relevant -- and the degraded mode should announce itself, not merely be documented. Grep for across the safety layer and check each one is either declared or loudly reported.

MY ANTI-HALLUCINATION GUARD WAS DISCARDING 60% OF CORRECT VERDICTS (found + fixed 2026-09-10). The tension judge returns which prior a candidate clashes with; TensionJudge validates that the cited id was actually among the priors shown, so an invented reference cannot become a surfaced insight. Sound guard, but implemented as strict string equality. SYMPTOM: the ship-gate eval flapped -- the gold case passed at 0.95 twice, then failed at 0.00 on a later run, with everything else identical. I nearly wrote it off as model sampling noise. MEASURED INSTEAD by repeating the identical case 5 times: the judge found the contradiction ALL FIVE TIMES. On three of them it wrote the id as 'PRIOR 429' rather than '429' -- echoing the '[PRIOR 429]' label MY OWN PROMPT used to present the priors. Exact match rejected those as hallucinations, so a working detector looked 60% unreliable and its true-positive rate was silently cut by more than half. TWO FIXES, both needed: (1) the prompt now labels priors '[id=429]' and asks for the id 'exactly as it appears after id=, digits only'; (2) _match_prior normalises before comparing -- strips a leading PRIOR/KB/entry/id token, brackets and whitespace, then falls back to a digit extraction that only resolves when EXACTLY ONE prior matches. The guard is not weakened: an id never shown still resolves to None (asserted by T13f). Stability after the fix: gold positive 5/5, hard negative 3/3. THIRD INSTRUMENTATION LESSON IN TWO DAYS: ScanReport now counts 'discarded (uncitable prior)' SEPARATELY from 'judge said NONE', because conflating them is exactly how a 60% suppression rate hid inside a plausible-looking zero. DIRECTIVE: a validator that rejects malformed-but-correct output is a false-negative generator, and it fails silently by construction. When a guard drops something, COUNT the drops as their own category -- never fold them into the legitimate-negative bucket. And check whether your own prompt's formatting is what the model is echoing back.

PATTERN: distrusts_an_aggregate_until_someone_reads_the_rows -- and it paid off measurably (2026-09-09/10, Antigravity corpus review on the personal laptop). The user asked Antigravity to judge training readiness. It answered with char/token shares and a confident verdict. The user's SECOND prompt is the whole event, VERBATIM: 'okay, you've judged the training corpus based on the chars and tokens, but have you actually looked at each training line and the conent in each of them? do they qualify as a training data for personalization and engineer models?' THE FIRST PASS FOUND: ratio asymmetry (87.1% engineer vs 12.9% personalization chars), zero SFT pairs, no loss collator -- all true, all derivable from aggregates. THE SECOND PASS FOUND THE THING THAT ACTUALLY MATTERS: ~40% of kb_identity/kb_judgment records are Claude's THIRD-PERSON clinical observations about the user ('PATTERN: ...', 'the user prefixed it'), which as raw next-token training would teach the adapter to write analyst notes ABOUT him rather than speak AS him. Verified independently: 101 of 246 such records (41%) carry third-person assistant voice; contamination is localized (user_voice 2%, professional_reasoning 0%), so the diagnosis is precise, not a smear. DIRECTIVE: when a verdict about DATA rests only on aggregates, read a stratified sample of the actual rows before accepting it. Counts describe volume; they are structurally blind to voice, person, truncation and provenance.

WORKFLOW PROTOCOLS FIRE BY REQUEST-SHAPE, AND CARRY NO SELF-INVENTED DISCRETION LAYER ON TOP (fixed 2026-07-15; rescued 2026-09-10 from machine-local memory that had ZERO KB representation). Since dev work in this repo happens conversationally ('do it', 'build the guard'), the workflows never fired -- dev.md's Design Review verdict, Stress Test bullets, Debug Hooks section, and closing Memory-suggestion/Cognitive-scan rituals were silently skipped even while file-header/code-style conventions kept looking followed, creating an illusion of compliance. FIX: trigger is now request-SHAPE matched against each workflow's stated purpose, regardless of literal slash typing. THE CORRECTION THAT MATTERS MORE THAN THE FIX ITSELF: while drafting it, I proposed broadening the trigger AND adding a 'skip the full ritual for trivial asks' discretion layer on top.
