 when adding checks to a non-UC path, audit what they *output*, not just what
 they read.

## Cloud capacity: quota, VM generations, and spot

- **Azure vCPU quota is per VM *family*, per region, per subscription — not per
 pool, per cluster, or per workload.** Names like `standardESv5Family`,
 `standardDDSv5Family`, `standardDSv5Family` are the actual buckets, and an
 `AZURE_QUOTA_EXCEEDED_EXCEPTION` names the one you exhausted. The practical
 consequence is unintuitive: **changing node size can change which quota you
 draw from**, so a "smaller, cheaper" node may succeed where a larger one
 failed purely because it lands in a different, emptier bucket. Spreading a
 fleet across families is a legitimate capacity strategy.
- **Compute peak concurrent vCPU before shipping a fan-out, and do it as a
 sum.** Every chunk of a parallel fan-out is its own cluster, and independent
 tiers run *at the same time*, so peak = Σ over all chunks of
 (workers + 1 driver) × cores-per-node. One job at concurrency 3 and 12 needed
 1,344 cores of one family against a limit of 350 — a 4× overrun that was
 entirely predictable from the YAML, and wasn't predicted because nobody did
 the arithmetic.
- **Spot draws from a *separate* quota, and it can be far larger.** In the same
 region and subscription: 350 cores for the on-demand family, **10,000** for
 `Total Regional Spot vCPUs`. The spot pool was the *same VM* as the on-demand
 one. So when a per-family limit blocks you, moving to spot is not a downgrade
 in hardware at all — it's a change of accounting bucket, and it may be the
 only way to keep your intended concurrency while a quota increase is pending.
- **Quota is not capacity.** Having headroom in the limit says nothing about
 whether the provider has spare VMs of that SKU in that region right now,
 which matters most for spot. Treat "quota available" and "allocation will
 succeed" as two separate questions.
- **A pool with no `max_capacity` cannot be a contention point.** If pools are
 uncapped, two clusters sharing one pool draw exactly the same VMs from
 exactly the same quota as two clusters on two pools — splitting them to
 "avoid contention" buys nothing. Scarcity lives at the quota layer, not the
 pool layer. Worth checking `max_capacity` and `min_idle_instances` before
 designing around imagined pool contention.
- **VM *generation* can be a compliance gate, independent of everything else.**
 One region enforced a

 "avoid contention" buys nothing. Scarcity lives at the quota layer, not the

- **VM *generation* can be a compliance gate, independent of everything else.**
 One region enforced a standard requiring Azure VNet encryption, which only

 region can therefore have pools that *exist* and are *quota-available* and
 still cannot start a single cluster.
- **Compliance rules shrink the usable inventory dramatically, and asymmetrically
 between regions.** Of 12 pools in the constrained region, 8 were v5 and
 startable; of those, 4 were on-demand. An "on-demand only, no spot" policy
 plus a v5-only compliance rule left exactly **four** usable pools, and only
 **two** of them memory-optimised — both drawing on the same 350-core family.
 Enumerate the intersection of all constraints early; the answer is often much
 smaller than the pool list suggests.
- **The same pool name can be different hardware in different regions.** One
 region's `ondemand_memory_optimised_32core_256gb` was E32s_v5, the other's
 E32s_v3; the 4-core standard pool was D4s_v5 in one and DS3_v2 in the other.
 Name-based resolution is what lets one config serve two regions, and it is
 also what hides the fact that the two regions are running different silicon.
- **Insufficient quota does not always fail loudly.** Sometimes you get a clean
 `AZURE_QUOTA_EXCEEDED_EXCEPTION`; sometimes the cluster simply sits pending
 and the fan-out waits on it indefinitely. The second is how a run silently
 becomes a two-day run. Loud failure is the good case.

## Infrastructure-as-code: deploy time vs run time

- **The single most expensive confusion: a bundle deploys the whole job
 definition to *every* target, so every cluster spec is validated in every
 region — including clusters for tasks that can never run there.** A comment
 reading "this task is SE-only, so the East constraint doesn't apply" was
 correct about runtime and wrong about deployment, and it blocked a prod
 deploy. **Runtime reachability and deploy-time validation are different
 properties.** Ask separately: will this task ever *execute* here, and will
 this spec ever be *validated* here.
- **Know exactly which checks happen at each stage.** Deploy time: does the
 resource name resolve, and does the spec satisfy any attached policy. Cluster
 start time: quota, compliance rules, actual capacity. A v3 pool that no
 region-local task uses will deploy perfectly and only fail if something
 eventually tries to start it — which makes it a latent trap rather than a
 visible one.
- **A cluster *policy* validates at deploy, and its allowlist can be
 fundamentally incompatible with your standards.** The single-node policy in
 one region allowed only **spot** pools. Combined with an "on-demand only"
 rule, no compliant configuration existed at all — the two requirements were
 mutually exclusive and no amount of pool-swapping would have satisfied both.
 When a policy blocks you, check whether the policy's allowlist and your own
 policy can *ever* both hold before searching for the pool that squares them.
- **A policy that requires a property does not impose it.** A single-node
 policy rejected a cluster that hadn't declared itself single-node — the spec
 had the policy attached and none of `num_workers: 0`, the `ResourceClass`
 tag, or the `cluster.profile` conf. "Single node via the policy" was the
 assumption; "single node *or rejected* by the policy" was the reality.
- **Dropping a policy is a legitimate fix when nothing mandates one.** Twelve of
 fourteen cluster profiles in the repo carried no

- **Dropping a policy is a legitimate fix when nothing mandates one.** Twelve of

 the very apply that the one policed cluster failed — direct evidence the
 workspace didn't require policies. Matching the configuration that
 demonstrably works beats inferring what a policy wants from its error text.
- **Referencing anything that exists in only one workspace breaks the other's
 deploy.** A pool present in one region and absent in the other fails the
 lookup, and the error names the missing resource rather than the reasoning
 that introduced it.
- **A resource referenced only by a never-running task is a standing
 fragility.** Nobody in that region has any reason to keep it, and if it's
 cleaned up the deploy starts failing with an error unrelated to whatever
 change exposed it.
- **Deploying the same bundle twice with different config between runs is
 possible but leaves the repo correct for only one target at a time.** Any
 redeploy of the other region — a rollback, a hotfix, an automated pipeline
 run — then fails, and nothing in the repo records which region the committed
 state is currently aimed at. Prefer configuration that is valid everywhere;
 where you can't, make the asymmetry loud in the file itself.

## Validation / testing methodology

- **A binary pass/fail hides the difference between "wrong" and "couldn't
 tell."** A third verdict — NOT MEASURED — for permission errors, extractor
 bugs, and unsafe time-travel windows keeps "the clone lost data" distinct
 from "we weren't able to check," which otherwise collapse into the same
 alarming-looking failure count.
- **Comparing an evolving source against a frozen target is not a fair
 test**, no matter how good the comparator is — the fix has to happen at the
 measurement layer (pin both sides to the same version), not in how
 differences get reported afterward.
- **A retention/safety gate should be scoped to what it actually protects,
 not applied blanket.** Gating *all* checks on the data-file retention window
 when only two of twelve checks touch data files threw away ~20,000 valid
 measurements per run — the gate's blast radius should match its actual
 cause.
- **Guard against "confident wrong answer" more than against "crash."** A
 function that returns `0` or `{}` on an edge case it can't actually handle
 is worse than one that raises — the caller can route an exception to NOT
 MEASURED, but a silently-wrong zero looks exactly like a real, passing
 measurement.
- **A mode switch beats a parallel implementation.** Adding a second family of
 checks as an `inc=true/false` mode on the existing notebooks — rather than
 duplicating them — avoided copying ~1,800 lines of renderer and comparator
 logic that would then have drifted. The condition for this being safe is that
 the two modes are genuinely mutually exclusive; if both could run at once
 you'd be building a flag, not a mode.
- **Put the mode gate at the single point every path already passes through.**
 One four-line guard inside the function every check card is rendered by beat
 wrapping twenty-odd call sites, and it cannot be forgotten when a new card is
 added later. Finding that convergence point is usually the whole design.
- **Derive the output shape from one named set, never from a second list.**
 Column ordering, the extractor loop, and the written schema all deriving from
 a single `ACTIVE_CHECKS` list means a mode switch changes one line. An earlier
 version iterated a different dict for the column headers and would have
 emitted nine all-NaN columns that look exactly like measurements nobody took.
- **Prove the old path is unchanged; don't assert it.** After

- **Prove the old path is unchanged; don't assert it.** After adding a mode
 switch, executing the registry cells from the *pre-change commit* and from

 added an else branch" into evidence. Cheap to write, and it catches the
 reordering that a set comprehension or a dict-iteration change silently
 introduces.
- **Choose deliberately what a new mode does *not* fold in.** Excluding the
 long-running full diff from the incremental report was a design decision, not
 an omission: including it would have forced a dependency edge onto a task
 that runs for 22 hours and serialised a four-hour report behind it. Worth
 recording the reasoning next to the exclusion, or someone "fixes" it later.
- **Classify failures by side and by cause before drawing any conclusion from
 the count.** A recovered run showed 465 passes and **88 failures**, which read
 as a serious clone defect. Breaking them down changed the story completely:
 all 88 were **source-side** (three storage accounts, all in the source
 region), **zero** were row-count mismatches, and the causes were 52
 `FAILED_READ_FILE.DBR_FILE_NOT_EXIST` plus 35 `FileNotFoundException` 404s —
 i.e. source files vacuumed away between clone time and validation time. Not
 one of them said anything about the clone. **Forward rule:** a failure count
 is not a finding. Group by side, by error class, and by object before
 reporting — the grouping usually *is* the diagnosis, and an ungrouped count
 will send people to debug the wrong component.
- **An absolute threshold is an absolute answer to a relative question — and
 the obvious statistical fix has its own degenerate case.** A fixed 50 GB tier
 boundary was applied to an estate whose largest table was under 50 GB, so
 every table classified "small": the large-tier cluster started, found zero
 tables, and exited eight minutes later while the small tier ran past twelve
 hours. Switching to a population statistic is the right instinct, but the
 *median* was also degenerate here, because most tables reported zero size —
 the median of a zero-heavy population is zero, which routes the entire estate
 the other way. The mean over non-zero values was the workable choice.
 **Forward rule:** derive split points from the data, but inspect the
 distribution first — count the zeros and nulls before choosing a statistic,
 and keep a sanity check that raises when a computed threshold would put every
 item on one side.

## Job orchestration (Databricks Jobs)

- **A `for_each` repair must resolve to the same iteration count as the
 original run.** Change the `inputs:` array from 8 entries to 12 and every
 in-flight or historical run becomes **permanently unrepairable** — the
 scheduler can't map old iterations onto the new array. So: deploys that
 change pools, parameters or notebook code leave old runs repairable; deploys
 that change an `inputs:` array do not. Worth knowing before you promise
 someone a repair.
- **In a fan-out, the chunk divisor and the scheduled iteration count are two
 different numbers and both directions of mismatch matter.** Iterations >
 divisor is wasteful but safe — surplus iterations exit on the guard. Divisor
 > iterations is **silent data loss**: whole modulo groups get no runner at
 all, nothing fails, and the only trace is an absent output file. Reconcile
 row-level coverage before overwriting the scope file, not after.
- **The UI task-edit is a real escape hatch when redeploys are expensive.** You
 can repoint a task's cluster in the Jobs UI and repair the run immediately,
 without another deploy; the next IaC deploy

- **The UI task-edit is a real escape hatch when redeploys are expensive.** You
 can repoint a task's cluster in the Jobs UI and repair the run immediately,
 without another deploy; the next IaC deploy reverts it. That converts "we get
 one deploy attempt" into "we get one deploy attempt plus a manual override,"
 which materially changes how much risk a change can carry.
- **Job parameters silently override task base parameters of the same name.**
 A job-level `max_parallel` beat every per-tier `base_parameter` of that name
 on every task, so per-tier tuning had no effect at all and looked like a
 stale deploy. Namespacing the job-level parameters (`default_max_parallel`,
 `scope_chunks`) fixed it. Check for name collisions between the two layers
 before concluding a value "isn't taking effect."
- **A default nobody runs with is a bug waiting to surface.** A concurrency
 default of 1 was survivable only because operators overrode it by hand every
 time; the first run that used the default would have been ~8× slower with no
 error. Defaults should be the value you actually want.
- **Serverless bills for the wall-clock you hold it, so the worst possible fit
 is a long-lived task that does no compute.** A live progress dashboard — sleep
 60s, list a few small files, one API call, render text — sat on serverless for
 **22h46m** on a single run, because it exits only once every sibling task is
 terminal. It performed no Spark work in that entire window and was billed at a
 rate meant for real query compute. Moving it to the cheapest classic
 single-node cluster cost about five minutes of startup, which is irrelevant
 against a 22-hour run. **Forward rule:** classify every task as
 compute-bound or wall-clock-bound before choosing its compute. Serverless is
 excellent for short bursty work and actively wrong for anything that mostly
 waits.
- **A cosmetic task must be structurally incapable of failing or delaying the
 run.** Two properties made that true for the dashboard, and both are
 counter-intuitive: **nothing depends on it** (so it can never block a
 successor), and it carries **no `timeout_seconds`** — because a Databricks
 task timeout marks the task Failed, and a failed task fails the whole run. A
 timeout on a monitoring task would mean a cosmetic component could kill a
 22-hour validation. It self-exits on its own internal limit instead, with
 success. **Forward rule:** for any observability or reporting sidecar, check
 both edges — can it block anything, and can it fail anything — and prefer an
 in-notebook self-exit over a platform timeout.
- **A task that watches the run it is part of must exclude itself.** The
 dashboard's exit condition was "all tasks terminal", which it can never
 observe — it is itself running whenever it asks. Without passing the task its
 own key so it can filter itself out, the condition is unsatisfiable and every
 run sits until the backstop limit. **Forward rule:** any self-referential
 monitoring loop needs an identity and a self-exclusion; if you find yourself
 wondering why a watcher always runs to its maximum duration, this is the first
 thing to check.

- **A job in region A can fire and then await a job in region B, and the whole
 mechanism is just the REST API plus an Entra service principal.** There is no
 special "cross-workspace" feature to enable. Region A obtains an OAuth token
 for a service principal, then calls region B's ordinary Jobs API with it. Once
 you have the token, the remote workspace is just a hostname.

 `grant_type=client_credentials`, the SP's `client_id`

- **`DATABRICKS_RESOURCE` is a fixed, well-known Azure constant** —
 `2ff814a6-3304-4ab8-85cb-cd0e6f879c1d`, the AzureDatabricks first-party
 application ID. It is the same for every tenant and every workspace on earth,
 so it belongs in code as a constant, not in config. Worth committing to memory;
 it is the piece that looks like it must be environment-specific and isn't.
- **The full checklist to make the connection work**, in the order things fail:
 the **tenant ID**; a **service principal** (client ID + secret) that exists in
 the tenant *and* has been granted access **in the target workspace** — being
 registered in the tenant is not enough; the secret stored in a **secret scope
 in the calling workspace**; the **target workspace host**
 (`https://adb-<workspace-id>.<n>.azuredatabricks.net`); and the **target
 `job_id`**. Everything else is a normal API call.
- **`job_id` is workspace-scoped and is the fragile link.** It is a number that
 means nothing in the calling region, and it changes if the target job is ever
 recreated rather than updated — which in IaC terms means changing the resource
 key destroys and re-issues it. That single integer is the tightest coupling
 between the two regions; treat it as an interface.
- **Preflight with `GET /api/2.1/jobs/get` before `run-now`.** One extra call
 proves the job exists *and* the SP can see it, so a wrong ID or a missing
 grant surfaces as a clear error rather than an opaque failure buried in a
 `run-now` response. Two failure modes separated for the cost of one request.
- **`run-now` rejects any `job_parameters` key the target job does not
 declare.** That silently couples the two jobs' parameter lists: adding a
 parameter on the calling side and forwarding it breaks *every* run until the
 target is redeployed too. Deploy the callee first, always.
- **Serverless compute cannot make the call.** Serverless egress fails the
 cross-workspace trust check, so the triggering and waiting tasks must run on
 classic VNet compute. This is the kind of constraint that only appears at
 runtime and forces a cluster into a job that otherwise wanted none.
- **Derive which region you are in at runtime; do not configure it.** One IaC
 target deployed byte-identically to two physical workspaces, so a deploy-time
 "my region" value would be correct in one and wrong in the other. Detecting
 the executing workspace and firing the *opposite* one makes direction a
 derived property. Configured direction is a bug waiting for the second
 deployment.
- **Per-workspace names you assume are symmetric often aren't.** The two
 workspaces' Key Vault-backed secret scopes were named differently
 (`secret-kv101` vs `secret-kv01`) despite one bundle serving both — so the

- **Fire-and-exit, then wait in a separate task.** `run-now` returns as soon as
 the remote run is queued; the returned `run_id` is published as a task value

- **`life_cycle_state` and `result_state` are two different fields and you need

 which. And some terminal states (`SKIPPED`, `INTERNAL_ERROR`) arrive with no

 hours against a 22-hour job is the right shape of margin.
- **A cross-region trigger should fail loud, unlike a best-effort one.** If
 everything downstream is meaningless without the remote run, swallowing the
 error just moves the failure somewhere less diagnosable.

## Diagnosing infrastructure failures

- **Read the error's own numbers before theorising.** The quota failure stated
 Current Limit 350, Current Usage 320, Additional Required 160, Minimum New
 Limit 480 — enough to compute both the immediate fix and the real ask (~1,400
 for the full fan-out) without a single assumption. Cloud errors are often
 more quantitative than they look.
- **Ask for the number you actually need, not the minimum the error suggests.**
 480 would have unblocked one cluster and failed on the next. The error tells
 you what the *current* request needed, not what your workload needs.
- **Terminated-cluster history is free evidence.** A 30-day cluster list showed
 three successful spot clusters and two successful runs on the exact SKU that
 later hit quota — proving "spot works in this region" and "this SKU works in
 this region" as separate facts, without creating anything. When you can't run
 an experiment, look for one that already ran.
- **Decompose an unknown into the parts that are already proven.** "Will spot
 E32s_v5 work here" split into three: does the pool exist (yes), is the SKU
 compliant (yes, v5), does spot allocate in this region (yes, evidenced on
 another SKU). What remained unproven was only the *combination* — a far
 smaller risk than the original question, and small enough to accept with a
 retry as cover.
- **Identical round numbers across unrelated metrics are a smell.** Three
 different quota families all reading exactly "0 of 350" was the tell that the
 region filter was wrong — those were untouched defaults for a region nobody
 deploys to. Real usage is lumpy.
- **Check the filter before trusting the reading.** The above happened because
 an autocomplete matched **Austria** East instead of **Australia** East. Any
 console with a region, subscription, or environment selector will eventually
 hand you correct-looking numbers for the wrong scope.
- **Verify you can perform the diagnostic action before you need it.** Cluster
 creation was denied, so the intended five-minute capacity smoke test was
 impossible — discovered mid-incident. Jobs create their own clusters as the
 run-as identity, so a human can lack a permission the pipeline has, and it
 only surfaces when you try to debug interactively.
- **A comment that encodes a *reason* is load-bearing, and a wrong one is worse
 than none.** "SE-only, so the East VNet constraint does not apply" was
 plausible, survived review, and blocked a prod deploy — because it forecloses
 the check it appears to

 it is the only reason the truncation here was detectable at all.

## Command-line and scripting gotchas (Windows / Databricks CLI)

- **PowerShell's `` `v `` is a vertical-tab escape, not a literal "v".** So
 `"standard$tag`v$ver`Family"` silently produced `standardES3Family` instead of
 `standardESv3Family`. Use `${}` around every variable in an interpolated
 string: `"standard${tag}v${ver}Family"`.
- **Passing multi-line or quote-containing arguments to native executables from
 PowerShell is genuinely hostile.** Here-strings (`@'…'@`) need the terminator
 at column 0 and break inside `;`-chained commands; double quotes embedded in a
 single-quoted string still break argument boundaries when the call is
 reconstructed. For anything non-trivial, write the text to a file and pass the
 file (`git commit -F`), or use repeated single-line flags.
- **`Format-Table` truncates at console width and drops the right-hand columns
 with no indication.** Pipe through `Out-String -Width 4096` when the output
 matters.
- **The Databricks CLI emits a UTF-8 BOM when redirected to a file**, which
 makes `json.load` fail with "Unexpected UTF-8 BOM". Read with `utf-8-sig`.
- **Prefer one API call that already returns what you need.** `instance-pools
 list` includes each pool's `stats` block, so per-pool `get` calls to fetch
 instance counts are wasted round-trips. Check the list response's shape before
 fanning out.

## PySpark / pandas gotchas worth remembering on sight

- **`dict(a_spark_row)` doesn't do what it looks like.** `Row` supports
 iteration over its *values*, not `(key, value)` pairs, so `dict()`
 misreads it — use `.asDict()`.
- **`spark.read.json()` infers any nested JSON object as a STRUCT, never a
 true `MapType`**, even for a field that's logically `map<string,string>` —
 code that expects a dict has to normalize this explicitly regardless of
 source.
- **CSV round-trips between pandas and Spark need explicit escape
 handling.** `pandas.to_csv()` doubles embedded quotes (RFC 4180); Spark's
 reader defaults to backslash-escaping. Without `.option("escape", '"')`, a
 quoted value with an internal comma silently shifts every later column — no
 error, just corrupted rows.

**CSV round-trips between pandas and Spark need explicit escape
 handling.** `pandas.to_csv()` doubles embedded quotes (RFC 4180); Spark's
 reader defaults to backslash-escaping. Without `.option("escape", '"')`, a
 quoted value with an internal comma silently shifts every later column — no
 error, just corrupted rows.
- **`groupBy().agg(F.max(col))` doesn't guarantee other columns come from
 that same max row.** If you need several columns tied to "the latest row,"
 use a window function (`row_number() over partitionBy(...).orderBy(...
 desc())`) — an aggregate can silently mix values from different rows when
 there's more than one candidate.
- **Multi-statement `%sql` notebook cells only display the last statement's
 result.** Earlier statements still ran; their output is just not rendered —
 an easy thing to misread as "didn't execute."
- **Serverless/Spark Connect compute blocks reading certain Spark confs
 outright**, distinct from "the value isn't set." The error looks like a
 runtime failure but is really a compute-tier restriction.
- **Databricks notebooks compile each cell independently, so control flow
 cannot span cells.** An `if` opened in one cell does not indent the next —
 attempting it produces `unexpected indent` on every following cell, which
 reads as a dozen unrelated syntax errors rather than one structural mistake.
 This is what forced a mode switch to be implemented as a guard *inside* the
 single function every code path already passes through, rather than as an `if`
 wrapped around twenty-odd cells. **Forward rule:** in a notebook, conditional
 behaviour has to live inside a function or be repeated per cell — so when you
 need to gate a lot of code, first go looking for the one function everything
 funnels through. A related consequence: `from __future__ import annotations`
 in any cell but the first makes the whole file fail `py_compile` while
 remaining perfectly valid at runtime, so validate notebooks cell-by-cell
 (`ast.parse` per cell) rather than as one file.
- **A pandas CSV round-trip silently converts an integer column containing any
 blank into float.** A version column written as `836` comes back as `836.0`,
 and `"836.0" != "836"` fails every downstream string comparison — on every
 row, so it looks like a total mismatch rather than a formatting artifact. The
 blank is enough to do it: pandas has no integer dtype with missing values by
 default, so one NA promotes the whole column. **Forward rule:** normalise
 through `int(float(x))` at every read boundary, or use the nullable `Int64`
 dtype explicitly. Treat any CSV hop as lossy for numeric types, and be
 suspicious of a comparison that fails 100% rather than partially — that
 pattern is nearly always a type or format issue, not a data issue.
- **`~col.isin([...])` silently drops NULLs, because SQL's `NOT IN` is
 three-valued.** `NULL != 'X'` is NULL, not true, so rows with a null in the
 filtered column fail the predicate and vanish from scope — no error, no
 warning, just a smaller working set than intended. In a scope-building filter
 that is silent data loss at the very first step. **Forward rule:** whenever
 you write an exclusion filter, decide explicitly what NULL should mean, and
 count the nulls you are dropping. The implementation here counts them and
 prints a loud warning if any exist, so the rule can be made explicit the
 moment it actually matters rather than being inherited by accident from
 three-valued logic.

 kind: CLASSIC_PREVIEW
 node_type_id: Standard_D4ds_v5
 is_single_node: true
 enable_elastic_disk: true
 azure_attributes:
 first_on_demand: 1
 spot_bid_max_price: -1
 spark_env_vars:
 PYSPARK_PYTHON: /databricks/python3/bin/python3
 DR_CLONE_INTRA_CHUNK_PARALLELISM: "2"
 # 4-core single node: 4 concurrent read/IO-bound recon
 # scans overlaps well without thrashing 4 cores. Higher
 # over-subscribes the local[*] executor.
 DR_RECON_INTRA_CHUNK_PARALLELISM: "4"
 # Per-table wall-clock cap (30 min). One pathological
 # table (millions of tiny files / huge un-checkpointed
 # _delta_log / throttled cross-region account) would
 # otherwise pin a thread and make a whole 64-table
 # chunk run 12-15h. On timeout the table's Spark job
 # group is cancelled, a Recon - ERROR row is written,
 # and the thread is freed so the chunk finishes.
 DR_RECON_TABLE_TIMEOUT_SEC: "9000"
 # Heavy-table guard: skip the column_stats FULL SCAN
 # (the only scanning check) when either side has > this
 # many files. A small-byte table with a huge file count
 # is brutally slow to scan cross-region; schema /
 # row_count / delta_version still run.
 DR_RECON_MAX_SCAN_FILES: "50000"
 spark_conf:
 spark.scheduler.mode: FAIR
 spark.sql.adaptive.enabled: "true"
 spark.sql.adaptive.coalescePartitions.enabled: "true"
 spark.databricks.delta.optimizeWrite.enabled: "false"
 spark.databricks.delta.autoCompact.enabled: "false"
 # Cap the driver's retained job/stage/task + SQL-exec
 # metadata. Recon runs THOUSANDS of small Spark jobs on
 # ONE long-lived single-node driver (every for_each
 # chunk reuses it). Defaults let the driver heap grow
 # monotonically -> GC thrash. These low limits keep the
 # driver footprint flat.
 spark.ui.retainedJobs: "200"
 spark.ui.retainedStages: "200"
 spark.ui.retainedTasks: "5000"
 spark.sql.ui.retainedExecutions: "200"
 spark.hadoop.fs.azure.io.retry.max.retries: "30"
 spark.hadoop.fs.azure.io.retry.backoff.interval: "1000"
 spark.hadoop.fs.azure.io.retry.max.backoff.interval: "60000"
 tasks:
 - task_key: dr_failover_restore_schema_task
 for_each_task:
 task:
 job_cluster_key: nonuc_singlenode

 job_clusters:

 new_cluster: *test_recon_singlenode

# DR ADLS Folder-Structure Sync Job
#
# Recreates the CONTAINER + DIRECTORY (folder) structure of a SOURCE ADLS
# Gen2 storage account onto a TARGET account — no file data is copied, only
# the empty container/directory skeleton. Useful for pre-provisioning a DR
# target account's layout before a deep clone / data copy.
#
# Compute: classic single-node job cluster (single_node_ondemand_cluster_profile,
# defined in resources/system_settings/bundle_config.yml). ON-DEMAND (not spot)
# so that when this job fans out up to 10 concurrent runs (one per source->target
# account mapping), none of the 10 single-node clusters can be spot-evicted
# mid-run -> deterministic allocation. The notebook talks
# to ADLS via the Azure Data Lake SDK using a ClientSecretCredential built
# from the client_id / secret_key job parameters (an Entra ID app / SP).
#
# run_as: pinned per-environment in databricks.yml to the OPERATION service
# principal. The target-level run_as is a DIFFERENT SP in every env, so this
# job overrides it explicitly under each target's resources.jobs:
# dev -> sp-svc-bdp4-operation-dev (58bb0ae3-...)
# test -> sp-svc-bdp4-operation-test (a79ffa62-...)
# preprod -> sp-svc-bdp4-operation-preprod (485cb420-...)
# prod -> sp-svc-bdp4-operation-prod (d064b061-...)
#
# Runtime knobs (job parameters, no redeploy needed):
# * source_account ADLS Gen2 account name to read the layout FROM
# * target_account ADLS Gen2 account name to recreate the layout ON
# * client_id Entra ID app (SP) client id used to auth to ADLS
# * secret_key that app's client secret (prefer a secret-scope ref)
resources:
 jobs:
 dr_adls_folder_structure_sync_job:
 name: dr_adls_folder_structure_sync_job
 tags:
 application: bupa_bdp4_deepclone_workload
 environment: ${bundle.target}
 type: adls_folder_sync
 # Allow fanning out one run per source->target account mapping (7-8
 # today) concurrently; 10 gives headroom. Each run gets its OWN
 # single-node job cluster from the pool below, so runs never share state.
 max_concurrent_runs: 10
 # timeout_seconds: 21600
 
 email_notifications:
 on_failure:
 - ${var.deepclone_product_owner_email}
 
 parameters:
 - name: source_account
 default: ""
 - name: target_account
 default: ""
 - name: client_id
 default: ""
 - name: secret_key
 default: ""
 # Performance knobs (tunable per run, no redeploy):
 # max_workers -> concurrent directory-create requests
 # container_workers -> containers enumerated in parallel
 # leaf_only -> create only leaf dirs (HNS auto-creates parents)
 - name: max_workers
 default: "64"
 - name: container_workers
 default: "16"
 - name: leaf_only
 default: "false"
 
 # Classic single-node ON-DEMAND cluster. single_node_ondemand_cluster_profile
 # is the complex variable defined in resources/system_settings/bundle_config.yml;
 # it must be attached here via a job_clusters entry before a task can reference it.
 # On-demand (vs the spot single_node_cluster_profile) guarantees all 10
 # concurrent runs get a node that won't be reclaimed mid-run.
 job_clusters:
 - job_cluster_key: single_node_ondemand_cluster_profile
 new_cluster: ${var.single_node_ondemand_cluster_profile}

 tasks:
 - task_key: dr_adls_folder_structure_sync_task
 job_cluster_key: single_node_ondemand_cluster_profile
 # No serverless environment on a classic cluster, so install the
 # Azure SDK dependencies as cluster libraries (pip).
 libraries:
 - pypi:
 package: azure-identity
 - pypi:
 package: azure-storage-file-datalake
 notebook_task:
 notebook_path: ../../../src/bdp4_lh/gld_deepclone/dr_adls_folder_structure_sync.ipynb
 base_parameters:
 source_account: "{{job.parameters.source_account}}"
 target_account: "{{job.parameters.target_account}}"
 client_id: "{{job.parameters.client_id}}"
 secret_key: "{{job.parameters.secret_key}}"
 max_workers: "{{job.parameters.max_workers}}"
 container_workers: "{{job.parameters.container_workers}}"
 leaf_only: "{{job.parameters.leaf_only}}"

# DR Deep Clone Full Orchestrator — Full Clone Job
#
# Single SE-workspace job, mixed compute:
# Task 1 (inventory) -> serverless (UC): information_schema,
# ctlfwk, registering tables in dr_clone_config.
# Writes dr_clone_tasks, emits chunk IDs + run_id /
# chunk_size / stream_name / sync_direction taskValues.
# Task 2 (executor) -> NON-UC cluster (NO_ISOLATION_SHARED). for_each over
# chunk IDs. SP OAuth + path-based clone bypasses
# UC masking.
# Task 3 (finalizer) -> serverless (UC): upserts dr_clone_status + cleanup.
#
# Used for: initial DR setup, full table refresh, disaster recovery failback.
#
# Parameter design:
# Only RUN-TIME knobs (things a human reasonably changes per execution)
# appear in `parameters:` and surface in "Run with different parameters".
# Deploy-time values (storage credential, catalog, SP refs, etc.) are wired
# directly into `base_parameters` from DAB variables so they are not
# override-able at runtime — single source of truth lives in
# databricks.baseline.yml / databricks.yml target overrides.
resources:
 jobs:
 dr_deep_clone_full_load_orchestrator_job:
 name: dr_deep_clone_full_load_orchestrator_job
 tags:
 application: bupa_bdp4_deepclone_workload
 environment: ${bundle.target}
 type: full_clone
 max_concurrent_runs: 1
 queue:
 enabled: true

 # Run-time-only parameters. Everything else (config_catalog, SP creds,
 # storage mappings, etc.) is read directly from DAB variables below.
 parameters:
 - name: stream_name
 default: FULL_CLONE
 - name: catalog_name
 default: ""
 - name: sync_direction
 default: ""
 - name: clone_type
 default: FULL
 # Comma-separated schemas for clone_type=SCHEMA (e.g.
 # "brz_peoplesoft,brz_epicor"). Ignored by SYNC and FULL modes.
 - name: schema_names
 default: ""
 # Comma-separated table refs for clone_type=TABLE. Each entry may be
 # 'table', 'schema.table', or 'catalog.schema.table'. A bare 'table'
 # present in >1 schema is rejected as ambiguous (qualify as schema.table).
 - name: table_names
 default: ""
 # IDEMPOTENT RESUME: when set, skip discovery + registration in
 # Task 1 and re-process only the failed/un-attempted tables of
 # the previous run. Leave empty for a fresh run.
 - name: resume_run_id
 default: ""
 # 2-TIER PERFORMANCE: tables >= this many GB are routed to the
 # large-cluster executor; smaller tables run on the small-cluster
 # executor. Both run in parallel. If the threshold leaves one
 # tier with < 10% of tables, the inventory task auto-rebalances
 # (top ~35% by size → Tier-L, rest → Tier-S) so both clusters
 # are utilised. Set to a very large value (e.g. 999999) to force
 # everything onto Tier-L (single-cluster, equivalent to v1).
 - name: tier_threshold_gb
 default: "50"
 # SINGLE-TIER mode: route EVERY table to ONE tier so only the small
 # executor runs (Tier-L gate stays closed -> its cluster never starts) --
 # the whole clone runs as one for_each on one cluster. Used by the
 # dev/test single-node targets (set to "true" there). Default "false"
 # keeps the 2-tier size-aware split for preprod/prod.
 - name: single_tier
 default: "false"
 # FORCE METADATA RE-EXTRACT: re-capture UC tags / comments / PK-FK from
 # the SOURCE for EVERY in-scope table, ignoring the incremental skip of
 # tables already present in dr_clone_table_metadata. Use "true" to
 # back-fill metadata (e.g. primary keys) onto schemas cloned before the
 # PK/FK carry-over existed. Default "false" keeps the fast incremental
 # extract (only newly-cloned tables).
 - name: refresh_existing_metadata
 default: "false"
 # Reconcile each table right after it is cloned (fast metadata-only
 # recon: file_match, clone_version, structure, column_mapping,
 # deletion_vectors). Default "false".
 - name: recon_table
 default: "false"
 # Delta time-travel window (days) applied to every cloned target as
 # inline TBLPROPERTIES on the DEEP CLONE -- widens both
 # logRetentionDuration and deletedFileRetentionDuration so old
 # versions stay queryable through VACUUM. "0" (or

metadata-only
 # recon: file_match, clone_version, structure, column_mapping,
 # deletion_vectors). Default "false".
 - name: recon_table
 default: "false"
 # Delta time-travel window (days) applied to every cloned target as
 # inline TBLPROPERTIES on the DEEP CLONE -- widens both
 # logRetentionDuration and deletedFileRetentionDuration so old
 # versions stay queryable through VACUUM. "0" (or empty) keeps the
 # source's own retention untouched. Default "30" gives a full month.
 - name: target_retention_days
 default: "30"
 environments:
 - environment_key: deepclone_serverless
 spec:
 client: "2"

 job_clusters:
 # Tier-L cluster: fewer/fatter D16 workers, network-bound clones.
 - job_cluster_key: nonuc_cluster_l
 new_cluster: ${var.nonuc_cluster_profile_tier_l}
 # Tier-S cluster: many cheap D8 workers, metadata-bound clones.
 - job_cluster_key: nonuc_cluster_s
 new_cluster: ${var.nonuc_cluster_profile_tier_s}

 tasks:
 # Task 1: Bootstrap + scan information_schema, register tables in
 # dr_clone_config, persist dr_clone_tasks, classify into
 # S/L tiers, emit two chunk-descriptor lists.
 - task_key: dr_table_inventory_identifier_task
 environment_key: deepclone_serverless
 notebook_task:
 notebook_path: ../../../src/bdp4_lh/gld_deepclone/dr_table_inventory_identifier.ipynb
 base_parameters:
 # Run-time parameters
 stream_name: "{{job.parameters.stream_name}}"
 catalog_name: "{{job.parameters.catalog_name}}"
 sync_direction: "{{job.parameters.sync_direction}}"
 # workspace_region is bundle-provided (databricks.yml per target)
 # and drives ONLY the ExternalLocationManager cross-region
 # suffix -- it is NOT an operator-facing param and is decoupled
 # from sync_direction so the operator remains free to run any
 # direction from any region.
 workspace_region: ${var.workspace_region}
 clone_type: "{{job.parameters.clone_type}}"
 schema_names: "{{job.parameters.schema_names}}"
 table_names: "{{job.parameters.table_names}}"
 resume_run_id: "{{job.parameters.resume_run_id}}"
 tier_threshold_gb: "{{job.parameters.tier_threshold_gb}}"
 single_tier: "{{job.parameters.single_tier}}"
 refresh_existing_metadata: "{{job.parameters.refresh_existing_metadata}}"
 recon_table: "{{job.parameters.recon_table}}"
 # Deploy-time values, wired directly from DAB variables
 config_catalog: ${var.bdp4_system_catalog}
 config_schema: ${var.config_schema}
 metadata_storage_path: ${var.metadata_storage_path}

 # Gate-S: only start Tier-S cluster if inventory found small tables.
 # Without this gate, an empty tier still triggers cluster boot
 # (~3-5 min wasted) just to run a no-op for_each.
 - task_key: gate_has_small_tables
 depends_on:
 - task_key: dr_table_inventory_identifier_task
 condition_task:
 op: GREATER_THAN
 left: "{{tasks.dr_table_inventory_identifier_task.values.n_chunks_small}}"
 right: "0"

 # Gate-L: only start Tier-L cluster if inventory found large tables.
 - task_key: gate_has_large_tables
 depends_on:
 - task_key: dr_table_inventory_identifier_task
 condition_task:
 op: GREATER_THAN
 left: "{{tasks.dr_table_inventory_identifier_task.values.n_chunks_large}}"
 right: "0"

# DR Deep Clone Orchestrator — Sync (Incremental) Clone Job
#
# Triggered by ADF ParentJobDeepClone_UC pipeline. Single SE-workspace job,
# mixed compute:
# Task 1 (inventory) -> serverless (UC): ctlfwk lookup + register tables,
# write dr_clone_tasks, classify tables into S/L
# size tiers, emit two chunk-descriptor lists +
# run_id / chunk_size / stream_name / sync_direction.
# Gates (S/L) -> serverless condition tasks: start a tier cluster
# only if inventory found tables of that size class.
# Task 2-S / 2-L -> NON-UC pool-backed tier clusters (E8 small / E32
# large), running in PARALLEL: for_each over chunk
# IDs, SP OAuth + path-based clone (masking-safe).
# Task 3 (finalizer) -> NON-UC cluster: upsert dr_clone_status + cleanup.
# Task 4 (notification) -> serverless (UC): email/webhook, runs ALL_DONE.
#
# Parameter design: see full_load orchestrator -- only run-time knobs surface
# in `parameters:`; deploy-time values (SP creds, catalog, storage mappings)
# are wired directly from DAB vars into `base_parameters`.
resources:
 jobs:
 dr_deep_clone_orchestrator_job:
 name: dr_deep_clone_orchestrator_job
 tags:
 application: bupa_bdp4_deepclone_workload
 environment: ${bundle.target}
 type: sync_clone
 # Parallel runs — one per stream_name can be triggered concurrently by
 # ADF. Each run gets a globally-unique run_id (inventory adds a uuid
 # suffix), so all dr_clone_tasks / dr_clone_status / dr_clone_audit_log
 # rows are fully isolated by run_id even though runs share the metadata
 # tables. Concurrent Delta writes retry on conflict; locked source
 # tables retry the DEEP CLONE per-table with backoff.
 #
 # BOUNDED fan-out (was 1000). 1000 was a stampede risk: 150-200+ ADF
 # triggers would each cold-claim their own tier cluster and blow past
 # the Esv3 regional vCPU quota + VNet subnet IPs -> AZURE_QUOTA_EXCEEDED.
 # With queue.enabled=true, triggers BEYOND this cap WAIT instead of
 # failing, so 200+ triggers still "work" — they drain in waves within a
 # footprint the region can actually satisfy. No trigger is dropped, no
 # quota error.
 #
 # Set this to: floor( Esv3_regional_vCPU_quota / per_run_peak_vCPU )
 # per_run_peak_vCPU (this design) ~= tier-S 16-72 + tier-L 0-224.
 # Use ~150 vCPU as a planning midpoint. e.g. 7,500-vCPU quota -> ~50.
 # 50 is a safe preprod default; confirm with:
 # az vm list-usage --location <region> -o table | findstr ESv3
 # and raise only after the quota + subnet free-IP headroom is verified.
 max_concurrent_runs: 50
 timeout_seconds: 28800
 queue:
 enabled: true
 health:
 rules:
 - metric: RUN_DURATION_SECONDS
 op: GREATER_THAN
 value: 21600

# DR Deep-Clone Metadata Refresh Job
#
# Region-aware DAILY refresh of the SOURCE region's UC table metadata
# (comments, tags, primary/foreign keys, column structure) into the shared
# dr_clone_table_metadata table. Runs on serverless in whichever region it is
# deployed to (each region is the SOURCE for its own direction) and force
# re-extracts the whole scope, so DRIFT on already-cloned tables is captured --
# something the SYNC clone path never does (its inventory only extracts
# metadata for NEW tables).
#
# The job knows which region it runs in from databricks.yml: workspace_region
# ('se' | 'east') is wired from the per-target var below and is NOT an operator
# parameter. The notebook derives the SOURCE side of sync_direction and refuses
# to run if it does not match workspace_region, so a mis-scheduled run cannot
# overwrite the true source metadata with the target's copy.
#
# Bidirectional: this SAME job is deployed to BOTH regions and scheduled in
# each at the same time. The direction is NOT hardcoded -- it is DERIVED from
# workspace_region (databricks.yml, per region) in the notebook, so the SE
# deploy runs SOUTHEAST_TO_EAST and the East deploy runs EAST_TO_SOUTHEAST.
# Each region is the SOURCE for its own direction, so it captures its live
# source-of-truth metadata and never clobbers the peer's copy. When a refresh
# detects changed metadata it fires the OPPOSITE region's
# dr_table_registration_job cross-region (fire-and-forget, gated on
# changed_count > 0) so drift is applied promptly; that region's own daily
# dr_table_registration_job remains the backstop. It is drift-aware and
# applies the refreshed metadata ONLY to the changed tables.
#
# config_catalog / config_schema / metadata_storage_path / workspace_region are
# wired automatically from databricks.yml vars. Run as the datacopy service
# principal (target-level run_as).
#
# Schedule: runs ONCE A DAY (23:00 / 11 PM Sydney) in BOTH regions but ships
# PAUSED -- confirm scope + workspace_region, then UNPAUSE in each region.

 name: dr_deepclone_metadata_refresh_job

 application: bupa_bdp4_deepclone_workload
 environment: ${bundle.target}
 type: metadata_refresh
 max_concurrent_runs: 1
 # A full-catalog information_schema extract of tens of thousands of tables
 # can run beyond an hour; 6h ceiling avoids premature TIMEOUT kills.

 schedule:
 # 23:00 (11 PM) Sydney -- scheduled in BOTH regions at the same time.
 # Bidirectional: the SE deploy runs SOUTHEAST_TO_EAST and the East

 # call does NOT need a 2-node E8 tier cluster, so this uses the
 # pre-warmed single-node 4-core pool: near-instant start, exactly one
 # node, no infra request. Safe because this job is max_concurrent_runs=1.

 - task_key: dr_metadata_refresh_task
 environment_key: deepclone_serverless

 config_schema: ${var.config_schema}
 metadata_storage_path: ${var.metadata_storage_path}

 # Control-flow gate -- runs on the CONTROL PLANE, starts NO cluster.
 # Evaluates changed_count (tables whose metadata ACTUALLY changed vs what
 # is already stored for THIS sync_direction). Only the "true" branch
 # (changed_count > 0) lets the trigger task below run; when nothing
 # changed the trigger is SKIPPED and its VNet cluster is NEVER started --
 # zero compute on a no-change day.
 - task_key: gate_has_metadata_changes
 depends_on:
 - task_key: dr_metadata_refresh_task
 condition_task:
 op: GREATER_THAN
 left: "{{tasks.dr_metadata_refresh_task.values.changed_count}}"
 right: "0"

 - task_key: gate_has_metadata_changes
 outcome: "true"
 job_cluster_key: nonuc_trigger_cluster
 notebook_task:
 notebook_path:

# DR Deep Clone Mute / Unmute Job
# Protects tables from the incremental deep-clone sync (mute) -- or releases
# them (unmute) -- by flipping the is_active flag in dr_clone_config. Incremental
# discovery only clones rows where COALESCE(is_active,'Y')='Y', and the
# registration MERGE preserves is_active on already-registered rows, so a mute
# survives future re-discovery.
#
# The job flips the flag ONLY on tables that already exist in dr_clone_config
# (it never inserts placeholder rows). A table that has never been registered is
# reported as NO_CHANGE_OR_NO_MATCH.
#
# Runtime knobs (job parameters, no redeploy needed):
# * action MUTE | UNMUTE
# * scope_type CATALOG | SCHEMA | TABLE
# * scope_value inline, comma-separated targets (blank when csv_path is set):
# CATALOG -> 'cat1, cat2'
# SCHEMA -> 'cat.sch1, cat.sch2'
# TABLE -> 'cat.sch.tbl1, cat.sch.tbl2'
# * csv_path path to a header CSV (abfss:// | /Volumes | dbfs:/); when set,
# scope_value must be blank. Columns matched by NAME, COUNT must
# match the scope exactly (CATALOG=catalog; SCHEMA=catalog,schema;
# TABLE=catalog,schema,table).
# * dry_run true -> report what WOULD change without writing.
resources:
 jobs:
 dr_deepclone_mute_job:
 name: dr_deepclone_mute_job
 tags:
 application: bupa_bdp4_deepclone_workload
 environment: ${bundle.target}
 type: deepclone_mute
 max_concurrent_runs: 1
 timeout_seconds: 21600

 parameters:
 - name: action
 default: MUTE
 - name: scope_type
 default: TABLE
 - name: scope_value
 default: ""
 - name: csv_path
 default: ""
 - name: dry_run
 default: "false"

 environments:
 - environment_key: deepclone_serverless
 spec:
 client: "2"

 tasks:
 - task_key: dr_deepclone_mute_task
 environment_key: deepclone_serverless
 notebook_task:
 notebook_path: ../../../src/bdp4_lh/gld_deepclone/dr_deepclone_mute.ipynb
 base_parameters:
 config_catalog: ${var.bdp4_system_catalog}
 config_schema: ${var.config_schema}
 metadata_storage_path: ${var.metadata_storage_path}
 action: "{{job.parameters.action}}"
 scope_type: "{{job.parameters.scope_type}}"
 scope_value: "{{job.parameters.scope_value}}"
 csv_path: "{{job.parameters.csv_path}}"
 dry_run: "{{job.parameters.dry_run}}"
 clone_direction: "SOUTHEAST_TO_EAST"

# DR Failover Restore Orchestrator
#
# Mirrors dr_deep_clone_full_load_orchestrator_job topology (without the S/L tier
# split, since failover is point-restore not catalog-wide):
# Task 1 (get_tables) -> serverless (UC). Reads dr_clone_config, groups
# tables by schema, bootstraps dr_failover_audit_log,
# emits failover_batches taskValue. UC-safe -- only
# touches metadata tables, never table data.
# Task 2 (restore) -> NON-UC cluster (data_security_mode: NONE).
# for_each over schema batches. SP OAuth + path-based
# delta reads/writes -> works on masked + non-masked
# tables alike.
#
# Triggered manually via "Run now with different parameters" or via API.
#
# Parameter design:
# Only RUN-TIME knobs (FAILOVER_TYPE / CATALOG / SCHEMA / TABLE_NAMES / etc.)
# appear in `parameters:` and surface in "Run with different parameters".
# Deploy-time values (config catalog, SP creds, storage mappings, etc.) are
# wired directly into `base_parameters` from DAB variables.

 name: dr_failover_restore_orchestrator_job

 max_concurrent_runs: 1

 health:
 rules:
 - metric: RUN_DURATION_SECONDS
 op: GREATER_THAN
 value: 21600

 parameters:
 - name: FAILOVER_TYPE
 default: ""
 - name: CATALOG
 default: ""
 - name: SCHEMA
 default: ""
 - name: TABLE_NAMES
 default: ""
 - name: SOURCE_VERSION
 default: ""
 - name: RESTORE_POINT
 default: ""
 - name: AFFECTED_DATE
 default: ""
 - name: START_DATE
 default: ""
 - name: END_DATE
 default: ""

 # DR metadata source: PRIMARY (default, normal) or REPLICA (read the
 # cross-region metadata replica during a disaster when SE metadata is
 # unreachable). REPLICA makes get_tables read dr_clone_config and write
 # its audit log from the gld_deepclone_dr replica schema/path instead.

 default: "PRIMARY"

 environments:
 - environment_key: deepclone_serverless
 spec:
 client: "2"

 job_clusters:
 # Non-UC cluster for the restore task (Task 2). NONE-mode is required
 # so UC is fully off and path-based abfss reads bypass Immuta masking
 # + CheckPathAccess on managed-storage locations.

 new_cluster: ${var.nonuc_cluster_profile}

 tasks:
 # Task 1: Read job parameters, query dr_clone_config, group tables by
 # schema, bootstrap dr_failover_audit_log, emit failover_batches.
 - task_key: dr_failover_get_tables_task
 environment_key: deepclone_serverless
 notebook_task:
 notebook_path: ../../../src/bdp4_lh/gld_deepclone/dr_failover_get_tables.ipynb
 base_parameters:
 # Run-time parameters
 FAILOVER_TYPE: "{{job.parameters.FAILOVER_TYPE}}"
 CATALOG: "{{job.parameters.CATALOG}}"
 SCHEMA: "{{job.parameters.SCHEMA}}"
 TABLE_NAMES: "{{job.parameters.TABLE_NAMES}}"
 SOURCE_VERSION: "{{job.parameters.SOURCE_VERSION}}"
 RESTORE_POINT: "{{job.parameters.RESTORE_POINT}}"
 AFFECTED_DATE: "{{job.parameters.AFFECTED_DATE}}"
 START_DATE: "{{job.parameters.START_DATE}}"
 END_DATE: "{{job.parameters.END_DATE}}"
 DATE_COLUMN: "{{job.parameters.DATE_COLUMN}}"
 # Deploy-time values, wired directly from DAB variables
 CONFIG_CATALOG: ${var.bdp4_system_catalog}
 CONFIG_SCHEMA: ${var.config_schema}
 metadata_storage_path: ${var.metadata_storage_path}
 # DR metadata replica wiring (PRIMARY default = unchanged). In
 # REPLICA mode get_tables derives the replica from these + reads/
 # writes the gld_deepclone_dr schema instead of the down primary.
 metadata_source: "{{job.parameters.metadata_source}}"
 storage_mappings_json: ${var.storage_mappings_json}
 clone_direction: "SOUTHEAST_TO_EAST"

 # Task 2: Restore one schema batch per for_each iteration on the
 # non-UC cluster. Tables within each schema processed sequentially;
 # schemas processed in parallel (capped by concurrency below).
 - task_key: dr_failover_restore_schema_task
 depends_on:
 -

"{{job.parameters.metadata_source}}"
 storage_mappings_json: ${var.storage_mappings_json}
 clone_direction: "SOUTHEAST_TO_EAST"

 # Task 2: Restore one schema batch per for_each iteration on the

 - task_key: dr_failover_restore_schema_task

 - task_key: dr_failover_get_tables_task

# DR Metadata Replication Job (read-only cross-region copy of gld_deepclone)
# Keeps a READ-ONLY replica of the entire DR metadata schema (gld_deepclone) on the
# paired region's storage account, so a failover can be recovered even if the
# primary region / primary metadata storage account is unavailable, or the
# metadata is accidentally deleted or corrupted (metadata SPOF fix, L1).
#
# It enumerates every base table in gld_deepclone from information_schema (so NEW
# metadata tables are picked up automatically -- it does NOT read dr_clone_config),
# reads each table's current snapshot in the SOURCE region, and writes it to the
# replica path on the DR-region account (one atomic Delta overwrite per table).
# It NEVER writes the primary metadata path -- read-only on the primary.
#
# CIRCUIT BREAKER: before overwriting a table's replica it compares the source
# row count to what is already in the replica; if the source dropped below
# min_row_ratio of the replica (or went to zero while the replica had rows), that
# table is SKIPPED and the last good replica is kept -- so an accidental delete /
# corruption on the primary is NOT propagated into the DR copy. If any table trips
# the breaker or errors and fail_on_circuit_breaker is true, the run RAISES at the
# end (after the good replicas + watermark are written) so alerting fires.
#
# The DR-region account is resolved from dr_storage_account_mapping (the account
# paired with the primary metadata account for clone_direction); the path swaps
# metadata_tables -> metadata_tables_dr. Pass replica_storage_account to override.
# The recovery jobs point their metadata_storage_path_override at this replica.
#
# Runtime knobs (job parameters, no redeploy needed):
# * clone_direction SOUTHEAST_TO_EAST (default) or EAST_TO_SOUTHEAST
# * replica_storage_account blank = resolve from dr_storage_account_mapping
# * min_row_ratio circuit breaker threshold (default 0.9)
# * fail_on_circuit_breaker raise/fail the run on any trip or error (default true)
# * include_tables/exclude_tables optional CSV filters on table name
#
# Run in the SOURCE workspace (SE for SOUTHEAST_TO_EAST) as the datacopy SP. A UC
# external location + storage credential must cover the replica path on the DR
# account (the notebook pre-flights this and fails with a clear message if not).
# Schedule: hourly but PAUSED -- review, then UNPAUSE. Tune the cron for RPO/cost.
resources:
 jobs:
 dr_metadata_replication_job:
 name: dr_metadata_replication_job
 tags:
 application: bupa_bdp4_deepclone_workload
 environment: ${bundle.target}
 type: metadata_replication
 max_concurrent_runs: 1
 timeout_seconds: 7200

 # Failure alerting: any failed run — an errored table OR a circuit-breaker
 # trip (both raise and fail the run) — emails the recipient(s) below.

 on_failure:
 - ${var.deepclone_product_owner_email}

 schedule:
 # Every 12h (00:00 and 12:00 Sydney). The recovery-critical config tables
 # change rarely, so a 12h RPO on them is safe and cheap; tighten the cron

 - name: replica_storage_account # blank = resolve from dr_storage_account_mapping
 default: ""
 - name: min_row_ratio # circuit breaker: trip if source < ratio * replica rows

 - name: include_tables # optional CSV filter (blank = all gld_deepclone tables)

 environment_key: deepclone_serverless
 notebook_task:
 notebook_path:

# Runs ANY notebook whose workspace path is supplied at run time via the
# `notebook_path` job parameter. Useful for ad-hoc / on-demand execution of a
# notebook (e.g. dr_setup_metadata, a one-off backfill, a verification book)
# without wiring a dedicated job per notebook.

# HOW IT WORKS: DAB can only bundle a notebook task whose path is a fixed local
# file, so a dynamic `{{job.parameters.notebook_path}}` cannot be the task path
# directly (validation fails: "notebook ... not found"). Instead the task runs a
# small bundled DISPATCHER notebook (dr_notebook_runner.ipynb) which reads the
# `notebook_path` widget and calls dbutils.notebook.run(...) on the target.
#
# Usage (run-now with parameters):
# notebook_path -> absolute workspace path of the notebook to run, e.g.
# /Workspace/deploy/system/bupa_bdp4_deepclone/dev/files/
# src/bdp4_lh/gld_deepclone/dr_setup_metadata
# notebook_params -> optional JSON object of widget values forwarded to the
# target notebook, e.g. {"config_catalog":"bdp4_dev_lh"}
# notebook_timeout -> max seconds to wait for the child notebook (default 3600)
#
# Compute: serverless (UC) so no cluster config is needed.

 dr_notebook_runner_job:
 name: dr_notebook_runner_job

 application: bupa_bdp4_deepclone_workload

 - name: notebook_params

 - name: notebook_timeout

# DR Recon Orchestrator — validates one clone direction end-to-end.
#
# Mirrors the structure of dr_deep_clone_full_load_orchestrator_job.yml:
# Task 1 (inventory) -> serverless. Joins dr_clone_config x dr_clone_audit_log,
# persists dr_recon_tasks, emits chunk descriptors +
# recon_run_id / recon_direction / deep-clone knobs.
# Task 2 (executor) -> NON-UC cluster. for_each over chunks. Reconciles
# EVERY table (managed AND external) by its abfss
# LOCATION -- SP OAuth + path-based delta.`abfss://...`
# reads (managed __unitystorage paths included). Bulk
# Delta append per chunk to dr_recon_audit_log.
# Task 3 (finalizer) -> serverless. Aggregates recon outcomes; raises if
# fail_on_recon_failure=true and any non-passing rows.
#
# Used for: validating a completed full clone (or, in future, an incremental
# sync) — runs separately from the clone job, against the same metadata.
resources:
 jobs:
 dr_recon_orchestrator_job:
 name: dr_recon_orchestrator_job
 tags:
 application: bupa_bdp4_deepclone_workload
 environment: ${bundle.target}
 type: recon
 max_concurrent_runs: 1
 # No JOB-level timeout. A job-level timeout CANCELS the whole run, which
 # would skip the ALL_DONE finalizer and leave the status table
 # un-updated -- exactly the failure we are fixing. Instead the runtime
 # is bounded per CHUNK on the executor task (timeout_seconds there), and
 # a slow-but-progressing run is allowed to finish so the finalizer
 # always runs. The health rule below still raises a warning at 10h.
 timeout_seconds: 0
 queue:
 enabled: true
 health:
 rules:
 - metric: RUN_DURATION_SECONDS
 op: GREATER_THAN
 value: 36000

 # Run-time-only parameters. Deploy-time values flow from DAB variables.
 #
 # ── THE ONLY KNOBS MOST RUNS NEED ────────────────────────────────────
 # scope_type/scope_value + recon_direction
 # Everything below the "ADVANCED" marker can be left at defaults.
 #
 # This recon is purpose-built for DEEP CLONE: it runs ONE fixed set of
 # eight deep-clone checks (file_match, clone_version, row_count,
 # structure, read_test + protocol, column_mapping, deletion_vectors).
 # It does NOT re-sum/re-hash data -- DEEP CLONE copies files byte-for-byte
 # at a frozen sourceVersion, so the checks are metadata-only + a cheap
 # COUNT(*) and a small LIMIT read. Safe for an ALL-scope 40k sweep.
 parameters:
 # Direction the clone was performed in. The recon reads SE as source
 # and East as target when SOUTHEAST_TO_EAST (or vice versa).
 - name: recon_direction
 default: SOUTHEAST_TO_EAST
 # How to anchor the SOURCE comparisons (row count, file metrics):
 # CLONE_VERSION (default) -> the frozen sourceVersion recorded in the
 # target's CLONE commit. Correct even if the source has moved on.
 # LIVE -> the current source (only valid if the source is unchanged
 # since the clone).
 - name: source_comparison_basis
 default: CLONE_VERSION
 # Run the real LIMIT read smoke test (check #5). true | false.
 - name: enable_read_test
 default: "true"
 # Row cap for the read test.
 - name: read_test_limit
 default: "100"
 # Scope: ALL | CATALOG | SCHEMA | TABLE | RUN_ID
 - name: scope_type
 default: ALL
 # Comma-separated values matching scope_type. Examples:
 # scope_type=CATALOG, scope_value=bdp4_dev_lh
 # scope_type=SCHEMA, scope_value=brz_peoplesoft,brz_epicor
 # scope_type=TABLE, scope_value=bdp4_dev_lh.brz_peoplesoft.t1,...
 - name: scope_value
 default: ""
 # When true, finalizer raises RuntimeError if any FAILED/ERROR rows
 # exist for this recon_run_id (loud-and-blocking). Default false:
 # surface counts, do not fail the job.
 - name: fail_on_recon_failure
 default: "false"

 # === ADVANCED (leave at defaults unless you know why) ===============
 # When scope_type=RUN_ID, validate exactly the tables the given
 # clone run_id touched. ALSO: when failed_only=true (and scope_type is
 # NOT RUN_ID), this is read as a recon_run_id -- the retry is pinned to
 # the FAILED/ERROR tables of that one past recon run.
 - name: run_id_filter
 default: ""
 #

default: "false"

 # === ADVANCED (leave at defaults unless you know why) ===============
 # When scope_type=RUN_ID, validate exactly the tables the given
 # clone run_id touched. ALSO: when failed_only=true (and scope_type is
 # NOT RUN_ID), this is read as a recon_run_id -- the retry is pinned to
 # the FAILED/ERROR tables of that one past recon run.
 - name: run_id_filter
 default: ""
 # Skip tables whose latest dr_clone_audit_log status is not SUCCESS.
 - name: succeeded_only
 default: "true"
 # Retry-failed mode. When true, recon ONLY the tables whose MOST RECENT
 # recon row (dr_recon_audit_log, this direction) ended FAILED/ERROR.
 # Composes with scope_type: leave scope_type=ALL to retry every failed
 # table, or set scope_type=SCHEMA/CATALOG to narrow the retry. Tables
 # never reconciled before are not selected. Default false (recon all).
 - name: failed_only
 default: "false"
 # Skip intermediate / materialized-view backing / event-log tables
 # (names starting with an underscore, e.g. `_materialised...`). Their
 # large streaming Delta logs make DESCRIBE HISTORY recon pathologically
 # slow and can hang a whole for_each chunk for hours.
 # Default true -- set false only to deliberately recon those internal
 # tables (scope_type=TABLE always targets an exact name regardless).
 - name: exclude_intermediate_tables
 default: "true"

 environments:
 - environment_key: deepclone_serverless
 spec:
 client: "2"

 job_clusters:
 - job_cluster_key: nonuc_cluster_recon
 new_cluster: ${var.nonuc_cluster_profile_recon}

 tasks:
 # Task 1: Inventory + bootstrap. Serverless because the workload is
 # pure metadata (information_schema joins, Delta DDL).
 - task_key: dr_recon_inventory_task
 environment_key: deepclone_serverless
 notebook_task:
 notebook_path: ../../../src/bdp4_lh/gld_deepclone/dr_recon_inventory.ipynb
 base_parameters:
 # Run-time
 recon_direction: "{{job.parameters.recon_direction}}"
 scope_type: "{{job.parameters.scope_type}}"
 scope_value: "{{job.parameters.scope_value}}"
 run_id_filter: "{{job.parameters.run_id_filter}}"
 succeeded_only: "{{job.parameters.succeeded_only}}"
 failed_only: "{{job.parameters.failed_only}}"
 exclude_intermediate_tables: "{{job.parameters.exclude_intermediate_tables}}"
 source_comparison_basis: "{{job.parameters.source_comparison_basis}}"
 enable_read_test: "{{job.parameters.enable_read_test}}"
 read_test_limit: "{{job.parameters.read_test_limit}}"
 # Deploy-time
 config_catalog: ${var.bdp4_system_catalog}
 config_schema: ${var.config_schema}
 metadata_storage_path: ${var.metadata_storage_path}

 # Gate: only spin the recon cluster up when there is work to do.
 - task_key: gate_has_recon_tasks
 depends_on:
 - task_key: dr_recon_inventory_task
 condition_task:
 op: GREATER_THAN
 left: "{{tasks.dr_recon_inventory_task.values.total_tasks}}"
 right: "0"

 # Task 2: Executor — for_each over chunks.
 # NOTE: the nested task uses a SHARED job cluster (nonuc_cluster_recon),
 # so Databricks runs chunk iterations SEQUENTIALLY on it -- a
 # concurrency > 1 here does not spawn parallel iterations on one
 # shared cluster. Real parallelism comes from INSIDE each chunk:
 # chunk_size (>=128) tables fanned over DR_RECON_INTRA_CHUNK_PARALLELISM
 # (48) driver threads, saturating the autoscaling 4-16 worker cluster.
 # (To parallelise chunks themselves you'd give each iteration its own
 # new_cluster -- 8x the cost/startup -- which we deliberately avoid.)
 - task_key: dr_recon_executor_task
 depends_on:
 - task_key: gate_has_recon_tasks
 outcome: "true"
 for_each_task:
 inputs: "{{tasks.dr_recon_inventory_task.values.clone_tasks}}"
 concurrency: 8
 task:
 task_key: dr_recon_runner
 job_cluster_key: nonuc_cluster_recon
 # Per-CHUNK timeout (Databricks only allows timeout on the inner
 # task, not on the for_each). This caps a single pathological
 # chunk so it can't hang the run forever. When a chunk times
 # out the for_each ends as FAILED, but the run is NOT cancelled,
 # so the ALL_DONE finalizer

concurrency: 8
 task:
 task_key: dr_recon_runner
 job_cluster_key: nonuc_cluster_recon
 # Per-CHUNK timeout (Databricks only allows timeout on the inner
 # task, not on the for_each). This caps a single pathological
 # chunk so it can't hang the run forever. When a chunk times
 # out the for_each ends as FAILED, but the run is NOT cancelled,
 # so the ALL_DONE finalizer below still runs and updates the
 # status table. A repaired ("Repair run") executor then resumes:
 # the notebook skips tables already validated under this
 # recon_run_id and only finishes the remainder.
 timeout_seconds: 201600 # 56h per chunk (safety cap)
 notebook_task:
 notebook_path: ../../../src/bdp4_lh/gld_deepclone/dr_recon_executor_nonuc.ipynb
 base_parameters:
 task_json: "{{input}}"
 config_catalog: ${var.bdp4_system_catalog}
 config_schema: ${var.config_schema}
 metadata_storage_path: ${var.metadata_storage_path}
 storage_mappings_json: ${var.storage_mappings_json}

 # Task 3: Finalizer. ALL_DONE so we still summarize after a partial
 # executor failure. Serverless — pure SQL aggregation.
 - task_key: dr_recon_finalizer_task
 depends_on:
 - task_key: dr_recon_executor_task
 run_if: ALL_DONE
 environment_key: deepclone_serverless
 notebook_task:
 notebook_path: ../../../src/bdp4_lh/gld_deepclone/dr_recon_finalizer.ipynb
 base_parameters:
 config_catalog: ${var.bdp4_system_catalog}
 config_schema: ${var.config_schema}
 recon_direction: "{{job.parameters.recon_direction}}"
 fail_on_recon_failure: "{{job.parameters.fail_on_recon_failure}}"

# First run / re-seed -> FULL baseline snapshot. Daily -> only CDF changes since
# the last watermark (staging APPEND, bronze MERGE live-mirror). Each run commits
# a new Delta version to the DR table = that day's snapshot (recover any day via
# TIMESTAMP AS OF). DR tables get ~20yr retention so snapshots are never VACUUMed.

# staging/bronze table). Populate it once per environment. The DR-region storage
