- **VM *generation* can be a compliance gate, independent of everything else.**
 One region enforced a standard requiring Azure VNet encryption, which only
 v4/v5 SKUs support: `INVALID_PARAMETER_VALUE … must use instances that
 support Azure Virtual Network encryption`. That is a property of the VM
 generation alone — orthogonal to spot vs on-demand, to size, and to price. A
 region can therefore have pools that *exist* and are *quota-available* and
 still cannot start a single cluster.
- **Compliance rules shrink the usable inventory dramatically, and asymmetrically
 between regions.** Of 12 pools in the constrained region, 8 were v5 and
 startable; of those, 4 were on-demand. An "on-demand only, no spot" policy
 plus a v5-only compliance rule left exactly **four** usable pools, and only
 **two** of them memory-optimised — both drawing on the same 350-core family.
 Enumerate the intersection of all constraints early; the answer is often much
 smaller than the pool list suggests.
- **The same pool name can be different hardware in different regions.** One
 region's `ondemand_memory_optimised_32core_256gb` was E32s_v5, the other's
 E32s_v3; the 4-core standard pool was D4s_v5 in one and DS3_v2 in the other.
 Name-based resolution is what lets one config serve two regions, and it is
 also what hides the fact that the two regions are running different silicon.
- **Insufficient quota does not always fail loudly.** Sometimes you get a clean
 `AZURE_QUOTA_EXCEEDED_EXCEPTION`; sometimes the cluster simply sits pending
 and the fan-out waits on it indefinitely. The second is how a run silently
 becomes a two-day run. Loud failure is the good case.

## Infrastructure-as-code: deploy time vs run time

- **The single most expensive confusion: a bundle deploys the whole job
 definition to *every* target, so every cluster spec is validated in every
 region — including clusters for tasks that can never run there.** A comment
 reading "this task is SE-only, so the East constraint doesn't apply" was
 correct about runtime and wrong about deployment, and it blocked a prod
 deploy. **Runtime reachability and deploy-time validation are different
 properties.** Ask separately: will this task ever *execute* here, and will
 this spec ever be *validated* here.
- **Know exactly which checks happen at each stage.** Deploy time: does the
 resource name resolve, and does the spec satisfy any attached policy. Cluster
 start time: quota, compliance rules, actual capacity. A v3 pool that no
 region-local task uses will deploy perfectly and only fail if something
 eventually tries to start it — which makes it a latent trap rather than a
 visible one.
- **A cluster *policy* validates at deploy, and its allowlist can be
 fundamentally incompatible with your standards.** The single-node policy in
 one region allowed only **spot** pools. Combined with an "on-demand only"
 rule, no compliant configuration existed at all — the two requirements were
 mutually exclusive and no amount of pool-swapping would have satisfied both.
 When a policy blocks you, check whether the policy's allowlist and your own
 policy can *ever* both hold before searching for the pool that squares them.
- **A policy that requires a property does not impose it.** A single-node
 policy rejected a cluster that hadn't declared itself single-node — the spec
 had the policy attached and none of `num_workers: 0`, the `ResourceClass`
 tag, or the `cluster.profile` conf. "Single node via the policy" was the
 assumption; "single node *or rejected* by the policy" was the reality.
- **Dropping a policy is a legitimate fix when nothing mandates one.** Twelve of
 fourteen cluster profiles in the repo carried no

 had the policy attached and none of `num_workers: 0`, the `ResourceClass`
 tag, or the `cluster.profile` conf. "Single node via the policy" was the
 assumption; "single node *or rejected* by the policy" was the reality.
- **Dropping a policy is a legitimate fix when nothing mandates one.** Twelve of
 fourteen cluster profiles in the repo carried no policy and deployed fine, in
 the very apply that the one policed cluster failed — direct evidence the
 workspace didn't require policies. Matching the configuration that
 demonstrably works beats inferring what a policy wants from its error text.
- **Referencing anything that exists in only one workspace breaks the other's
 deploy.** A pool present in one region and absent in the other fails the
 lookup, and the error names the missing resource rather than the reasoning
 that introduced it.
- **A resource referenced only by a never-running task is a standing
 fragility.** Nobody in that region has any reason to keep it, and if it's
 cleaned up the deploy starts failing with an error unrelated to whatever
 change exposed it.
- **Deploying the same bundle twice with different config between runs is
 possible but leaves the repo correct for only one target at a time.** Any
 redeploy of the other region — a rollback, a hotfix, an automated pipeline
 run — then fails, and nothing in the repo records which region the committed
 state is currently aimed at. Prefer configuration that is valid everywhere;
 where you can't, make the asymmetry loud in the file itself.

## Validation / testing methodology

- **A binary pass/fail hides the difference between "wrong" and "couldn't
 tell."** A third verdict — NOT MEASURED — for permission errors, extractor
 bugs, and unsafe time-travel windows keeps "the clone lost data" distinct
 from "we weren't able to check," which otherwise collapse into the same
 alarming-looking failure count.
- **Comparing an evolving source against a frozen target is not a fair
 test**, no matter how good the comparator is — the fix has to happen at the
 measurement layer (pin both sides to the same version), not in how
 differences get reported afterward.
- **A retention/safety gate should be scoped to what it actually protects,
 not applied blanket.** Gating *all* checks on the data-file retention window
 when only two of twelve checks touch data files threw away ~20,000 valid
 measurements per run — the gate's blast radius should match its actual
 cause.
- **Guard against "confident wrong answer" more than against "crash."** A
 function that returns `0` or `{}` on an edge case it can't actually handle
 is worse than one that raises — the caller can route an exception to NOT
 MEASURED, but a silently-wrong zero looks exactly like a real, passing
 measurement.
- **A mode switch beats a parallel implementation.** Adding a second family of
 checks as an `inc=true/false` mode on the existing notebooks — rather than
 duplicating them — avoided copying ~1,800 lines of renderer and comparator
 logic that would then have drifted. The condition for this being safe is that
 the two modes are genuinely mutually exclusive; if both could run at once
 you'd be building a flag, not a mode.
- **Put the mode gate at the single point every path already passes through.**
 One four-line guard inside the function every check card is rendered by beat
 wrapping twenty-odd call sites, and it cannot be forgotten when a new card is
 added later. Finding that convergence point is usually the whole design.
- **Derive the output shape from one named set, never from a second list.**
 Column ordering, the extractor loop, and the written schema all deriving from
 a single `ACTIVE_CHECKS` list means a mode switch changes one line. An earlier
 version iterated a different dict for the column headers and would have
 emitted nine all-NaN columns that look exactly like measurements nobody took.
- **Prove the old path is unchanged; don't assert it.** After

from a second list.**
 Column ordering, the extractor loop, and the written schema all deriving from
 a single `ACTIVE_CHECKS` list means a mode switch changes one line. An earlier
 version iterated a different dict for the column headers and would have
 emitted nine all-NaN columns that look exactly like measurements nobody took.
- **Prove the old path is unchanged; don't assert it.** After adding a mode
 switch, executing the registry cells from the *pre-change commit* and from
 HEAD and diffing the resulting check lists element-by-element turned "I only
 added an else branch" into evidence. Cheap to write, and it catches the
 reordering that a set comprehension or a dict-iteration change silently
 introduces.
- **Choose deliberately what a new mode does *not* fold in.** Excluding the
 long-running full diff from the incremental report was a design decision, not
 an omission: including it would have forced a dependency edge onto a task
 that runs for 22 hours and serialised a four-hour report behind it. Worth
 recording the reasoning next to the exclusion, or someone "fixes" it later.
- **Classify failures by side and by cause before drawing any conclusion from
 the count.** A recovered run showed 465 passes and **88 failures**, which read
 as a serious clone defect. Breaking them down changed the story completely:
 all 88 were **source-side** (three storage accounts, all in the source
 region), **zero** were row-count mismatches, and the causes were 52
 `FAILED_READ_FILE.DBR_FILE_NOT_EXIST` plus 35 `FileNotFoundException` 404s —
 i.e. source files vacuumed away between clone time and validation time. Not
 one of them said anything about the clone. **Forward rule:** a failure count
 is not a finding. Group by side, by error class, and by object before
 reporting — the grouping usually *is* the diagnosis, and an ungrouped count
 will send people to debug the wrong component.
- **An absolute threshold is an absolute answer to a relative question — and
 the obvious statistical fix has its own degenerate case.** A fixed 50 GB tier
 boundary was applied to an estate whose largest table was under 50 GB, so
 every table classified "small": the large-tier cluster started, found zero
 tables, and exited eight minutes later while the small tier ran past twelve
 hours. Switching to a population statistic is the right instinct, but the
 *median* was also degenerate here, because most tables reported zero size —
 the median of a zero-heavy population is zero, which routes the entire estate
 the other way. The mean over non-zero values was the workable choice.
 **Forward rule:** derive split points from the data, but inspect the
 distribution first — count the zeros and nulls before choosing a statistic,
 and keep a sanity check that raises when a computed threshold would put every
 item on one side.

## Job orchestration (Databricks Jobs)

- **A `for_each` repair must resolve to the same iteration count as the
 original run.** Change the `inputs:` array from 8 entries to 12 and every
 in-flight or historical run becomes **permanently unrepairable** — the
 scheduler can't map old iterations onto the new array. So: deploys that
 change pools, parameters or notebook code leave old runs repairable; deploys
 that change an `inputs:` array do not. Worth knowing before you promise
 someone a repair.
- **In a fan-out, the chunk divisor and the scheduled iteration count are two
 different numbers and both directions of mismatch matter.** Iterations >
 divisor is wasteful but safe — surplus iterations exit on the guard. Divisor
 > iterations is **silent data loss**: whole modulo groups get no runner at
 all, nothing fails, and the only trace is an absent output file. Reconcile
 row-level coverage before overwriting the scope file, not after.
- **The UI task-edit is a real escape hatch when redeploys are expensive.** You
 can repoint a task's cluster in the Jobs UI and repair the run immediately,
 without another deploy; the next IaC deploy

data loss**: whole modulo groups get no runner at
 all, nothing fails, and the only trace is an absent output file. Reconcile
 row-level coverage before overwriting the scope file, not after.
- **The UI task-edit is a real escape hatch when redeploys are expensive.** You
 can repoint a task's cluster in the Jobs UI and repair the run immediately,
 without another deploy; the next IaC deploy reverts it. That converts "we get
 one deploy attempt" into "we get one deploy attempt plus a manual override,"
 which materially changes how much risk a change can carry.
- **Job parameters silently override task base parameters of the same name.**
 A job-level `max_parallel` beat every per-tier `base_parameter` of that name
 on every task, so per-tier tuning had no effect at all and looked like a
 stale deploy. Namespacing the job-level parameters (`default_max_parallel`,
 `scope_chunks`) fixed it. Check for name collisions between the two layers
 before concluding a value "isn't taking effect."
- **A default nobody runs with is a bug waiting to surface.** A concurrency
 default of 1 was survivable only because operators overrode it by hand every
 time; the first run that used the default would have been ~8× slower with no
 error. Defaults should be the value you actually want.
- **Serverless bills for the wall-clock you hold it, so the worst possible fit
 is a long-lived task that does no compute.** A live progress dashboard — sleep
 60s, list a few small files, one API call, render text — sat on serverless for
 **22h46m** on a single run, because it exits only once every sibling task is
 terminal. It performed no Spark work in that entire window and was billed at a
 rate meant for real query compute. Moving it to the cheapest classic
 single-node cluster cost about five minutes of startup, which is irrelevant
 against a 22-hour run. **Forward rule:** classify every task as
 compute-bound or wall-clock-bound before choosing its compute. Serverless is
 excellent for short bursty work and actively wrong for anything that mostly
 waits.
- **A cosmetic task must be structurally incapable of failing or delaying the
 run.** Two properties made that true for the dashboard, and both are
 counter-intuitive: **nothing depends on it** (so it can never block a
 successor), and it carries **no `timeout_seconds`** — because a Databricks
 task timeout marks the task Failed, and a failed task fails the whole run. A
 timeout on a monitoring task would mean a cosmetic component could kill a
 22-hour validation. It self-exits on its own internal limit instead, with
 success. **Forward rule:** for any observability or reporting sidecar, check
 both edges — can it block anything, and can it fail anything — and prefer an
 in-notebook self-exit over a platform timeout.
- **A task that watches the run it is part of must exclude itself.** The
 dashboard's exit condition was "all tasks terminal", which it can never
 observe — it is itself running whenever it asks. Without passing the task its
 own key so it can filter itself out, the condition is unsatisfiable and every
 run sits until the backstop limit. **Forward rule:** any self-referential
 monitoring loop needs an identity and a self-exclusion; if you find yourself
 wondering why a watcher always runs to its maximum duration, this is the first
 thing to check.

## Cross-region orchestration: one job triggering and awaiting another

- **A job in region A can fire and then await a job in region B, and the whole
 mechanism is just the REST API plus an Entra service principal.** There is no
 special "cross-workspace" feature to enable. Region A obtains an OAuth token
 for a service principal, then calls region B's ordinary Jobs API with it. Once
 you have the token, the remote workspace is just a hostname.
- **The auth flow is Azure AD machine-to-machine client credentials.** POST to
 `https://login.microsoftonline.com/{TENANT_ID}/oauth2/v2.0/token` with
 `grant_type=client_credentials`, the SP's `client_id`

- **The auth flow is Azure AD machine-to-machine client credentials.** POST to
 `https://login.microsoftonline.com/{TENANT_ID}/oauth2/v2.0/token` with
 `grant_type=client_credentials`, the SP's `client_id` and `client_secret`, and
 `scope={DATABRICKS_RESOURCE}/.default`. The response's `access_token` goes
 straight into `Authorization: Bearer …` against the target workspace.
- **`DATABRICKS_RESOURCE` is a fixed, well-known Azure constant** —
 `2ff814a6-3304-4ab8-85cb-cd0e6f879c1d`, the AzureDatabricks first-party
 application ID. It is the same for every tenant and every workspace on earth,
 so it belongs in code as a constant, not in config. Worth committing to memory;
 it is the piece that looks like it must be environment-specific and isn't.
- **The full checklist to make the connection work**, in the order things fail:
 the **tenant ID**; a **service principal** (client ID + secret) that exists in
 the tenant *and* has been granted access **in the target workspace** — being
 registered in the tenant is not enough; the secret stored in a **secret scope
 in the calling workspace**; the **target workspace host**
 (`https://adb-<workspace-id>.<n>.azuredatabricks.net`); and the **target
 `job_id`**. Everything else is a normal API call.
- **`job_id` is workspace-scoped and is the fragile link.** It is a number that
 means nothing in the calling region, and it changes if the target job is ever
 recreated rather than updated — which in IaC terms means changing the resource
 key destroys and re-issues it. That single integer is the tightest coupling
 between the two regions; treat it as an interface.
- **Preflight with `GET /api/2.1/jobs/get` before `run-now`.** One extra call
 proves the job exists *and* the SP can see it, so a wrong ID or a missing
 grant surfaces as a clear error rather than an opaque failure buried in a
 `run-now` response. Two failure modes separated for the cost of one request.
- **`run-now` rejects any `job_parameters` key the target job does not
 declare.** That silently couples the two jobs' parameter lists: adding a
 parameter on the calling side and forwarding it breaks *every* run until the
 target is redeployed too. Deploy the callee first, always.
- **Serverless compute cannot make the call.** Serverless egress fails the
 cross-workspace trust check, so the triggering and waiting tasks must run on
 classic VNet compute. This is the kind of constraint that only appears at
 runtime and forces a cluster into a job that otherwise wanted none.
- **Derive which region you are in at runtime; do not configure it.** One IaC
 target deployed byte-identically to two physical workspaces, so a deploy-time
 "my region" value would be correct in one and wrong in the other. Detecting
 the executing workspace and firing the *opposite* one makes direction a
 derived property. Configured direction is a bug waiting for the second
 deployment.
- **Per-workspace names you assume are symmetric often aren't.** The two
 workspaces' Key Vault-backed secret scopes were named differently
 (`secret-kv101` vs `secret-kv01`) despite one bundle serving both — so the
 code carries *both* candidate scope names and selects once the region is
 known. Expect at least one such asymmetry per region pair.
- **Fire-and-exit, then wait in a separate task.** `run-now` returns as soon as
 the remote run is queued; the returned `run_id` is published as a task value
 and consumed downstream as `{{tasks.<trigger>.values.tgt_run_id}}`. Splitting
 trigger from wait is what lets other local work proceed in parallel with the
 remote run instead of blocking behind it.
- **You can wait on a single *task inside* the remote run, not just the whole
 run.** `GET /api/2.1/jobs/runs/get` returns a `tasks[]` array with per-task
 state, so you can release local work the

 run.** `GET /api/2.1/jobs/runs/get` returns a `tasks[]` array with per-task
 state, so you can release local work the moment the one upstream task you
 actually depend on finishes. That turned a full-run barrier into a precise
 synchronisation point and unlocked real parallelism — probably the single most
 useful thing in this section.
- **`life_cycle_state` and `result_state` are two different fields and you need
 both.** `TERMINATED` covers success and failure alike; `result_state` says
 which. And some terminal states (`SKIPPED`, `INTERNAL_ERROR`) arrive with no
 `result_state` at all, so treating its absence as "still running" produces a
 poll loop that never exits.
- **Be generous with a wait task's timeout, or make it unbounded.** A wait that
 times out marks the task failed and fails the whole run — so the timeout is
 not a safety net, it is an additional way to lose a good run. Sizing it at 48
 hours against a 22-hour job is the right shape of margin.
- **A cross-region trigger should fail loud, unlike a best-effort one.** If
 everything downstream is meaningless without the remote run, swallowing the
 error just moves the failure somewhere less diagnosable.

## Diagnosing infrastructure failures

- **Read the error's own numbers before theorising.** The quota failure stated
 Current Limit 350, Current Usage 320, Additional Required 160, Minimum New
 Limit 480 — enough to compute both the immediate fix and the real ask (~1,400
 for the full fan-out) without a single assumption. Cloud errors are often
 more quantitative than they look.
- **Ask for the number you actually need, not the minimum the error suggests.**
 480 would have unblocked one cluster and failed on the next. The error tells
 you what the *current* request needed, not what your workload needs.
- **Terminated-cluster history is free evidence.** A 30-day cluster list showed
 three successful spot clusters and two successful runs on the exact SKU that
 later hit quota — proving "spot works in this region" and "this SKU works in
 this region" as separate facts, without creating anything. When you can't run
 an experiment, look for one that already ran.
- **Decompose an unknown into the parts that are already proven.** "Will spot
 E32s_v5 work here" split into three: does the pool exist (yes), is the SKU
 compliant (yes, v5), does spot allocate in this region (yes, evidenced on
 another SKU). What remained unproven was only the *combination* — a far
 smaller risk than the original question, and small enough to accept with a
 retry as cover.
- **Identical round numbers across unrelated metrics are a smell.** Three
 different quota families all reading exactly "0 of 350" was the tell that the
 region filter was wrong — those were untouched defaults for a region nobody
 deploys to. Real usage is lumpy.
- **Check the filter before trusting the reading.** The above happened because
 an autocomplete matched **Austria** East instead of **Australia** East. Any
 console with a region, subscription, or environment selector will eventually
 hand you correct-looking numbers for the wrong scope.
- **Verify you can perform the diagnostic action before you need it.** Cluster
 creation was denied, so the intended five-minute capacity smoke test was
 impossible — discovered mid-incident. Jobs create their own clusters as the
 run-as identity, so a human can lack a permission the pipeline has, and it
 only surfaces when you try to debug interactively.
- **A comment that encodes a *reason* is load-bearing, and a wrong one is worse
 than none.** "SE-only, so the East VNet constraint does not apply" was
 plausible, survived review, and blocked a prod deploy — because it forecloses
 the check it appears to

clusters as the
 run-as identity, so a human can lack a permission the pipeline has, and it
 only surfaces when you try to debug interactively.

 than none.** "SE-only, so the East VNet constraint does not apply" was

- **Stale comments cause real regressions.** A note reading "parallelism is cut
 to 8 because East cannot offer a driver larger than 32 GB" was true for about
 a week. Anyone acting on it afterwards would have undone the fix that
 replaced it. Update the prose in the same commit as the value.
- **Know your recovery-source hierarchy before you need it — the friendliest
 artifact is often the lossy one.** When a 12-hour run was cancelled before
 writing any output, the results still existed in two places, and they were not
 equally good. **Notebook HTML exports were silently truncated**: 452 of 547
 results recovered, with a `*** WARNING` marker and visible gaps in the
 per-table counter — findable only because the output happened to be numbered.
 **Driver stdout was complete**: 171 + 169 + 213 = 553 results across three
 chunks, zero gaps. The polished, shareable artifact lost 17% of the data; the
 raw log lost none. **Forward rule:** when reconstructing from logs, prefer the
 rawest source available and *verify completeness independently* — a sequence
 counter or expected total in the output is what turns "looks complete" into
 "is complete". Design that counter in deliberately; it costs one integer and
 it is the only reason the truncation here was detectable at all.

## Command-line and scripting gotchas (Windows / Databricks CLI)

- **PowerShell's `` `v `` is a vertical-tab escape, not a literal "v".** So
 `"standard$tag`v$ver`Family"` silently produced `standardES3Family` instead of
 `standardESv3Family`. Use `${}` around every variable in an interpolated
 string: `"standard${tag}v${ver}Family"`.
- **Passing multi-line or quote-containing arguments to native executables from
 PowerShell is genuinely hostile.** Here-strings (`@'…'@`) need the terminator
 at column 0 and break inside `;`-chained commands; double quotes embedded in a
 single-quoted string still break argument boundaries when the call is
 reconstructed. For anything non-trivial, write the text to a file and pass the
 file (`git commit -F`), or use repeated single-line flags.
- **`Format-Table` truncates at console width and drops the right-hand columns
 with no indication.** Pipe through `Out-String -Width 4096` when the output
 matters.
- **The Databricks CLI emits a UTF-8 BOM when redirected to a file**, which
 makes `json.load` fail with "Unexpected UTF-8 BOM". Read with `utf-8-sig`.
- **Prefer one API call that already returns what you need.** `instance-pools
 list` includes each pool's `stats` block, so per-pool `get` calls to fetch
 instance counts are wasted round-trips. Check the list response's shape before

## PySpark / pandas gotchas worth remembering on sight

- **`dict(a_spark_row)` doesn't do what it looks like.** `Row` supports
 iteration over its *values*, not `(key, value)` pairs, so `dict()`
 misreads it — use `.asDict()`.
- **`spark.read.json()` infers any nested JSON object as a STRUCT, never a
 true `MapType`**, even for a field that's logically `map<string,string>` —
 code that expects a dict has to normalize this explicitly regardless of
 source.
- **CSV round-trips between pandas and Spark need explicit escape
 handling.** `pandas.to_csv()` doubles embedded quotes (RFC 4180); Spark's
 reader defaults to backslash-escaping. Without `.option("escape", '"')`, a
 quoted value with an internal comma silently shifts every later column — no
 error, just corrupted rows.
- **`groupBy().agg(F.max(col))` doesn't guarantee other columns come from

**CSV round-trips between pandas and Spark need explicit escape
 handling.** `pandas.to_csv()` doubles embedded quotes (RFC 4180); Spark's
 reader defaults to backslash-escaping. Without `.option("escape", '"')`, a
 quoted value with an internal comma silently shifts every later column — no
 error, just corrupted rows.
- **`groupBy().agg(F.max(col))` doesn't guarantee other columns come from
 that same max row.** If you need several columns tied to "the latest row,"
 use a window function (`row_number() over partitionBy(...).orderBy(...
 desc())`) — an aggregate can silently mix values from different rows when
 there's more than one candidate.
- **Multi-statement `%sql` notebook cells only display the last statement's
 result.** Earlier statements still ran; their output is just not rendered —
 an easy thing to misread as "didn't execute."
- **Serverless/Spark Connect compute blocks reading certain Spark confs
 outright**, distinct from "the value isn't set." The error looks like a
 runtime failure but is really a compute-tier restriction.
- **Databricks notebooks compile each cell independently, so control flow
 cannot span cells.** An `if` opened in one cell does not indent the next —
 attempting it produces `unexpected indent` on every following cell, which
 reads as a dozen unrelated syntax errors rather than one structural mistake.
 This is what forced a mode switch to be implemented as a guard *inside* the
 single function every code path already passes through, rather than as an `if`
 wrapped around twenty-odd cells. **Forward rule:** in a notebook, conditional
 behaviour has to live inside a function or be repeated per cell — so when you
 need to gate a lot of code, first go looking for the one function everything
 funnels through. A related consequence: `from __future__ import annotations`
 in any cell but the first makes the whole file fail `py_compile` while
 remaining perfectly valid at runtime, so validate notebooks cell-by-cell
 (`ast.parse` per cell) rather than as one file.
- **A pandas CSV round-trip silently converts an integer column containing any
 blank into float.** A version column written as `836` comes back as `836.0`,
 and `"836.0" != "836"` fails every downstream string comparison — on every
 row, so it looks like a total mismatch rather than a formatting artifact. The
 blank is enough to do it: pandas has no integer dtype with missing values by
 default, so one NA promotes the whole column. **Forward rule:** normalise
 through `int(float(x))` at every read boundary, or use the nullable `Int64`
 dtype explicitly. Treat any CSV hop as lossy for numeric types, and be
 suspicious of a comparison that fails 100% rather than partially — that
 pattern is nearly always a type or format issue, not a data issue.
- **`~col.isin([...])` silently drops NULLs, because SQL's `NOT IN` is
 three-valued.** `NULL != 'X'` is NULL, not true, so rows with a null in the
 filtered column fail the predicate and vanish from scope — no error, no
 warning, just a smaller working set than intended. In a scope-building filter
 that is silent data loss at the very first step. **Forward rule:** whenever
 you write an exclusion filter, decide explicitly what NULL should mean, and
 count the nulls you are dropping. The implementation here counts them and
 prints a loud warning if any exist, so the rule can be made explicit the
 moment it actually matters rather than being inherited by accident from
 three-valued logic.

── SIZE TIERING ────────────────────────────────────────────────
WHERE THE TIER IS ACTUALLY DECIDED: get_versions.py stamps a
PROVISIONAL tier per chunk from dr_clone_audit_log.copied_file_size,
but get_versions_merge_task OVERWRITES it across the whole merged
population before anything reads it. The merge is the only task that
can decide this correctly -- get_versions.py is a 5-chunk for_each,
so a statistic computed there would be computed five times over five
disjoint slices. Both tiered fan-outs below (the versioned extractor
and the full diff) INHERIT that column rather than deriving their
own, so the merge's single decision settles both.
tier_strategy picks HOW the l/s line is drawn:
mean Default. The split point is the mean of every non-zero
copied_file_size in scope. On the normal right-skewed
shape (a long tail of small tables, a few enormous ones)
the mean sits well above the median, so only genuine
outliers route to 'l' -- which is what tiering is for.
median An exact 50/50 split by count. Neither tier can be empty
while two distinct sizes exist, at the cost of sending
half the estate to the expensive large cluster. Use this
if 'mean' reports an empty tier.
absolute The previous behaviour: the fixed tier_threshold_gb
below, ignoring the population entirely.
WHY THIS IS NOT JUST tier_threshold_gb ANY MORE. A fixed 50 GB is an
absolute answer to a relative question. On an estate whose largest
table is under 50 GB, every table classified 's': the small cluster
carried the entire diff while the large one started, found
tables_in_scope=0 and exited 8 minutes later -- with tier-s still
running past 12 hours. A split point derived from the sizes
themselves cannot fail that way.
tier_threshold_gb is still used verbatim when tier_strategy=absolute,
and as the fallback when no table has a usable size at all (the merge
warns loudly in that case rather than accepting a 0-byte split point,
which would route the entire estate to 'l' -- the mirror image of the
bug above).
UNKNOWN size still routes to 'l' deliberately: an unexpectedly large
table starving the small cluster is worse than a small table wasting
capacity on the large one. A genuine 0 is a KNOWN size and lands 's'.

Per-tier chunk counts and concurrency. Each tier is an independent
population on its own cluster, so each gets its own numbers.
SAME CAVEAT AS total_chunks: each of these MUST stay in sync with
the matching `inputs:` literal on its for_each_task -- DAB cannot
expand a parameter into an array, so lowering one alone wastes
iterations and RAISING one alone breaks the merge (it would look
for chunk files no iteration wrote).
The versioned extractor and the full diff carry SEPARATE numbers on
purpose: the extractor is latency-bound (thousands of tiny log
reads -- wants high concurrency), while the diff is shuffle-bound
(a full exceptAll per table -- over-subscribing it starves every
table of the cores it needs). This is the same tension
dr_clone_full_diff_standalone.py's DIFF_MAX_PARALLEL_CEILING clamp
exists to defend against; giving them separate knobs means the
clamp should no longer have to fire at all.
── SCALING THE FULL DIFF: OUT, NOT UP ──────────────────────────
When this job moves to an estate with more/larger tables (prod is
20k+, each substantially bigger than preprod's), raise the CHUNK
counts -- diff_chunks_l / diff_chunks_s -- and leave
diff_max_parallel_l / _s alone. The two knobs are not
interchangeable and only one of them adds capacity:
+1 chunk = one more CLUSTER = genuinely more cores.
Cores per in-flight table stays constant.
+1 max_parallel = the SAME cores divided among more tables.
Cores per in-flight table FALLS.
The relevant invariant is cores-per-concurrent-table, which
dr_clone_full_diff_standalone.py puts at ~16 minimum. At E64 nodes:
tier l 4-8 workers x 64c = 256-512c / 4 tables = 64-128 c/table
tier s 3-6 workers x 64c = 192-384c / 16 tables = 12-24 c/table
Scaling UP is what produced the 30-hour livelock recorded in that
notebook's clamp comment (max_parallel=500 on 512 cores -> ~1 core
per table, 609 Spark jobs admitted at once, throughput to zero).
Note that failure came from the PARAMETER side; the small tier's
1-2 workers reached the same 4-8 c/table from the CLUSTER side
(now 3-6 -- see bundle_config.yml). Both sides of the ratio have to
hold, so raise chunks and let each chunk keep its own full cluster.
BEFORE RAISING CHUNKS, CHECK QUOTA. Every chunk is a whole cluster
drawing E64s_v3 (64 vCPU) nodes from the dedicated full-diff pools,
and both tiers run CONCURRENTLY, so the peak is the sum:
today l 3x(4-8 +1 driver) + s 4x(3-6 +1) = 31-55 nodes
= 1,984-3,520 vCPU
l=5,s=6 l 5x(4-8 +1) + s 6x(3-6 +1) = 49-87 nodes
= 3,136-5,568 vCPU
Workers are SPOT, so that is spot Esv3 quota plus one VNet IP per
node. Confirm both in the target subscription first -- a chunk that
cannot allocate does not fail loudly, it sits pending and the
for_each waits on it.

is one more CLUSTER (more cores); +1 max_parallel divides the SAME

67% more capacity for the tier. If the table list splits evenly that

taking the full diff's peak from 55 to 73 nodes / 4,672 vCPU, plus one

── FULL RE-VERIFICATION vs INCREMENTAL ─────────────────────────
false (DEFAULT) -- incremental. dr_clone_full_diff_standalone.py
skips tables already proven to match in an earlier run, so a run
only chases what is still outstanding. Observed live: 13,320 in
scope narrowed to 497, and a tier-s chunk finished in 13 minutes
instead of 10h48m.
true -- re-diff EVERY table in scope, ignoring what any previous
run concluded. The skip-list file is NOT deleted, only ignored for
that run; the merge rebuilds it from the merged result either way.
WHY THIS IS A PARAMETER AND NOT A CONVENTION. The two modes support
different CLAIMS. An incremental run can only say "N tables verified
as of whenever each was last checked"; only a full run can say "the

forget to put back.

THREE VERDICTS, NOT TWO -- this is the important design point.
PASS source and target agree
FAIL source and target genuinely differ
NOT MEASURED the value could not be read at all (permission denied,
extractor error), so NO verdict is possible
NOT MEASURED is never folded into FAIL. A target extract that hit
PERMISSION_DENIED on 10 of 19 columns would otherwise report
"DC-04 FAIL 35/35", which reads as "the clone lost all the data" when the
truth is "we were not allowed to look". Those are opposite conclusions and
must never be conflated.
Related: an extractor that collapses "denied" into a plain "false" (DC-01,
DC-11) is indistinguishable from a real absence when read in isolation. So
an object with ANY permission error on ANY of its columns is marked
EXTRACTION BLOCKED, and its boolean-false checks are reported NOT MEASURED
rather than FAIL. The blocked count is always shown, never hidden.

── Target-location collisions in dr_clone_config ───────────────────────────
TWO active rows pointing at the SAME physical storage path is a registration
defect with a silent and destructive consequence: both tables' clones write
to one location, so whichever ran last OVERWROTE the other's data, and every
row count this report then reads from that path belongs to the survivor.
The symptom that exposed it: two unrelated tables in different schemas
reporting an identical target row count (79,882) from different source
counts (80,877 / 80,892). Both were reported as "TARGET IS SHORT" -- i.e. as
clone fidelity defects -- when the real finding is that one table's DR copy
had been destroyed by another's and neither source can match the survivor.
Checked from dr_clone_config directly rather than from the extract CSVs,
which do not carry storage paths (the versioned extractor consumes
_own_location and drops it). BOTH location columns are examined so the check
is direction-agnostic. Degrades to {} on any failure -- no UC access, table
absent, column renamed -- exactly like AUDIT_STATUS above: losing this
annotation must never cost the whole report.

── Canonical test-case registry ─────────────────────────────────────────────
The single source of truth for DC ids, ADO work items and official
descriptions. Everything rendered below reads from here, so the HTML can
never drift from the ADO test plan the way ad-hoc per-cell titles did.

Every FAIL / NOT MEASURED row from every card, accumulated across the whole
run and written out as ONE csv at the end (see FINDINGS_CSV).
This exists because display() is the wrong artifact to rely on for
completeness: the Databricks grid caps what it renders (the UI says
"1,000+ rows / Truncated data"), and that cap is a product behaviour, not
something a notebook can raise from code. The grid stays as the interactive
preview; the CSV is the thing that actually holds every row, and it is what
to open when the question is "which tables exactly".

test_id -> Counter of NOT MEASURED reason buckets for that card.
Keyed by test_id rather than accumulated into one global Counter so that
re-running a single DC cell REPLACES that card's contribution instead of
double-counting it -- the same reason _emit rewrites RESULTS by id.
Exists because the dashboard banner used to assert a hardcoded cause
("overwhelmingly target-side PERMISSION_DENIED / missing USE SCHEMA") for
every not-measured check. On the 13,574-table run that was flatly wrong:
permission-blocked objects were ZERO, and the real causes were an extractor
ValueError and the retention skip. A banner that names the wrong cause is
worse than no banner -- it sends the reader to fix access they already have.

multiLine=True: defence in depth against any extractor column
that embeds a raw newline (e.g. an unstripped stacktrace) --
without it, Spark's CSV reader treats each embedded newline as
a new row, shredding one erroring object into several bogus
rows with garbled/blank identity columns.
escape='"' is equally MANDATORY, and for a different reason. The
extracts are written by pandas .to_csv(), which escapes an
embedded quote by DOUBLING it ("") per RFC-4180, while Spark's
CSV reader defaults to BACKSLASH. On a doubled quote Spark loses
the quoted-field context and (under its default
unescapedQuoteHandling=STOP_AT_DELIMITER) splits the value at the
next comma -- so a json.dumps blob such as dc_10_tblproperties or
dc_13_pk_fk_constraints becomes 2+ fields, every later column
shifts right, and the row tail falls off the end. It never
raises: row count and header stay correct, so the damage is
silent. Observed in a real 22,585-table prod run as ~132,000
phantom "failures" and ~99% of the target tag columns destroyed.

tst_tables_info_versioned_standalone.py emits this when the retention check
ruled a table's pinned Delta version unsafe to time travel to, so its four
versioned checks were never run.
It is treated exactly like an extractor error -- NOT MEASURED -- because that
is literally true: nothing was measured. Critically it must NOT fall through
to a normal comparison: when both sides skip the same table their two skip
markers are identical strings, so cmp_exact would call that a PASS and
manufacture a clean result for a table nobody actually checked.

── EMPTY TABLE -- two signatures, one underlying condition ─────────────────
A table created but never written: it carries a _delta_log, but no schema and
no rows. Still NOT MEASURED (nothing WAS measured), but emphatically NOT a
clone defect, and it must not read as one -- there was never anything on the
source for the clone to carry.
get_versions.py deliberately emits a version for EVERY table, and for one of
these the only truthful value is Delta's own marker, sourceVersion = -1
("no committed version to clone from"). That -1 is pinned like any other
version, so `VERSION AS OF -1` really is issued and really does fail -- the
bare minus is a SQL PARSE error, not a read error. The raw ParseException is
kept verbatim in source_value / target_value as the evidence of what ran.
What is NOT acceptable is leaving the operator to decode that. On its own the
parse error reads as a malformed query someone wrote by hand; it says nothing
about the table. So the reason column below reconstructs the causal chain --
empty table -> sourceVersion -1 -> pinned -> parse error -- and names the
actual finding.
_EMPTY_VERSION_MARKERS the pin failed: -1 reached the SQL (source side)
_EMPTY_TABLE_MARKERS the read failed: Delta says the table has no
columns (typically the target side)

── RUNTIME too old for the table's Delta protocol ──────────────────────────
Delta reader TABLE FEATURES are a hard protocol gate, not a hint: when a
table declares one, a reader must support EVERY declared feature or refuse
the table outright. There is no partial read -- that is deliberate, so a
runtime cannot silently misinterpret data written by a newer one.
`catalogManaged` postdates DBR 15.4 LTS, which every cluster profile in this
bundle pins. So these tables are unreadable BY THIS RUNTIME while being
perfectly healthy in themselves. Reporting the raw
DeltaUnsupportedTableFeatureException invites someone to go looking for a
data problem that does not exist; the finding is "our reader is too old".
It also very likely explains an accompanying PATH_NOT_FOUND on the other
side: the CLONE job runs the same 15.4 runtime, so if it could not read the
source either, no target copy was ever produced. One root cause, two
symptoms -- worth saying out loud, because they otherwise read as unrelated.

── NEVER REGISTERED in dr_clone_config ─────────────────────────────────────
The most serious finding this report can carry, and the one most easily
mistaken for noise. The table was never recorded by the SE inventory task,
so the clone job never ran for it and NOTHING exists in East. It is not a
fidelity defect and not a runtime problem -- it is a DR COVERAGE GAP: after
a failover the table would simply not be there.
It reaches this notebook by TWO different routes, which is why both are
matched here:
NoPathResolved our own extractor, when dr_clone_config
yields no _own_location for the table
"not found in dr_clone_config" the clone job's own audit error_message,
carried in via _augment_with_audit_reason.
On this route the CELL only says
PATH_NOT_FOUND -- indistinguishable from a
clone that ran and failed -- so the audit
text is the only thing that tells them
apart.

One comparator per kind of check. Each returns (verdict, detail).
Every comparator must return NOT_MEASURED -- never FAIL -- when the inputs
are unreadable, so a permissions problem can never masquerade as a defect.

Delta generates these row-tracking column names per table with a random
suffix. A clone necessarily gets NEW ones, so comparing them can never
pass and says nothing about clone fidelity -- they are an internal Delta
implementation detail, not user metadata. Observed differing on 32 of 35
tables purely for this reason.

BEFORE the generic "ERROR: <ExceptionType>" regex below, which would
otherwise bucket these as "extractor error -- ParseException" /
"-- AnalysisException" and bury them among unrelated failures. Both
signatures fold into ONE bucket because they are one cause: the table is
empty. Which of the two symptoms appeared (a failed -1 version pin, or a
failed no-columns read) is a detail of where it was caught, not a
different problem to go and fix.

FIRST among the error buckets, and before the generic regex. On the
audit route the cell only says PATH_NOT_FOUND, so this would otherwise
bucket as "extractor error -- AnalysisException" alongside genuine clone
failures -- burying the one finding here that means a table is missing
from East entirely rather than merely mis-copied.

Also before the generic regex -- it would otherwise read as
"extractor error -- Py4JJavaError", which describes the transport and
not the cause. This is a runtime-version ceiling, and it is actionable
in a completely different way from every other bucket here.

Joins source to target on object identity, applies the comparator per object,
and renders the card. Objects present in SOURCE but absent from the TARGET
extract are a real FAIL (the clone did not produce them) -- distinct from an
object that is present but unreadable, which is NOT MEASURED.
Distinguishes "the target extract has no row for this object at all" from
"the target row exists and its value is genuinely empty" -- two different
findings that would otherwise both render as a blank target_value cell.

NEVER REGISTERED is called out explicitly rather than being folded into
the generic "clone attempt status=SKIPPED: <raw audit text>" line.
This is the ONLY route by which that finding is visible for most of
these tables: the extract cell says nothing more than PATH_NOT_FOUND,
which reads identically to a clone that ran and failed. The two have
completely different owners -- one is a registration gap upstream of the
clone job, the other a defect inside it -- and only the audit
error_message distinguishes them. Buried mid-sentence in raw log text it
was reliably missed.

MODE GATE. DC cards are skipped on an INC run and INC cards on a DC run,
keyed purely on the test_id prefix.
Enforced HERE rather than by wrapping the calls in `if not INC:` because
the DC cards span twenty-odd notebook CELLS, and Databricks compiles each
cell independently -- an `if` in one cell cannot indent the next. One
guard at the single point every card already passes through is both
smaller and impossible to forget when a card is added.

A source column blank for EVERY object while the target is populated
means the source side is not emitting that column at all -- one

35/35 failing purely because dc_08_column_order_src is NULL on every
row after the extractor for it was reverted, while the target measures

Deliberately requires ALL rows blank. A single object with an empty
value (a table with no comment, say) is a real, comparable measurement

A blocked object's bare "false" cannot be distinguished from a real
absence, so downgrade that FAIL to NOT MEASURED. Applied ONLY to a
FAIL: a check that genuinely agrees (both sides blank, for instance)
stays a PASS -- an over-broad rule here would bury real passes as

Findings are no longer rendered INTO the card. They used to be an HTML

# Merge the parallel chunks of dr_clone_full_diff_standalone
Runs as `dr_clone_full_diff_merge_task`, immediately after the
`dr_clone_full_diff_task` for_each fan-out (each chunk on its own
`nonuc_cluster_profile_tier_l` cluster) finishes. Reads each chunk's
`dr_clone_full_diff_result.chunk{i}.csv`, concatenates them, sorts by
`table`, and writes the merged result to the plain
`dr_clone_full_diff_result.csv`.
Each chunk's OWN summary (written alongside its result file) is
necessarily PARTIAL -- only its own slice of tables -- so this notebook
recomputes the TRUE summary from the full merged result set and writes it
to `dr_clone_full_diff_summary.csv`, exactly reproducing the aggregate
counts a single non-chunked run would have produced.
Runs on `nonuc_cluster_l` (same as the chunks) for the same SP OAuth
reason -- this cluster has no UC storage credential. `env=src` only, same
gating as the raw notebook; `dc_test_dir`/`clone_direction` arrive as task
values from `dr_clone_full_diff_prep_task`, same as the chunks receive
them (that task is not fanned out, so this reference is unambiguous).

Per-tier chunk counts. The two size tiers are independent populations on
differently sized clusters, so they carry independent chunk counts -- 3
large chunks alongside 4 small ones is normal. Both are probed regardless;
a tier that did not run simply contributes no files.

Echoed from the same job parameter the diff workers received, purely so the
summary CSV can record WHICH MODE produced it. Without this, someone reading
dr_clone_full_diff_summary.csv months later cannot tell whether "12,823
matched" means the estate was verified that day or that most tables were
skipped because an earlier run had cleared them. This task does not act on
the flag -- it only stamps it.

Bundle-resolved, NOT operator-facing -- same SP + secret the chunks use;
this cluster has no UC storage credential, so SP OAuth via
fs.azure.account.* Spark configs is the only way to reach abfss:// paths.
Two secret-scope candidates, not one -- see tst_tables_info_versioned_standalone.py's
widget comment for why (SE/East scopes are genuinely named differently).

Unrecognised values are NOT silently treated as false -- a typo would stamp
the summary INCREMENTAL on a run that was actually full, or vice versa, and
the whole point of recording it is that it can be trusted.

Chunk paths across BOTH size tiers. dr_clone_full_diff_standalone.py fans
out twice -- once per tier, each onto its own cluster with its own chunk
count -- writing dr_clone_full_diff_result.{tier}.chunk{i}.csv. The two
tiers are independent populations with independent chunk counts, so both
have to be collected here. The untiered name is probed too, so a
standalone/manual run (or tiering switched off) still merges correctly.

escape='"' is MANDATORY -- pandas .to_csv() doubles embedded quotes ("")
while Spark's reader defaults to backslash, so without this the `error`
column (which can carry a comma-bearing message) is split into extra fields
and every later column shifts right. Silent: no exception, correct row count.
multiLine='true' matters at least as much here: `error` is written as a raw
str(exc), which on current Databricks runtimes carries a multi-line "JVM
stacktrace:" block. Without this each stacktrace line is read as its own
record -- a phantom row whose `table` field holds "at com.databricks..." --
and those rows then survive the drop_duplicates below AND get counted
against the coverage gate, so a single failing table can both pollute the
final result and skew the reconciliation that is supposed to catch problems.
Missing paths are skipped rather than fatal: a tier with fewer chunks than
configured, or an absent tier entirely, is a legitimate state. A run that
finds NOTHING is a real failure and raises -- writing an empty result over
a good one would look like "every table passed" to the summary and skip
list below.

Captured BEFORE the carry-forward below, so it means "tables actually
re-diffed this run" rather than "rows in the final file". On an incremental
run these two numbers differ by the size of the skip list, and conflating
them is exactly how an incremental result gets mistaken for a full one.

The workers skip tables already proven to match (see SKIP_LIST_FILE in
dr_clone_full_diff_standalone.py), so the chunk files above cover only what
was still outstanding. Without folding the previous result back in, this file
would silently SHRINK to just the latest slice -- a partial validation that
looks like a complete one.
Read BEFORE the overwrite below, since it is the same path.

The result must account for EVERY table in the scope CSV, not just the ones
this run happened to process. Reconcile explicitly rather than trusting the
arithmetic above.
THIS GATE IS FATAL, and it has to be. It used to print "*** INCOMPLETE ***"
and then return SUCCESS, which is the worst of both worlds: the run reported
green, the summary below described only the tables that happened to be
processed, and the skip list was rebuilt as though the missing ones simply
had nothing to report.
It is the ONLY check that can catch a whole class of silent shortfalls,
because it reconciles the final result against the scope regardless of CAUSE.
Both causes seen so far pass every other check in this job:
- a chunk divisor that does not match the scheduled iteration count
(total_chunks=5 against 4 for_each inputs left one modulo group with no
runner at all: 2,490 tables, no error, no missing file)
- a tier whose chunk ran against a stale scope, found 0 tables, and
succeeded in one second (867 tables)
Neither produced a failed task or an absent chunk file, so ALL_SUCCESS on
this task's depends_on was satisfied and every chunk file the merge looked
for was present and readable. Only the row-level reconciliation notices.

Every column round-trips through CSV as a plain string (no inferSchema
anywhere in this pipeline). "error == ''" is safe that way -- pandas writes
Python None as an empty string. THE NUMERIC COLUMNS ARE NOT.
The previous version compared them as text on the stated assumption that
each was "a canonical int-as-string with no formatting ambiguity". That
holds only while every row succeeded. A chunk writes None for all three
numeric fields on an error row, and pandas widens a column holding None
alongside ints to float64, so .to_csv() renders EVERY value in that column
with a decimal point. A clean table's zero arrives here as "0.0".
Both consumers then broke silently, in opposite directions:
"0.0" != "0" -> true for every clean table, so a real run
reported 9,805 of 9,822 tables as
mismatched when ~21 actually were
"0.0" not in ("", "0") -> the skip list below matched nothing and was
written EMPTY, so every run re-diffed the
entire estate from scratch
Hence _num(): compare numbers as numbers. Note the per-chunk summaries were
always right -- they count in memory, on real ints, before any CSV write.

Both counts actually present. NaN != NaN is TRUE in pandas, so without this
an error-free row with unreadable counts would be reported as a mismatch on
the strength of two values neither of which exists.

`compared` counts every table with a verdict in the final file, which on

proven to match in an earlier run are skipped, so a run only chases what is
still outstanding. true = diff every table in scope regardless of what a
previous run concluded.
This exists because the two modes support different CLAIMS. An incremental
run can only say "N tables verified as of the date they were last checked";
only a full run can say "the estate is verified as of today". The skip list
is keyed on table NAME with no version component, so a table verified last
week that has changed since is not re-checked in incremental mode.
Previously the only way to force a full run was to delete the skip-list file

max_parallel is ONE job parameter shared by every task in this job. The
metadata extractors (tst_tables_info_*) are latency-bound on thousands of
tiny catalog lookups and genuinely want a high value; this notebook is the
opposite -- each table is a full row-count plus an exceptAll that shuffles
BOTH sides -- so the same number is actively harmful here.
Measured on a real prod run at max_parallel=500 against a 512-core cluster
(8-16 workers x 32 cores): ~1 core per concurrent table with nothing left
for parallelism WITHIN a table, 609 Spark jobs admitted at once, individual
jobs sitting at 0/2345 tasks for 15+ minutes, throughput sawtoothing from
2,325 tables/hr to 1/hr and flat-lining entirely after hour 12 -- 10,801 of
22,352 tables in 30 hours, then nothing. Not a slowdown; a livelock.
So the shared value is CLAMPED here rather than merely defaulted, because a
default cannot protect this task from a parameter set for a different one.
~16 cores per concurrent table is the target: enough to shuffle a large
table, while keeping enough tables in flight that small ones don't queue.
Raise DIFF_MAX_PARALLEL_CEILING only alongside a bigger cluster.

exceptAll fully shuffles both sides, so partition count matters a lot --
but a single fixed number can't be right for both a 300K-row table and a
1.08B-row table sharing this same notebook/session. 2048 was picked to size
the large tables properly, on the theory that AQE's post-shuffle coalescing
(spark.sql.adaptive.coalescePartitions.enabled=true, already set on this
cluster profile) collapses it back down for small tables with "no downside
either way". That theory doesn't hold: coalescing only MERGES partitions
after the fact, it does not undo the planning-time cost of 2048 partitions
on a 10-file table -- every table still pays for as many map-side shuffle
writes as the shuffle-partition count, regardless of how few rows it holds.
'auto' lets AQE size shuffle partitions from the query plan's own actual
input-size statistics instead of one static guess applied to every table --
confirmed via Spark's own performance-tuning docs and the original AQE
engineering blog as the recommended mode over hand-picking a fixed count.
Coalescing and skew-splitting (both already on this cluster profile) then
continue to apply on top of whatever AQE plans, same as before.

already had. This notebook does nothing but read those files, aggregate, and

anything the pipeline reads.

-- the fork where BOTH the extractor branch (`tst_tables_info` / views /

SUCCESS, and it has three independent exit conditions. See the "Isolation"
cell below -- that behaviour is the point, not an afterthought.

This task must never fail the run and must never keep it alive after the
real work is done.
* **Cannot block anything** -- it is a leaf. No task lists it in `depends_on`.
* **Cannot fail the run** -- the whole body is wrapped, and every path ends in
`dbutils.notebook.exit(...)` with SUCCESS. A missing directory, a torn JSON
read, an unreachable API: all degrade the view, none raise.
* **Cannot stall the run** -- three independent exits: all *other* tasks
terminal, `max_hours`, or too many consecutive API failures.
* **The trap:** this notebook is itself a task in the run it polls, so
"all tasks terminal" is never true -- it is always RUNNING when it asks.

monitored keys (which silently rots when a task is renamed), it monitors
*every* task except itself.

task Failed, which fails the run. `max_hours` exits SUCCESS instead.

Runs as `get_versions_merge_task`, immediately after the
`get_versions_task` for_each fan-out finishes. Each chunk wrote BOTH
`tst_tables_info_ver_tgt.chunk{i}.csv` AND
`tst_tables_info_ver_src.chunk{i}.csv` from the same per-table loop --
this notebook merges each, independently, back to its plain unsuffixed
filename.
`wait_for_tgt_get_versions_completion.py` (the src leg's cross-workspace
wait) watches THIS task, not the raw `get_versions_task` for_each wrapper
-- the wrapper reaches SUCCESS as soon as all chunks finish, which is
before this merge has actually assembled `tst_tables_info_ver_src.csv`.
Self-gates on `test_tables` exactly like `get_versions.py` itself. No
`env` gate is needed here: `get_versions_task`'s own `depends_on` (on
`env_is_tgt_gate`'s true branch) already means this whole for_each --
and therefore this merge task, which depends on it -- is simply never
admitted on the src leg.
**It also decides the final `tier`.** `get_versions.py` stamps a
provisional l/s tier per chunk against a fixed GB threshold; this task
overwrites it across the whole merged population using a split point
derived from the sizes themselves (`tier_strategy`). It is the only task
that can: it is the first to see every row, and both tiered fan-outs --
`tst_tables_info_versioned_task_{large,small}` and
`dr_clone_full_diff_task_{large,small}` -- inherit this column rather
than deriving their own, so one decision here settles both.

── Size-tier split point ───────────────────────────────────────────────
get_versions.py stamps a provisional l/s tier per chunk using a FIXED
threshold (tier_threshold_gb, 50 GB). That is an absolute answer to a
relative question: on an estate whose largest table is under 50 GB, EVERY
table classifies 's', the small cluster carries the entire workload and the
large one starts, finds nothing in scope and exits. Observed exactly --
dr_clone_full_diff_chunk_l reported tables_in_scope=0 and finished in 8
minutes while chunk_s was still running at 12h+.
This task is where that gets corrected, for two reasons:
1. It is the FIRST task that sees the COMPLETE population. get_versions.py
itself runs as a 5-chunk for_each, so a statistic computed there would
be computed five times over five disjoint 1/5th slices -- five
different thresholds, and a table's tier would depend on which chunk
happened to process it.
2. Every downstream fan-out INHERITS this tier rather than deriving its
own -- tst_tables_info_source_standalone.py carries it as `_tier` for
tst_tables_info_versioned_task_{large,small}, and
dr_clone_full_diff_prep.py carries it as `tier` for
dr_clone_full_diff_task_{large,small}. Fixing it once here therefore
fixes BOTH tiered fan-outs; fixing it in either downstream notebook
would fix only that one.
mean -- the default. On the normal right-skewed shape (a long tail of
small tables, a few enormous ones) the mean sits well above
the median, so only genuine outliers route to 'l' -- which is
what the tiering exists for: stopping a few billion-row
tables from holding up thousands of small ones.
median -- an exact 50/50 split by count. Neither cluster can ever be
empty, at the cost of sending half the estate to the
expensive large cluster.
absolute -- the previous fixed-threshold behaviour, unchanged.

multiLine='true' for the same read-then-rewrite reason as escape: these
files carry free-form reason text, and an embedded newline read as a

escape='"' is MANDATORY, not optional. Every chunk file was written by
pandas .to_csv(), which escapes an embedded quote by DOUBLING it ("") per
RFC-4180. Spark's CSV reader defaults to backslash as its escape character,
so on a doubled quote it loses the quoted-field context and (under its

next comma, quotes and all. Any json.dumps blob -- dc_10_tblproperties,
dc_13_pk_fk_constraints -- then becomes 2+ fields, every later column shifts
right, and the row tail falls off the end. It never raises: row count and
header stay correct, so the damage is silent and gets written straight back
out by the dbutils.fs.put below.

with an embedded newline (an unstripped stacktrace) is otherwise read as
several records -- phantom rows with a stacktrace line in `catalog` and blank
schema/table_name -- and the put below persists them, turning a transient
read artifact into permanent on-disk corruption.

into a warning: on a real run the equivalent leniency in the tiered merges

The untiered tst_tables_info_{env}.chunk{i}.csv name is ALSO probed, so a

escape='"' is MANDATORY -- pandas .to_csv() doubles embedded quotes ("")
while Spark's reader defaults to backslash, so without this any json.dumps
blob is split at its internal commas and every later column shifts right.
Silent: no exception, correct row count. multiLine='true' is mandatory for

Both tiers are disjoint by construction (a table is 'l' or 's', never
both), but dedupe defensively on identity -- a re-run of one tier while

This merge overwrites the very file the chunks read from, so an incomplete
merge does not merely under-report -- it DESTROYS the scope. Every table it
failed to cover would vanish from tst_tables_info_{env}.csv, and re-running
the versioned fan-out afterwards would read the truncated file and "cover"
it perfectly. The damage would look like success. So this reconciles first
and raises while the original file is still intact.
Right now _final_path still holds the pre-versioned scope, which is exactly
what every chunk filtered on -- so it is the authoritative expected key set.
(Re-running this merge after a good one is harmless: the file then holds the
same tables, so the same reconciliation passes.)
WHAT THIS CATCHES, and nothing else in this notebook does: a chunk divisor
that disagrees with the scheduled iteration count. The two directions are
not symmetric --
inputs > total_chunks : surplus iterations exit on the chunk guard.
Wasteful, SAFE, and intended (observed live:
versioned_s had 8 inputs against total_chunks=5,
so iterations 5-7 exited and groups 0-4 still
covered every table -- no data lost).
inputs < total_chunks : whole modulo groups get NO runner at all. Silent
loss, no failed task, no absent chunk file --
because the missing groups were never assigned to
anything that could fail. Only a row-level
reconciliation sees it.
A worker cannot detect this itself: it knows its own index and the divisor,
never how many siblings were scheduled.

Sort on content (not file-read order) before splitting -- spark.read.csv's
row order for a given file is not a guaranteed-stable contract, and all

Unknown/blank tier counts as 'l', matching _size_tier()'s own default: a

DC-05 -- num files + size bytes, AT THE PINNED VERSION
These two used to live in tst_tables_info_source_standalone.py, computed with
DESCRIBE DETAIL. That call has no time-travel syntax -- it always describes
the table's CURRENT version -- so the check compared a LIVE source against a
target frozen at the clone. Measured on a real 22,585-table prod run: only
48% matched, the rate was a FLAT ~48% whether the two sides were measured 1
minute or 6 hours apart (proving it was clone-age, not measurement drift),
and 92-96% of every mismatch bucket was a staging table that gets truncated
and reloaded each ETL cycle. The check was reporting "has this table changed
since the clone", not "did the clone copy it correctly".
There is no `DESCRIBE DETAIL ... VERSION AS OF`, so the snapshot is
reconstructed from the transaction log instead. This is not an approximation:
DESCRIBE DETAIL's own numFiles/sizeInBytes are themselves computed by summing
the active AddFile set, which is exactly what is rebuilt below.

Refuse to reconstruct from an incomplete log rather than returning a
confident-looking undercount.
The replay below needs either a checkpoint at/before the target (a
complete snapshot to start from) or the commit history all the way back
to version 0. If log cleanup has removed the early commits and left no
usable checkpoint, the AddFiles from the missing range are simply absent
and the sum silently comes back too low -- or 0, if nothing at all is in
range. That would compare against the target's real count as a FALSE
FAIL, which is the one outcome this framework must never produce from a
measurement gap.
Previously unreachable: every table this could hit was blanket-skipped
by the 168h retention gate. Splitting that gate per-check (log-only
checks now run out to logRetentionDuration) opens this path, so the
guard lands with it. Raising here surfaces as ERROR -> NOT MEASURED.

A Delta data file path is added once and removed once and is never
re-added, so cancelling adds against removes by path is order-independent
-- which is what lets the whole commit range be read in ONE Spark job
rather than replayed commit by commit.

DC-14 -- table comment + column comments, AT THE PINNED VERSION
These two also used to live in tst_tables_info_source_standalone.py, read
from `information_schema.tables` / `.columns` -- Unity Catalog's LIVE view,
with no time travel of any kind.
This is not hypothetical drift. On a real 22,585-table prod run DC-14b had 33
differences, and splitting them by DIRECTION showed 5 where the TARGET had
column comments and the SOURCE did not. A deep clone cannot invent comments
the source never had, so on those tables the source must have HAD them at
clone time and lost them since. Once drift is proven in that direction, the
other 28 (source-populated, target-blank) cannot be read as clone gaps
either: unpinned, the check simply cannot tell "the clone never copied this"
apart from "the source changed afterwards".
Delta stores both natively -- the table comment in `metaData.description`,
the column comments in each field's `metadata.comment` inside
`metaData.schemaString` -- so reading the log at the pinned version answers
the intended question instead. Output format is unchanged, so these stay
comparable with previously-captured extracts.

Nothing found anywhere in range. This is NOT a table that legitimately
has no metaData/protocol -- every Delta table writes both at version 0,
and every checkpoint snapshots them -- so the only way to reach here is
a log that has been cleaned past the target version.
Returning {} instead would be silently wrong in the worst direction:
the callers would read an empty metaData as real answers -- no table
comment, no column comments, partitioning "cols=[]", columnMapping
"none", deletionVectors "false", tblproperties "{}" -- and each would
compare as a confident FALSE FAIL against the target's real values.
Raising surfaces as ERROR -> NOT MEASURED, which is the honest verdict.
Same reasoning and same trigger as the guard in _delta_snapshot_stats:
unreachable until the retention gate was split per-check, since these
tables used to be blanket-skipped before any of this ran.

All four previously read live state in the non-versioned notebook -- DC-08/

has time-travel syntax, so each compared an evolving source against a target
frozen at the clone.
They showed ZERO differences on the prod run that exposed DC-05 and DC-14, so
they were not causing false failures yet. That is a fact about one moment,
not a property of the checks: it held only because nobody had run ALTER TABLE
... SET TBLPROPERTIES, enabled column mapping or deletion vectors, or
repartitioned any of 22,585 tables in the window between clone and
validation. DC-14b then proved drift is real on this estate (5 tables where
the comment existed on the TARGET and not the source -- impossible for a
clone to produce). These four carry the identical exposure, so they are
pinned now rather than after they misreport.
Every value here comes from the SAME metaData/protocol pair already resolved
for DC-14, so this adds no extra log reads per table.

row_count's exemption is evidence-based, not just theoretical: a real prod

readable in practice, which is the one thing the retention check was

The "ERROR: " prefix is load-bearing, not cosmetic: it is what
Comparison_test_case_result_deepclone.py's is_error() keys on to
rule the cell a non-measurement. Without it this sentinel was read
as an ordinary VALUE, which broke both ways -- one-sided it became a
false FAIL (a string compared against a real measurement), and
two-sided the two identical sentinels compared EQUAL and
manufactured a false PASS for a table nothing was ever read from.

row_count is deliberately UNCONDITIONAL -- computed regardless of
skip_reason, before the skip check below even runs.
dr_clone_full_diff_standalone.py has never checked retention at all --
it just pins VERSION AS OF on the recorded source version and reads --
and a real prod run (10,802+ tables, apple-to-apple via row counts +
exceptAll) completed with every comparison a clean MATCH, proving those
same pinned-source reads succeed in practice regardless of how long ago
the clone ran. That is direct evidence for the ONE thing skip_reason
was guarding row_count against: deletedFileRetentionDuration, i.e.
whether the DATA FILES backing an old version might be vacuumed. They
evidently aren't, at least not in a way that breaks this read.
This does NOT make row_count immune to every failure -- if the
_delta_log itself is gone (logRetentionDuration well and truly
exceeded), VERSION AS OF cannot resolve at all and row_count() throws,
same as always -- caught by its own try/except, reported as
"ERROR: ..." and read as NOT MEASURED downstream. That failure is just
no longer pre-empted by a proactive skip; it is discovered the same way
dr_clone_full_diff_standalone.py discovers it -- by attempting the read.
Skipped entirely in INC mode -- it is a FULL TABLE SCAN and row_count is
not one of the two checks INC-02 borrows. This is the single biggest cost
the mode switch avoids.

tst_tables_version_retention_check.py flagged this row: its recorded
version is past logRetentionDuration AND the table has been written
since, so VERSION AS OF <that version> is not safe to trust for the
OTHER ten checks below -- unlike row_count, none of them have prod
evidence backing an exemption, and the log itself (not just the data
files) is what is in question here. Refuse to pin on it for those.
Deliberately NOT falling back to latest: these checks exist to
compare the SAME version on both sides, and silently swapping in a
different one produces a confident-looking result that answers a
different question. Reporting the skip is the honest outcome.

`env=src` only (self-gated). Polls the run that `trigger_tgt_test_case_job`
submitted in the opposite region, but -- unlike

actually finished writing that file before this leg reads it. This task
closes that gap without waiting for the target's OWN extractors

Mechanism 5 — REPLACE WHERE flow (Beta) for targeted backfill/correction. A FLOW REPLACE WHERE <predicate> defines a predicate on the target; on each run all rows matching the predicate are deleted and replaced by re-evaluating the source query for that same range — rows outside the predicate are untouched. The source must be a batch (non-streaming) source (a streaming source throws), so this handles late data, upstream reprocessing, and backfills without streaming semantics (no watermark management), and can target a window the streaming engine would have dropped. Requires the PREVIEW channel (set the pipelines.channel table property to "PREVIEW"); Databricks recommends Unity Catalog + serverless (incremental refresh of the flow is serverless-only). BY NAME is required and the predicate must be deterministic. Gotcha: a full refresh re-runs the source query using only the current predicate — if a 7-day-predicate pipeline ran for a year, a full refresh leaves only the last 7 days and permanently deletes older rows. Guard with pipelines.reset.allowed = 'false'. (REPLACE WHERE and ONCE are mutually exclusive.)

pipelines.reset.allowed	Table property	true	When false, blocks full refresh of that table (full refresh resets streaming-table state/checkpoints and re-derives from source, dropping records if the source no longer has them). Incremental writes and new data still flow in. Protects backfilled / manually-corrected / short-retention-source tables.
pipelines.autoOptimize.managed	Table property	true	Enables/disables SDP's automatically-scheduled optimization (file compaction + layout) for that table. Not used when the table is governed by predictive optimization.
pipelines.trigger.interval	Table property (via spark_conf / SET) or pipeline configuration	Streaming queries: 5 s; complete (batch) queries all-Delta sources: 1 min; complete queries with any non-Delta source: 10 min	Micro-batch cadence per flow. Because a triggered pipeline processes each table once, it is honored only in continuous pipelines. Set per-table — streaming and batch defaults differ, so a pipeline-wide value is usually wrong.
CLUSTER BY AUTO / cluster_by_auto=True	Table clause / decorator kwarg	off	Automatic liquid clustering — predictive optimization picks and maintains clustering keys from query history (requires PO; needs DBR 15.4 LTS+ for intelligent key selection). Replaces PARTITIONED BY and Z-ordering; skew-resistant and incremental.
Other SDP-specific knobs:

Knob	Scope	Default	Notes
pipelines.autoOptimize.zOrderCols	Table property	None	Comma-separated Z-order columns. Legacy — docs recommend CLUSTER BY AUTO instead.
cluster_by=[...] / CLUSTER BY (cols)	Table clause / kwarg	off	Manual liquid clustering keys. Mutually exclusive with PARTITIONED BY.
pipelines.cdc.tombstoneGCThresholdInSeconds	Table property (on the AUTO CDC target)	172800 (2 days)	How long SCD2 delete tombstones are retained before GC. "What the measurements imply
The signal is absence of resolution, not absence of activity. And resolution state should be recorded, not inferred — the same move that replaced domain_guess (keyword hint) with domain_labels.jsonl (explicit projection).

Tier 1 — a commitment registry. When a decision defers something, write the deferral structurally: what, the condition that resolves it, a review horizon. Your repo already does this informally and those cases are machine-checkable today — 4.6 GraphRAG ⏭ DEFERRED (trigger-gated: first KB-logged multi-hop retrieval failure) is a real open loop with an explicit trigger. Make that shape first-class and detection becomes a boring scan with zero inference.

Tier 2 — the detector, mirroring tension.py's proven architecture: candidates → LLM judge with an abstention option → confidence floor → watermark so nothing nags twice. Critically, build the gold eval set first, as eval_tension.py did. Without it you can't distinguish a working detector from a broken one — which is exactly how the previous volume detector died, producing zero insights for months with nobody noticing.

Tier 3 — statistical clustering. Only if 1–2 fall short. Measurement 1 says the data is bursty and coarse; this is speculative.

The one thing not to do is ship something that says "you have 51 stale items." Most are finished work, and a false-positive firehose trains you to ignore the channel — an ignored channel being indistinguishable from a broken one, which is the failure this whole organ exists to prevent.
